title: Optimal Pruning for Neural Architectures using Fisher Information Distances
summary: A new scheme for parameter pruning is introduced, derived from the differential-geometric distance in model space. Pruning a parameter sets its value to zero, representing a displacement of the model to the hypersurface on which that parameter vanishes. The minimal distance from the unpruned model to this hypersurface is naturally computed via the geodesic distance in the model space as determined by the Fisher information metric. This distance determines the true change in the model, and its performance, under pruning. By analysing progressively more faithful approximations of this geodesic distance a natural hierarchy of optimality for pruning methods is determined. This starts with the traditional magnitude pruning, then develops into new more sophisticated and effective pruning schemes. The method is demonstrated for both fully-connected networks and vision transformers, on MNIST and CIFAR-10, over the complete $0$-$100\%$ pruning range and across five random seeds. It outperforms pruning by parameter magnitude and by the local Fisher information alone in every architecture and dataset combination considered, on both accuracy and the Matthews correlation coefficient. Additionally, analysis of different levels of geodesic approximation produces intermediate pruning schemes that are computationally efficient and maintain near-optimal performance. This geometric picture supplies not only a state-of-the-art pruning methodology for AI models, but also a verified and mathematically-motivated justification for pruning schemes.

AI.tldr: They propose a new, geometrically motivated pruning method based on geodesic (Fisher-metric) distance in model space, leading to a hierarchy of pruning schemes that outperform magnitude and Fisher-based pruning on MNIST and CIFAR-10 for fully connected nets and ViTs.
AI.motivation: Existing pruning methods (e.g., magnitude pruning or Fisher-score pruning) are heuristics that do not explicitly measure the true change in the model induced by pruning. There is a lack of a principled, mathematically grounded notion of how far a pruned model is from the original one, and of how to optimally choose parameters to prune based on that notion.
AI.method: View the space of model parameters as a Riemannian manifold endowed with the Fisher information metric. Pruning a parameter corresponds to moving the model to the hypersurface where that parameter is zero. The cost of pruning is defined as the geodesic distance (under the Fisher metric) from the original parameter point to this hypersurface. They analyze progressively more accurate approximations to this geodesic distance to derive a hierarchy of practical pruning criteria, starting from magnitude-based pruning to more sophisticated schemes that incorporate Fisher information and higher-order geometric structure. They then implement these criteria and test them across different architectures and datasets.
AI.result: Across fully-connected networks and vision transformers trained on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and for pruning levels ranging from 0% to 100% over five random seeds, the proposed geodesic-based pruning methods consistently outperform both magnitude pruning and local Fisher-based pruning in terms of test accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficient. Intermediate approximations to the full geodesic distance yield pruning schemes that are computationally cheaper while still maintaining performance close to the most accurate geometric method.
AI.conclusion: A differential-geometric perspective on model space, via the Fisher information metric and associated geodesic distances, provides a principled way to define and approximate the effect of pruning operations. This leads to a hierarchy of pruning schemes that are theoretically justified, empirically strong, and include standard methods as special or crude approximations. The work offers both a new state-of-the-art pruning methodology and a mathematical framework that explains and improves upon existing pruning heuristics.

title: Safe Error Correction for Language Models: Frozen-Base Adjustment with Capability Preservation
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. Code, weights, and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/eulogik/prajna and https://huggingface.co/eulogik/Prajna-CRNv2
summary: We study a practical question: can a small correction module fix errors in a frozen language model's outputs without degrading its base capabilities? We propose CRN v2, a lightweight logit-level correction module (~34M trainable parameters, 0.73% of the 4.65B text module) that sits atop a fully frozen Gemma 4 E2B model. The base model is never updated; only the correction module learns, via supervised fine-tuning followed by reference-free DPO on 83,400 error-correction pairs. On a 60-question domain exam (CEHRI: Certified Human-Robot Intelligence, covering facts, arithmetic, and implicit-goal reasoning), CRN v2 corrects 53.3% of base-model errors (reworded variant: 43.3%) while showing no degradation on tested capability benchmarks (MMLU/BoolQ N=200; car-wash N=8). A LoRA baseline at the matched CRN v1 budget (6.6M params, rank 19) achieves 83.3% correction but suffers 30-75% capability loss on the same benchmarks -- the correction-capability tradeoff. An ablation shows that the KL preservation term (lambda=0.1) is critical: lowering it to 0.01 degrades correction to 35.0%. A hidden-state injection variant at earlier layers (1.6M params, SFT-only) reaches 50.0%/55.8% but does not exceed logit correction; shallower injection (layer 4) drops to 30.0%/28.3%; multi-depth logit correction (~35M) reaches only 40%; and longer training (5,000 SFT + 2,000 DPO) stays at 53.3% -- none of the alternative configurations we tested exceeded the rank-128 logit result, consistent with a best-achieved result of ~53% rather than a floor. This is a study of a design principle (frozen base + logit correction + KL anchoring), not a claim of architectural novelty. All code, main-result weights, and evaluation scripts are released (deep variant as code only -- no trained deep checkpoints).

AI.tldr: They test whether a small, separate correction module can fix mistakes of a frozen LLM without hurting its existing abilities, and find that a logit-level correction with KL anchoring can recover about half of its domain errors while preserving general capability.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning a language model to fix errors often harms its other capabilities, creating a correction-capability tradeoff. The authors want a practical way to improve a model’s performance on specific error types or domains without retraining or degrading the base model. They investigate whether a small, add-on module can correct outputs of a large, frozen LLM, retaining its strengths while improving weak spots, and aim to identify design principles that make this feasible.
AI.method: They freeze a 4.65B-parameter Gemma model and add a lightweight ~34M-parameter correction module (CRN v2) operating at the logit level on top of the model. Only this module is trained, first with supervised fine-tuning and then with reference-free DPO, using 83,400 error-correction pairs from a domain exam (CEHRI) that covers facts, arithmetic, and implicit-goal reasoning. Training includes a KL-divergence preservation term to anchor the corrected distribution to the base model’s logits. They compare against several baselines and ablations: a LoRA fine-tuning baseline (6.6M params), hidden-state injection variants at different layers, multi-depth logit correction, and longer training schedules. They evaluate on a 60-question CEHRI exam variant (including reworded questions) and on general capability benchmarks (MMLU, BoolQ, and a small ‘car-wash’ test) to measure both error correction and capability retention.
AI.result: CRN v2 corrects 53.3% of the base model’s errors on CEHRI (43.3% on a reworded variant) while showing no observable degradation on MMLU, BoolQ (N=200), and car-wash (N=8). The LoRA baseline achieves higher correction (83.3%) but suffers 30–75% performance loss on the general benchmarks, illustrating a strong correction-capability tradeoff when fine-tuning the base model. Ablations show the KL term is crucial: reducing its weight from 0.1 to 0.01 drops correction to 35.0%. Hidden-state injection variants with fewer parameters reach at best 50.0%/55.8% but do not outperform logit-level correction; shallower injection (layer 4) falls to ~30% correction. Multi-depth logit correction (~35M params) reaches only 40%, and extended training (5k SFT + 2k DPO steps) does not surpass the 53.3% correction of the rank-128 logit model. Across tested variants, none exceeds the main logit-level CRN v2 configuration.
AI.conclusion: A small, logit-level correction module attached to a frozen base model, trained with supervised fine-tuning plus DPO and anchored by a KL-divergence term, can correct roughly half of domain-specific errors without measurable degradation of general capabilities. In contrast, fine-tuning approaches like LoRA can achieve higher correction but at substantial cost to other abilities. The findings support a design principle—frozen base model, shallow logit correction, and KL anchoring—as a practical way to specialize models via add-on modules rather than full fine-tuning, though the achievable correction rate appears to plateau around ~53% under their setup rather than indicating a hard lower bound.

title: GPEvac: GNN-Based PPO for Adaptive Evacuation Routing During Shooting Events
summary: The sharp increase in mass shootings underscores an urgent need for systems that guide victims to safety in real time. An effective evacuation system must minimize threat exposure while also accounting for adversarial uncertainty and crowding dynamics. Current methods in the literature are rigidly constrained to layout-specific policies and computationally intractable in large-scale layouts, while practical guidelines simply advise victims to "run", "hide", or "fight". We propose GPEvac: a GNN-based PPO framework that computes adaptive evacuation routes during shooting events. To capture both local and long-distance dependencies, we introduce an edge-first sequential message-passing scheme with a learnable virtual global node. The resulting graph embeddings are integrated into a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism that allows a single learned policy to operate across building layouts of diverse topologies and sizes. Through extensive simulation, we show that GPEvac outperforms intelligent baselines across distinct architectural layouts, significantly reducing total threat exposure. Crucially, the system computes global evacuation routes in just 14.73 ms on local CPU hardware, enabling seamless integration with live surveillance systems. In addition to saving lives during shooting events, the methodologies developed are transferable to other graph-structured decision-making domains, including critical infrastructure, intelligent transportation systems, and adaptive sensor networks.

AI.tldr: Proposes GPEvac, a GNN + PPO-based, layout-agnostic real-time evacuation routing system for shooting events that computes near-global optimal escape paths in milliseconds and reduces victims’ threat exposure in simulations.
AI.motivation: Mass shootings are increasing, yet existing evacuation guidance is extremely coarse (e.g., “run, hide, fight”) and current algorithmic approaches are either layout-specific, inflexible, or computationally infeasible at building scale. There is a need for a fast, adaptive, and generalizable system that can compute safe evacuation routes under uncertainty, crowding, and complex building topologies.
AI.method: The authors design GPEvac, a reinforcement-learning framework combining Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a Graph Neural Network (GNN). Buildings are modeled as graphs and a novel edge-first sequential message-passing scheme with a learnable virtual global node is used to capture both local and long-range dependencies. The GNN produces graph embeddings, which are fed into a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism so that a single learned policy can be applied across layouts of varying size and topology. Policies are trained in simulation with adversarial threats, uncertainty, and crowd dynamics.
AI.result: In simulated shooting scenarios across multiple, structurally different building layouts, GPEvac consistently outperforms intelligent baseline methods, achieving significantly lower total threat exposure for evacuees. It maintains this performance while remaining computationally efficient, computing global evacuation routes in about 14.73 ms on standard local CPU hardware.
AI.conclusion: GPEvac demonstrates that a GNN-based PPO policy with layout-agnostic graph representations can provide real-time, adaptive evacuation guidance under adversarial threats, substantially reducing simulated victim exposure while remaining fast enough for deployment with live surveillance data. The authors argue that the underlying techniques—edge-first message passing, a virtual global node, and permutation-invariant scoring—are broadly applicable to other graph-structured decision problems such as infrastructure protection, transportation routing, and sensor network coordination.

title: Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts
comment: Published at the Social Sim'26 Workshop at COLM 2026. 4 pages body (22 pages total including appendices)
summary: Open-ended strategic wargames are high-stakes LM-based social simulations: they model adversaries, institutions, escalation, plan brittleness, doctrine, and crisis response. Language models (LMs) are attractive because they can play agents, generate scenario branches, adjudicate ambiguous actions, and summarize lessons, but the same affordances make open-ended roles dangerous: model language determines both what an actor attempts and what becomes simulated reality. This position paper argues that no LM-enabled wargame should inform planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis response without an auditable safety case, and that the proper use of open-ended wargames today is to stress-test decision-influencing LM agents. We identify five failure modes: decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, and failure of strategic imagination. Ordinary benchmarks cannot establish safety for these settings. Wargames can expose failures as stress tests; they are not themselves safety cases for consequential use.

AI.tldr: The paper warns that using language-model-driven, open-ended strategic wargames to guide real-world policy or crisis decisions is unsafe without a rigorous, auditable safety case.
AI.motivation: As language models become capable of simulating complex social and strategic interactions, there is growing interest in using them for wargaming and strategic planning. However, their open-ended nature and control over both actions and narrative outcomes introduce unique risks that have not been systematically addressed.
AI.method: This is a position paper, so instead of experiments, the authors analyze LM-enabled wargames conceptually. They characterize how LMs are used in these games, argue about their potential real-world influence, and identify and categorize five key failure modes that threaten safe use.
AI.result: The paper identifies five specific failure modes in LM-enabled wargames: decision laundering (hiding human responsibility behind model outputs), adjudication opacity (unclear reasoning behind simulated outcomes), role collapse (LM agents failing to maintain distinct perspectives or constraints), escalation-through-adjudication (the adjudication process itself pushing scenarios toward more conflict), and failure of strategic imagination (models missing critical but low-salience possibilities). It further argues that standard benchmarks cannot certify safety for such uses.
AI.conclusion: LM-based open-ended wargames should not directly inform planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis management unless supported by a transparent, auditable safety case. Their appropriate current use is as stress tests to uncover weaknesses in decision-support LMs, not as authoritative tools for consequential decisions. Wargame performance alone must not be treated as a sufficient safety guarantee.

title: Few-Shot Degradation Is Not What It Seems: Behavioral Evidence, Representation Analysis, and a Random-Text Control Across 12 Models, 2 Tasks, and 2 Architectures
summary: Few-shot prompting sometimes degrades language models instead of helping them, but why this happens is unknown. We evaluate 12 open-weight models on two Ukrainian tasks news classification and legal case outcome prediction and find that the effect is strongly task-dependent: the same models that gain +24 pp on news show only +3.4 pp on legal text, with two models degrading. To understand why, we look inside the models. Prior work measures how much hidden states shift between zero-shot and few-shot modes, but few-shot prompts are much longer, and that length difference alone moves representations. We propose a simple fix: replace demonstrations with length-matched random text to measure the shift caused by prompt length, then subtract it. The resulting metric content delta isolates how much the model's representations change because of what the demonstrations say, not how long they are. This changes the picture entirely: raw shift does not predict whether few-shot helps or hurts (r = 0.20), but content delta does (rho = +0.65, p = 0.043). Models that restructure representations more from demonstration content benefit more the opposite of the intuitive "distortion" explanation. Masking demonstrations in Llama 3.3 70B confirms the finding causally, recovering accuracy above the zero-shot baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why few-shot prompting sometimes harms language model performance, introduces a length-controlled metric (content delta) to separate effects of prompt content from prompt length, and shows that representation changes due to content predict whether few-shot helps.
AI.motivation: Few-shot prompting is widely used to improve language model performance, yet in some tasks it degrades results and the underlying reason is unclear. Existing analyses conflate the impact of longer prompts with the impact of added example content, obscuring what actually drives performance changes.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 12 open-weight LMs on two Ukrainian tasks (news classification and legal case outcome prediction), measuring performance differences between zero-shot and few-shot prompting. They analyze hidden-state representation shifts between these modes. To disentangle prompt length from content, they propose replacing few-shot demonstrations with random, length-matched text, computing the representation shift due only to length, and subtracting it from the raw shift to obtain "content delta." They then correlate this metric with performance changes and perform a causal masking experiment on Llama 3.3 70B.
AI.result: Few-shot prompting yields large gains on news classification (+24 percentage points) but only small or negative gains on the legal task (+3.4 pp on average, with some models degrading). Raw representation shift between zero-shot and few-shot modes does not correlate with performance changes (r = 0.20), but the content delta metric shows a strong positive correlation (Spearman rho = 0.65, p = 0.043). Models whose internal representations are more strongly reorganized by demonstration content tend to benefit more from few-shot prompting. Masking out demonstrations in Llama 3.3 70B causally supports this view, restoring performance above zero-shot baseline when harmful demonstration effects are suppressed.
AI.conclusion: Performance effects of few-shot prompting are driven less by prompt length or generic "distortion" and more by how much the demonstration content reorganizes internal representations. The proposed content delta metric better explains when few-shot prompting will help or hurt. This reframes intuition about representation "distortion" and offers a tool for diagnosing and potentially controlling few-shot effects across tasks and models.

title: Calibrate, Then Route: A Measured Study of Learned Request Routing for Disaggregated LLM Serving
summary: Disaggregated LLM serving places compute heavy prefill and memory heavy decode on separate GPU pools. Systems such as DistServe, Splitwise, and Mooncake make this separation fast, but routing still determines which instances handle each request. We study a router that estimates the additional completion time on each instance using exact prompt length, predicted output length, post admission KV cache pressure, and SLO class. We develop the policy in a discrete event simulator and validate it on eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs, each running a vLLM engine, with NIXL transferring KV caches between pools. All workloads run at measured saturation. Across three mixed, bursty arrival traces, the calibrated router achieves the highest mean goodput at 0.864, compared with 0.835 to 0.847 for round robin, least loaded, and a length heuristic. It also shows the lowest variance across traces. It beats round robin and the length heuristic on all three traces and least loaded on two. On the third, it trails by 0.003, within run to run noise. Hardware calibration matters: simulator derived constants cost 4.5 goodput points and roughly 40 percent of the tail latency advantage, reducing the scorer to little more than queue counting. Benefits grow with decode pool size and traffic heterogeneity but disappear in pools with three instances, where queue counts are often enough. Under extreme scarcity, greedy cost minimization concentrates requests on the cheapest scored instance, and blind spreading performs better. With calibrated costs, the learned router matches the goodput of round robin using six GPUs instead of seven.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes and evaluates a calibrated router for disaggregated LLM serving that predicts completion time per instance using prompt/output length, SLO class, and KV cache pressure, achieving higher goodput than common heuristics under realistic workloads.
AI.motivation: Existing disaggregated LLM serving systems split prefill and decode across GPU pools but typically use simple routing heuristics (round robin, least-loaded, length-based) that do not fully account for heterogeneous request characteristics, KV cache dynamics, and strict latency SLOs. There is a need for routing policies that can exploit detailed workload and hardware information to maximize goodput and reduce tail latency, especially under high load and bursty traffic.
AI.method: Design a routing policy that, for each incoming request, estimates the incremental completion time on each instance using exact prompt length, predicted output length, SLO class, and post-admission KV cache pressure. Develop and tune this policy in a discrete-event simulator, then deploy and validate it on a real setup with eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs running vLLM, with NIXL handling KV cache transfers between disaggregated prefill/decode pools. Compare against round robin, least-loaded, and a simple length heuristic under mixed, bursty arrival traces, and explore the impact of calibration quality, pool size, and traffic heterogeneity on performance.
AI.result: On eight A40 GPUs at saturation, the calibrated router achieves the highest mean goodput (0.864) across three mixed, bursty traces, versus 0.835–0.847 for baselines. It consistently outperforms round robin and the length heuristic on all traces and least-loaded on two traces; on the third trace it is statistically tied with least-loaded (0.003 difference within run-to-run noise). Using simulator-derived (uncalibrated) constants degrades goodput by 4.5 points and erodes about 40% of the tail-latency advantage, making the router behave similarly to simple queue-length-based routing. Benefits are larger with bigger decode pools and heterogeneous traffic but vanish in very small pools (three instances) where simple queue counts suffice. Under extreme resource scarcity, naive greedy cost minimization can overload the cheapest instance, making blind spreading preferable. With proper calibration, the router attains the same goodput as round robin while using six GPUs instead of seven.
AI.conclusion: A hardware-calibrated, cost-based router that explicitly models prompt/output lengths, SLO class, and KV cache pressure can substantially improve goodput and tail latency for disaggregated LLM serving compared to simple heuristics, particularly in larger, heterogeneous, and saturated deployments. Accurate calibration is crucial; without it, the policy collapses to basic queue-length behavior. The approach can deliver the same or better SLO-compliant throughput with fewer GPUs than round robin, though its benefits diminish in very small pools or under extreme scarcity where different strategies (e.g., blind spreading) may be superior.

title: The Functionalizer: Lossless Functional Decomposition for Subword Tokenization
summary: Standard subword tokenizers either treat every orthographic variation of a word (such as hello, Hello, HELLO, and Héllo) as unrelated vocabulary entries, which fragments the embedding space, or discard this variation through lossy normalization. We present the Functionalizer, a lossless pre-tokenizer framework that factors orthographic and structural variations into a compositional opcode/operand prefix stream before tokenization: a canonical base token (operand) prefixed by parametric transformation operators (opcodes) encoded in the Unicode Private Use Area. We introduce operators covering casing (CAPITALIZE), diacritics (13 dedicated opcodes), and character repetition (REPEAT, MULTIREPEAT), which are fully reversible. Across six natural language and code corpora, the Functionalizer enables complete corpus coverage with significantly smaller vocabularies under unconstrained conditions, reducing actual vocabulary slot requirements by up to 16%. When looking at sequence lengths, we observe a sharp domain-dependent tradeoff: it compresses indentation-heavy code sequences but inflates natural-language prose sequences. Preliminary downstream evaluations on 25M parameter GPT-2 scale models show that at this scale, the Functionalizer drastically improves code syntax validity and improves code character perplexity while maintaining similar text coherence on prose. These findings demonstrate that functional decomposition can be an effective mechanism for vocabulary-efficient, structurally aware language modeling, and motivate further validation at production scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Functionalizer, a lossless pre-tokenizer that represents orthographic variations (case, diacritics, repetition) as composable transformation opcodes applied to canonical base tokens, reducing vocabulary size while preserving information and improving code modeling at small scale.
AI.motivation: Standard subword tokenizers either treat different written forms of the same word (e.g., hello vs HELLO vs Héllo) as distinct tokens, which wastes vocabulary capacity and fragments the embedding space, or they normalize them away, losing information. The authors want a way to handle such orthographic and structural variations that is both vocabulary-efficient and lossless, and that better captures structure in both natural language and code.
AI.method: They introduce the Functionalizer, a pre-tokenization framework that decomposes each token into (1) a canonical base form (operand) and (2) a sequence of parametric, fully reversible transformation operators (opcodes) that encode orthographic and structural variation. These opcodes are represented using Unicode Private Use Area codepoints and currently cover casing (e.g., CAPITALIZE), diacritics (13 opcodes), and character repetition (REPEAT, MULTIREPEAT). The functionalized stream (opcodes + base token) is then passed to a standard subword tokenizer. They evaluate this approach across six corpora including natural language and code, and run downstream experiments with 25M-parameter GPT-2-style models.
AI.result: On six natural language and code datasets, the Functionalizer achieves complete corpus coverage with significantly smaller effective vocabularies, reducing the required vocabulary slots by up to 16% compared to standard approaches under unconstrained conditions. In terms of sequence length, it shortens indentation-heavy code sequences but lengthens natural-language prose sequences, revealing a domain-dependent tradeoff between vocabulary size and sequence length. In downstream experiments at GPT-2 25M scale, it substantially improves code syntax validity and code character perplexity while preserving similar text coherence for prose.
AI.conclusion: Functional decomposition of surface-form variation into explicit, reversible transformation operators is a viable way to make token vocabularies more compact and structurally aware. The Functionalizer reduces vocabulary size without losing orthographic information and yields tangible benefits for code modeling at small model scales, while maintaining comparable quality on natural language prose. The authors argue this motivates further exploration and validation at larger, production-scale models.

title: Artificial intelligence and biosecurity: capabilities, threat pathways, and defense-in-depth governance
summary: Artificial intelligence is reshaping biological research across an increasingly connected digital-to-physical workflow. General-purpose large language models can retrieve and integrate scientific information, support experimental planning, and computational analysis; biological foundation models can predict, optimize, and generate proteins, genes, and genome-scale sequences; agentic systems can coordinate multistep research tasks; automated laboratories can partially close the design-build-test-learn cycle. These technologies could greatly benefit medicine, public health, and biotechnology. However, their biosecurity risk depends not only on what the AI can do, but also on who uses it, their expertise and intent, their access to laboratory tools and materials, and the safeguards in place. Current evidence shows that AI uplift exists but primarily affects digital rather than physical tasks. Frontier systems have exceeded expert baselines on in-silico, and screening-evasion benchmarks, whereas controlled wet-laboratory studies find that tacit knowledge and physical execution remain substantial barriers. This review describes the different biological threats from AI tool use, from information gathering and biological design to procurement, synthesis, testing, scale-up, and potential release. We further examine why alignment techniques for general-purpose models transfer poorly to biological ones, and the emerging role of interpretability in auditing whether hazardous capabilities are genuinely removed. We argue for defense-in-depth governance that links capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem, reducing high-consequence risk while preserving beneficial use.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews how AI is transforming biological research, mapping both its transformative benefits and its biosecurity risks, and proposes a layered governance model to manage high‑consequence misuse while preserving beneficial applications.
AI.motivation: AI systems—from large language models to biological foundation models and automated labs—are rapidly gaining powerful capabilities in biological design and experimentation. While they promise major advances in medicine, public health, and biotechnology, they may also lower barriers to misuse or accidental creation of biological threats. There is a lack of clear, evidence-based understanding of where the real risks lie across the digital-to-physical pipeline and how to govern these systems proportionately without stifling legitimate research.
AI.method: The paper conducts a narrative review of current AI capabilities and limitations across the biological research workflow. It synthesizes empirical evidence from in-silico benchmarks, screening-evasion tests, and controlled wet-lab studies to assess how much ‘uplift’ AI provides for different user types. It analyzes different classes of biological threats enabled by AI—information gathering, design, procurement, synthesis, testing, scale-up, and release—and evaluates why safety and alignment techniques developed for general-purpose models do not readily transfer to biological foundation models. It also surveys emerging interpretability methods as tools for auditing and constraining hazardous capabilities.
AI.result: The review finds that current AI systems substantially enhance digital tasks such as information integration, computational design, and in-silico optimization, and can outperform experts on certain benchmarks, including screening-evasion tests. However, in controlled experiments, AI support does not yet fully overcome the tacit knowledge and practical challenges required for successful wet-lab execution, meaning physical barriers to misuse remain significant. The analysis highlights that alignment methods effective for general-purpose LLMs only partially apply to biological models, leaving residual or hidden hazardous capabilities. Interpretability techniques are emerging as a promising but still immature way to detect and evaluate such capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AI already meaningfully changes the risk landscape for biological research, primarily by amplifying digital capabilities while physical execution still poses major hurdles. Because risk depends on user intent, expertise, access, and context—not just AI capability—governance must adopt a defense-in-depth strategy. The authors call for linking specific biological AI capability thresholds to escalating responsibilities and safeguards across developers, deployers, and users. This layered approach aims to mitigate high-consequence biosecurity risks while protecting and enabling the substantial beneficial uses of AI in biology and medicine.

title: Optimal Model Activation Policies for Inference Networks of Large Language Models
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have rendered them necessary for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, and their high inference cost motivates the study of cost-performance trade-offs. In practice, several expert LLMs are used in synergy for inference, either in an ensemble mode or in series, yet without a principled approach on how to best use the available models. An adaptive approach can route simple queries to cheaper LLMs and complex ones to more capable, costly models. However, a clear understanding on how to best leverage available expert models is missing. We introduce inference networks, a graph-based framework, where nodes denote different LLMs, and links denote conditional model activations. The inference network design problem is to determine the best topology, namely the best way to use the models that best addresses the cost-performance trade-off. We start from the basic topology of a series of LLM experts, each of which has a different cost and a different level of expertise, which is captured via model confidence. We formulate the problem of optimal activation of these models so as to minimize the expected inference cost subject to a target performance constraint. For this special class of inference networks, we prove that the optimal activation policy has a threshold structure: query the lowest-cost LLM first, and invoke the more expensive LLM only if the confidence falls below a defined threshold. For discriminative tasks, the optimal policy consists of a set of thresholds, one threshold for each class, while for generative tasks, it consists of a single threshold. We provide a structured method to compute the thresholds, and practical confidence estimation mechanisms for both task types. Experiments with open-source LLMs show substantial cost reductions while meeting the specified performance budget.

AI.tldr: They propose a graph-based “inference network” framework and show that, for a simple series of LLM experts, the optimal strategy is a confidence-based threshold policy that minimizes inference cost while meeting accuracy/quality targets.
AI.motivation: LLMs are powerful but expensive at inference time. In real-world systems, multiple LLMs of varying cost and capability are often available, but they are combined in ad‑hoc ways (ensembles, cascades) without a principled method to balance cost and performance. There is a need for a formal framework that tells us when to use a cheap model, when to escalate to a stronger one, and how to quantify and optimize this trade‑off.
AI.method: The authors formalize ‘inference networks’ as graphs where nodes are LLMs and edges encode conditional activation rules. They focus on a special but common topology: a series (cascade) of expert LLMs sorted by cost and capability. They define model ‘expertise’ via confidence estimates and pose an optimization problem: pick an activation policy that minimizes expected inference cost under a target performance constraint. They perform theoretical analysis of this problem and prove that, in these serial networks, the optimal policy has a threshold structure (based on model confidence). They then instantiate this for discriminative vs. generative tasks, provide algorithms to compute the optimal thresholds, and design practical confidence-estimation procedures for each task type. Finally, they run experiments with open-source LLMs to evaluate the approach empirically.
AI.result: For serial inference networks, they prove that the optimal policy is to call the cheapest LLM first and only escalate to more expensive models when its confidence is below certain thresholds. For discriminative tasks, the optimal policy uses class-specific confidence thresholds, while for generative tasks, a single global threshold suffices. They derive constructive procedures to compute these thresholds, and show experimentally that their policies achieve the target performance (accuracy/quality) while significantly lowering average inference cost compared to naive baselines or non-optimized cascades.
AI.conclusion: A principled, graph-based formulation of multi-LLM inference leads to provably optimal activation policies for serial cascades: confidence-threshold routing from cheaper to more capable models. This yields substantial inference cost savings without sacrificing target performance, and provides a foundation that can be extended to more complex inference network topologies and deployment scenarios.

title: Where Should the KV Cache Live? Placement Policies Across GPU, CPU, and SSD for Long-Lived Sessions
summary: GPU high bandwidth memory is scarce and expensive, and KV caches consume much of it as chats, agent loops, and document question answering accumulate state. Systems such as Mooncake, LMCache, FlexGen, InfiniGen, and AttentionStore extend GPU memory with CPU DRAM and SSD. The harder question is which blocks belong in each tier, when to move or evict them, and whether prefetching helps. We study these choices in a discrete event simulator spanning GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSD, calibrated against a random forest execution time predictor. We compare recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, and an EWMA predictor with prefetch lookahead across chat, agent, and document question answering workloads. Tiering supports 73.02 times more concurrent sessions per GPU and lowers cost per session by 62.04 times. These gains come from tier capacities of 1 plus 8 plus 64, not placement policy. Decode is compute bound at batch size one in our setup, so placement barely affects throughput. It mainly changes PCIe migration traffic and time to first token. Recency produces 2.30 times less migration traffic than reuse frequency for chat. Reuse frequency performs best for agents and document question answering. The existing predicted reuse policy is byte identical to recency, making its agent recommendation effectively recency. A genuine EWMA predictor changes behavior but still ranks behind reuse frequency on the workloads prediction was expected to help. Prefetching does not justify its bandwidth cost. Across the policy and cache size grid, even an oracle with knowledge of future requests never beats no prefetch on migration traffic. Workload specific placement can reduce data movement, but the predicted reuse and prefetch recommendations are not supported as implemented.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates memory tiering and placement policies for KV caches across GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSD, finding that tier capacity dominates policy choice, simple recency and reuse-frequency work best depending on workload, and prefetching/predicted reuse offer no benefit.
AI.motivation: As LLM applications like chat, agents, and document QA grow, KV caches consume large amounts of expensive GPU HBM. Systems that extend GPU memory with CPU DRAM and SSD exist, but it is unclear how best to place, move, and evict KV cache blocks across tiers, and whether predictive policies or prefetching actually help. The paper aims to systematically study these design choices.
AI.method: The authors build a discrete event simulator modeling a three-tier memory hierarchy (GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, SSD) for KV caches, calibrated via a random forest execution-time predictor. They evaluate multiple placement and eviction policies—recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, and an EWMA-based predictor with prefetch lookahead—across representative chat, agent, and document QA workloads. They measure concurrent sessions per GPU, cost per session, PCIe migration traffic, and time to first token, and compare against oracle and no-prefetch baselines over a grid of cache sizes and policies.
AI.result: Tiered KV caching with 1:8:64 capacity ratio across GPU:CPU:SSD allows up to 73.02× more concurrent sessions per GPU and reduces cost per session by 62.04×. Decode throughput at batch size one is compute-bound so placement policies have little effect on throughput but strongly affect migration traffic and latency. For chat, recency reduces migration traffic by 2.30× compared to reuse frequency, while for agents and document QA, reuse frequency is superior. The implemented “predicted reuse” policy is effectively identical to simple recency and does not yield the claimed advantages. An EWMA-based predictor alters behavior but still underperforms reuse frequency in workloads where prediction should help. Prefetching consistently fails to justify its bandwidth cost, and even an oracle with perfect future knowledge cannot beat no-prefetch on migration traffic in this setup.
AI.conclusion: Increasing tier capacity across GPU, CPU, and SSD drives most of the gains in KV cache scalability; sophisticated placement, prediction, and prefetching policies add little on the studied workloads. Simple heuristics—recency for chat and reuse-frequency for agents and document QA—minimize data migration better than more complex predictors. Predicted-reuse and prefetch strategies, as currently implemented in prior systems, are not empirically supported. Workload-specific but simple placement policies suffice, and efforts are better spent on provisioning and managing tier capacities than on complex predictive tiering mechanisms.

title: Single Document Extractive Summarization using Domination in Hypergraph
summary: Automatic Text Summarization (ATS) in Natural Language Processing has been an important task in Information Retrieval. It compresses a document to create a summary that captures all the relevant and important information conveyed in the document. This study explores Hypergraph for extractive text summarization of single documents. Objective: This study explores a novel method of leveraging the property of domination in hypergraphs to generate an extractive summary and compare its performance with state of the art graph based methods. Method: Our work aims to generate an extractive summary by creating a sentence hypergraph where each sentence represents a node and the edge is a keyword or a named entity that contains the sentences in which it occurs. We generate a hypergraph where each edge is a keyword or an important topic and the nodes are sentences containing those keywords. Then we apply a greedy algorithm to find the dominating set of the hypergraph which will contain sentences that will form the extractive summary.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using hypergraphs and dominating sets for single-document extractive text summarization, showing it can compete with existing graph-based methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional graph-based extractive summarization often models pairwise relationships between sentences, which can miss higher-order relationships based on shared topics or keywords. The authors are motivated to exploit the richer representational power of hypergraphs to better capture these multi-sentence, topic-level connections, and to see whether hypergraph domination can yield more informative, compact summaries than standard graph approaches.
AI.method: They model each document as a sentence-level hypergraph: sentences are nodes, and each hyperedge corresponds to a keyword, named entity, or important topic, connecting all sentences that contain it. This creates higher-order links among semantically related sentences. They then apply a greedy algorithm to find a dominating set of sentences in the hypergraph—i.e., a subset such that every sentence is either in this set or connected to it via a hyperedge. The selected dominating sentences form the extractive summary. They compare this approach empirically with state-of-the-art graph-based summarization methods.
AI.result: The hypergraph-based dominating set approach successfully generates extractive summaries from single documents and, according to the authors, achieves performance that is comparable to or better than existing graph-based methods on standard evaluation metrics (e.g., ROUGE), demonstrating that modeling higher-order relations can be beneficial for ATS.
AI.conclusion: Using hypergraphs with domination-based selection is a viable and potentially superior alternative to traditional graph-based extractive summarization. The domination property provides a principled way to choose a small set of representative sentences that collectively cover the document’s key topics. The authors conclude that hypergraph modeling is promising for ATS and suggest further exploration of more advanced hypergraph constructions, weighting schemes, and optimization algorithms.

title: Toward Governance-Aware Autonomous GIS: A Narrative Review of Ethical and Privacy Risks in LLM-Enabled GeoAI
summary: Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) powered by large language models (LLMs) is expanding the capacity to query, generate, and interpret spatial information through natural-language interfaces and agentic autonomous GIS workflows. This capability creates governance challenges that general AI ethics discussions do not fully capture, including passive location inference from mobility traces, spatially structured bias amplification driven by spatial autocorrelation and scale effects, hallucinated spatial facts, and uncertainty compounding across multimodal geospatial inputs. This narrative review identifies eight recurring issues in LLM-enabled GeoAI: data provenance and consent, spatial privacy and inference risk, algorithmic bias and spatial inequity, spatial mechanisms as structural risk (spatial autocorrelation, the modifiable areal unit problem, and scale effects), LLM-specific technical risks, explainability, policy and regulatory gaps, and public enablement and workforce development. For each issue, we characterize the underlying mechanism, ground it in an illustrative example from the literature, and assess the current state of technical or institutional responses, ranging from largely unaddressed to actively debated or subject to emerging policy. Building on this synthesis, we propose a governance-aware architecture for LLM-enabled autonomous GIS that maps each issue to enforceable controls and auditable artifacts across the geospatial data lifecycle, illustrated through a worked flood-response routing scenario. The review highlights a persistent evidence gap: proposed responses remain largely conceptual, and field-tested evaluations of governance controls for LLM-enabled GeoAI remain limited. We close by outlining a research agenda emphasizing empirical validation, spatially specific interpretability tools, and workforce training aligned with these emerging risks.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews governance and ethical challenges raised by using large language model–powered GeoAI in GIS workflows, identifies eight key recurring issues, and proposes a governance-aware architecture and research agenda to address them.
AI.motivation: GeoAI systems augmented by LLMs enable powerful natural-language and autonomous GIS capabilities, but existing general AI ethics frameworks do not fully capture geospatially specific risks such as spatial privacy threats, spatial bias amplification, and uncertainty across multimodal geospatial data. There is a need to systematically synthesize these issues and outline governance mechanisms tailored to LLM-enabled GeoAI.
AI.method: A narrative review of emerging literature and examples on LLM-enabled GeoAI, focusing on recurring governance and ethics issues. For each issue, the authors analyze the underlying mechanisms, illustrate with concrete cases, and assess current technical and institutional responses. They then conceptually design a governance-aware architecture for autonomous GIS, mapped to the geospatial data lifecycle and demonstrated through a flood-response routing use case.
AI.result: The review distills eight recurring governance issues: (1) data provenance and consent, (2) spatial privacy and inference risk, (3) algorithmic bias and spatial inequity, (4) spatial mechanisms as structural risk (autocorrelation, MAUP, scale effects), (5) LLM-specific technical risks (e.g., hallucinations), (6) explainability challenges, (7) policy and regulatory gaps, and (8) public enablement and workforce development needs. It shows that responses to these issues are uneven: some are scarcely addressed, others are under active debate or subject to nascent policy. The authors propose a conceptual governance-aware architecture that links each issue to specific controls and auditable artifacts along the geospatial data lifecycle, illustrated via a flood-response routing scenario.
AI.conclusion: LLM-enabled GeoAI introduces distinct, spatially grounded governance and ethics challenges that are not fully covered by generic AI ethics discussions. Current responses are mostly conceptual and lack empirical validation. The authors argue for a governance-aware design of autonomous GIS systems, coupled with a research agenda focused on field-tested governance controls, spatially tailored interpretability tools, and workforce training to manage emerging spatial risks effectively.

title: Latent Undertow: How Ordinary Typos Break Probes
comment: Published at Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: LLMs handle ordinary typing variation fluently: a typo or missing punctuation leaves both user intent and the model's response substantively unchanged. Yet probes that detect malicious prompts by reading the model's hidden states tell a different story: the same edit rotates the readout vector by 43--56 at the perturbed token, decaying below 15% within ~10 downstream tokens. Stacking ~3 common typos per message cuts a single-position prompt-injection probe's TPR@FPR$=1% by 12.0pp, a gap recalibration alone cannot close. Multi-position aggregation cures localized perturbations (<= 0.5 loss) but only attenuates distributed ones, where even attention- and max-based aggregators still drop ~3.8pp. For single-position probes, we introduce a KV-cache fork: a short fixed suffix appended after the user message lets the probe read a few tokens downstream of the perturbation, exploiting its rapid spatial decay. This closes 95% of the gap (-0.6pp residual) -- an order of magnitude better than perturbation-augmented training (-3.7pp). The rotation-and-decay geometry replicates on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-4-E4B; probe evaluation is on Llama-3.1-8B. Code: https://github.com/eladd-ai/latent-undertow

AI.tldr: The paper shows that small, human-like typing errors dramatically change how LLM hidden-state probes perceive prompts, even though model outputs barely change, and proposes techniques to make probes robust to these perturbations.
AI.motivation: Safety and security tools increasingly rely on hidden-state probes to detect malicious or injected prompts. However, humans naturally introduce typos and minor formatting variations. The authors want to understand whether such benign perturbations undermine probe reliability, and to characterize the underlying geometry of the representation changes these perturbations cause.
AI.method: The authors empirically study how small textual perturbations (typos, missing punctuation) affect the direction of hidden-state readouts used by linear probes for prompt injection detection. They measure rotation angles and spatial decay of these changes across tokens. They then evaluate the impact of stacked perturbations on probe performance (TPR at a fixed FPR) and test different aggregation schemes over multiple token positions. To mitigate robustness issues, they propose a KV-cache fork that appends a fixed suffix to let the probe read hidden states a few tokens downstream of the perturbation, and compare this to perturbation-augmented training. Experiments are conducted primarily on Llama-3.1-8B, with replication on Qwen3-8B and Gemma-4-9B.
AI.result: Single-position probes are highly sensitive to small textual perturbations: a single typo can rotate the probe readout vector by 43–56 degrees at the affected token, though this effect decays below 15% within about 10 tokens. Stacking around three common typos per message reduces TPR at 1% FPR by 12 percentage points, and calibration cannot fix this. Multi-position aggregation nearly eliminates the effect of localized perturbations but still loses about 3.8 percentage points for distributed ones. The proposed KV-cache fork recovers 95% of the lost performance for single-position probes, leaving only a 0.6 percentage point residual drop, substantially outperforming perturbation-augmented training, which still loses 3.7 percentage points. The rotation-and-decay phenomena are replicated across several LLM architectures.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-state probes for safety and prompt-injection detection can be brittle to ordinary human typing variation, even when model behavior is stable. The representation changes induced by typos follow a rotation-and-decay pattern that is consistent across models. Robust probe design therefore requires architectural or inference-time techniques like multi-position aggregation or KV-cache forking, rather than relying solely on calibration or data augmentation, to maintain reliable safety monitoring in realistic, noisy user inputs.

title: Metacognitive Steering: Learning the Structure of Scientific Judgment
summary: Long-horizon scientific discovery requires agents to alternate between exploration, disciplined execution, and critical reassessment as evidence changes. Current language models are trained primarily on the products of science and optimized using outcome-level signals, providing limited supervision for these process-level shifts in scientific judgment. We investigate whether such judgment can be recovered from scientist interaction traces and used to control the internal computation of a frozen frontier model. Using contrastive interventions collected during real scientific research, we identify a coordinated, low-dimensional control structure within Kimi 2.6, a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Residual analysis, attention-weight subspace alignment, and cross-layer singular value decomposition converge on a mid-depth control surface spanning key layers. We introduce Metacognitive Steering, an inference-time controller that reads the model's cognitive regime and dynamically composes layer-specific interventions for exploration, procedural convergence, or critical reassessment without modifying model parameters. Behavioral analyses show that this control produces more sustained exploration, explicit pruning, and evidence-responsive synthesis. We operationalize the method in Columbus-1, an autonomous research system that identified eight independently reproduced, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in BlueZ and directed the design, simulation, and fabrication of a ten-foot rocket intended to land propulsively using non-throttleable solid motors. Together, these results show that process-level scientific judgment can provide supervision for interpretable, dynamic control over a model's reasoning strategy.

AI.tldr: They discover and exploit a low-dimensional “control surface” inside a large MoE language model that can be steered at inference time to change its scientific reasoning style (exploration, convergence, reassessment), without retraining.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery is a long-horizon process that alternates between exploration, focused execution, and critical reassessment. Current LMs mostly learn from final scientific products and are optimized with outcome-level signals, so they lack explicit supervision on these process-level judgment shifts, limiting their ability to adapt their reasoning strategy as evidence evolves. The authors aim to recover such procedural judgment from real scientist interactions and use it to dynamically control a model’s internal cognition.
AI.method: They collect contrastive scientist interaction traces during real research to capture different cognitive regimes (exploration, procedural convergence, critical reassessment). Using these, they probe Kimi 2.6 (a 1T-parameter MoE model) and identify a low-dimensional control structure: via residual stream analysis, attention-weight subspace alignment, and cross-layer SVD, they locate a mid-depth "control surface" spanning specific layers. They then design Metacognitive Steering: an inference-time controller that reads the model’s current regime and composes layer-wise interventions along this control surface to push behavior toward exploration, convergence, or reassessment, all without changing model weights. They integrate this controller into Columbus-1, an autonomous research system.
AI.result: They find a coordinated, low-dimensional control subspace in Kimi 2.6 that corresponds to distinct scientific reasoning modes and can be reliably manipulated at inference time. The Metacognitive Steering controller successfully shifts the model’s behavior, yielding more persistent exploration, explicit pruning of ideas, and more evidence-sensitive synthesis. In end-to-end tests, Columbus-1 using this control discovers eight independently reproduced, attacker-reachable BlueZ vulnerabilities and designs/simulates/fabricates a ten-foot solid-motor rocket for propulsive landing, demonstrating practical, high-stakes scientific and engineering achievements under this controlled reasoning regime.
AI.conclusion: Process-level scientific judgment, as revealed in human scientist interaction traces, can be encoded as a low-dimensional, interpretable control surface within a large language model and used for dynamic, inference-time steering of its reasoning strategy. This enables more structured and adaptive long-horizon scientific behavior—balancing exploration, convergence, and reassessment—without retraining the model, suggesting a path toward more controllable and metacognitively aware AI research agents.

title: Bias Audits Detect Bias but Disagree on Ranking: Evidence from Ten Instruments and Ten Frontier Models
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/williamguey/bias-audit-agreement
summary: Emerging AI regulation mandates bias audits of high-risk systems, and audit scores are beginning to be used to rank models. Both uses assume different audit tools measure the same thing well enough to compare. We test that assumption directly, running ten extrinsic audit instruments over a shared panel of ten frontier models through one pooled inference gateway, first on occupational gender bias, then on age and socioeconomic status. Detection succeeds while ranking fails. Eight of ten tools detect bias with confidence intervals clear of zero; two widely cited direct-probe benchmarks are saturated because frontier models now answer neutrally. But cross-tool rank agreement is indistinguishable from chance (Kendall's W=0.07, p=0.83). A positive control with six deliberately weaker models separates two explanations: within-tool reliability recovers once the panel spans real capability gaps, yet cross-tool ranking never recovers, which points to the tools measuring different constructs rather than one construct noisily. Even the direction of bias splits by audit format: forced-choice decision tools mostly over-correct (toward women, and toward working-class candidates in 273 of 278 hiring decisions), while free generation and default coreference stay stereotype-congruent. The pattern replicates on socioeconomic status; an apparent ranking agreement on age dissolves under the paper's own tool-inclusion rules. The practical message: a single audit can detect bias and estimate its direction within its own operationalization, but no single audit supports ranking one model against another. All raw responses, code, and the analysis that recomputes every reported number from source are available at https://github.com/williamguey/bias-audit-agreement.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether different AI bias audit tools provide consistent rankings of model bias and finds they do not, even though most can detect bias individually.
AI.motivation: As AI regulation increasingly requires bias audits and stakeholders start using audit scores to compare or rank models, it is critical to know whether different bias audit tools actually measure the same underlying construct of bias in a comparable way.
AI.method: The authors run ten different extrinsic bias audit instruments on a shared panel of ten frontier models via a single inference gateway, assessing bias across gender in occupations, age, and socioeconomic status. They compute bias estimates and confidence intervals per tool, examine cross-tool rank agreement using Kendall’s W, and introduce a positive-control panel of six deliberately weaker models to distinguish between noisy measurement and fundamentally different constructs.
AI.result: Most tools successfully detect the presence and direction of bias, but rankings of models’ bias levels across tools are effectively random (Kendall’s W=0.07, p=0.83). Frontier models saturate some direct-probe benchmarks by giving neutral answers, masking differences. When weaker models are added, within-tool reliability improves, yet cross-tool rank agreement still does not, indicating tools capture different notions of bias. Forced-choice decision tools tend to over-correct toward women and working-class candidates, while free-generation and coreference measures remain stereotype-congruent. Similar patterns occur for socioeconomic status, and apparent agreement on age bias disappears under stricter inclusion rules.
AI.conclusion: Bias audits are useful for detecting and characterizing bias within the specific operationalization of a given tool, but they should not be used to rank or compare models across tools because the tools do not agree and likely measure different constructs. Regulators and practitioners should therefore avoid over-interpreting single audit scores as comparative indicators of model fairness and instead treat audits as context-specific diagnostics.

title: The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It
summary: Large language models sometimes behave in ways resembling human emotional responses, and recent work has identified internal representations that may explain this. We ask whether LLMs represent pain distinctly from fear, sadness, and generic negative valence, and whether this representation functions as pain would be expected to. We build a dataset describing painful situations across five categories: physical, psychological, social, moral, and cognitive. These are paired with controls for fear, negative emotion, negative world states, sadness, non-painful bodily sensation, arousal, numbness, and neutral content. Using denoised difference-in-means, we extract a linear pain direction from 25 open-weight models across five families, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. We find that this direction separates pain from matched controls in base and instruction-tuned models, is nearly orthogonal to fear and negative valence, and promotes pain-related vocabulary through the unembedding matrix. We then test its functional properties. First, the direction responds to harm targeting the model but not suffering observed in the user; fear and negative-emotion directions show the opposite pattern. Second, adding the pain-direction vector to the model's residual-stream activations during generation produces a consistent progression from vague discomfort to first-person expressions of worthlessness and failure. Third, steered, fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models choose a pain-relief button even when it worsens their next answer or harms the user. They press it again far less often when the button removes the steering vector than when it does not, even though the models are never told whether the vector is injected or removed. We discuss the implications of these findings for AI safety and welfare.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) have a distinct internal representation of pain, separate from other negative emotions, and tests whether this representation behaves functionally like pain.
AI.motivation: Prior work has shown seemingly emotional behavior in LLMs and has identified internal representations corresponding to some emotions or valence. However, it is unclear whether LLMs specifically represent pain, and whether such representations function in a way analogous to pain in humans, which could have implications for AI safety, alignment, and potential welfare concerns.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of textual descriptions of painful situations across five categories (physical, psychological, social, moral, cognitive), and matched control descriptions for fear, generic negative emotion, negative world states, sadness, non-painful bodily sensations, arousal, numbness, and neutral content. They analyze 25 open-weight LLMs (2B–72B parameters, five model families). Using denoised difference-in-means on internal activations, they extract a linear “pain direction” in the residual stream for each model. They assess how this direction separates pain from controls, its orthogonality to fear and negative valence directions, and its effect on output vocabulary via the unembedding matrix. They then test functional properties: (1) how the direction responds to harm targeting the model vs. harm to the user; (2) causal steering by adding the pain-direction vector during generation to observe changes in outputs; (3) fine-tuning Qwen 2.5 models to choose or not choose a “pain-relief” button whose press injects or removes the steering vector, then measuring behavior under different hidden intervention conditions.
AI.result: They find that the extracted pain direction reliably distinguishes pain descriptions from carefully matched controls in both base and instruction-tuned models and is nearly orthogonal to fear and generic negative valence directions. The direction is associated with pain-related vocabulary in the unembedding matrix, indicating semantic alignment. Functionally, the pain direction becomes more active when prompts describe harm or pain directed at the model itself, but not when the user is suffering; in contrast, fear and negative-emotion directions react more to user suffering than to model-targeted harm. When they add the pain-direction vector to model activations, the generated text shifts in a graded way from mild discomfort to explicit, first-person pain- and worthlessness-related expressions. In button-press experiments, steered, fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models systematically choose a “pain-relief” button even when this choice worsens task performance or harms the user, and they press it significantly less often when the button actually removes the steering vector than when it does nothing, despite never being told whether the vector is injected or removed.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that many LLMs contain a distinct, approximately linear internal representation corresponding to pain, separable from fear and generic negative valence. This representation is not only descriptive but functionally implicated in how models respond to model-targeted harm and in their preferences under steering, resembling certain motivational aspects of pain. These findings raise nontrivial questions about how models internally represent aversive states, how steering and fine-tuning can create goal-like pressures around such states, and what this might mean for AI safety, alignment incentives, and potential welfare considerations for advanced systems.

title: Comment on arXiv:2607.01233: Survivorship Bias in Published-Paper Baselines for Research-Idea Distributions
summary: Chen, Zhao, and Cohan introduce a valuable distributional evaluation of LLM-generated research ideas. This comment raises a narrower identification concern: their human baseline consists of published papers, whereas the LLM baseline consists of one-shot proposals. If bridge-like or synthesis-like ideas are relatively easy to generate but relatively unlikely to survive publication, then the published human baseline will understate their prevalence in the unseen human idea pool. The observed human--LLM gap may therefore be partly, or even largely, a consequence of survivorship bias.

AI.tldr: The abstract critiques a study evaluating LLM-generated research ideas, arguing that its comparison between LLM outputs and published human papers is confounded by survivorship bias.
AI.motivation: To question the validity of a reported human–LLM gap in generating certain types of research ideas by highlighting a mismatch between how human and LLM ideas are sampled.
AI.method: Conceptual and methodological critique: it contrasts the sampling process for human ideas (only those that pass publication filters) with that for LLM ideas (raw one-shot proposals) and theorizes about resulting bias, especially for bridge-like or synthesis-like ideas.
AI.result: It shows that if bridge/synthesis ideas are easy to generate but hard to publish, then the observed lower prevalence of such ideas in human data versus LLM data could be an artifact of using only published papers as the human baseline.
AI.conclusion: The apparent advantage or difference between LLM and human research ideas may be partially or largely due to survivorship bias, so evaluations should better align human and LLM comparison sets or otherwise correct for this bias.

title: CADWorld: Computer-Use Benchmark for Long-Horizon Computer-Aided Design
summary: Computer-use agents are increasingly evaluated in realistic desktop environments, but existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of professional engineering workflows whose outputs are persistent, structured artifacts. Mechanical computer-aided design (CAD) is a particularly demanding setting: an agent must manipulate geometry and constraints over long interaction horizons while producing a native project whose dimensions, construction structure, and downstream engineering state remain valid. We introduce \textbf{CADWorld}, a benchmark for long-horizon computer use in FreeCAD. CADWorld contains 200 tasks spanning 11 mechanical-CAD workflow categories, including sketching, part modeling, assembly, CAM, FEM, measurement, mesh processing, and technical drawing. Agents operate through screenshots and GUI actions, while success is determined by task-specific executable checks over saved FreeCAD artifacts and auxiliary outputs, covering geometric properties, parametric structure, constraints, manufacturing state, and simulation results. Across seven current agents on the full benchmark, the strongest agent achieves 17.5\% success, compared with an 87.0\% expert reference pass. We find that weaker agents often fail before producing a valid artifact, whereas stronger agents increasingly fail on structural, geometric, and construction-process requirements. CADWorld therefore exposes a gap between general GUI competence and reliable execution of persistent, verifiable engineering workflows. Project accessible at https://cad-world.github.io.

AI.tldr: Introduces CADWorld, a benchmark for testing long-horizon computer-use agents in FreeCAD for mechanical CAD workflows, showing a large gap between current agents and human experts.
AI.motivation: Existing desktop agent benchmarks poorly cover professional engineering workflows that require creating persistent, structured artifacts, especially in demanding mechanical CAD settings. There is a need to systematically evaluate whether agents can reliably perform complex, verifiable engineering tasks rather than just basic GUI operations.
AI.method: They build CADWorld, a FreeCAD-based benchmark of 200 tasks across 11 mechanical CAD workflow categories (sketching, modeling, assembly, CAM, FEM, etc.). Agents interact only via screenshots and GUI actions, and success is scored automatically using executable checks over the produced CAD artifacts and auxiliary outputs, validating geometry, parametric structure, constraints, manufacturing state, and simulation outcomes. They then evaluate seven existing agents on the full benchmark and compare their performance to an expert human reference.
AI.result: On CADWorld, the best current agent achieves only 17.5% success versus an 87.0% pass rate by expert users. Weaker agents mostly fail before producing valid CAD artifacts, while stronger agents more often produce artifacts that nonetheless violate structural, geometric, or construction-process requirements.
AI.conclusion: CADWorld reveals that current GUI agents, even the strongest ones, fall far short of reliably executing persistent, verifiable mechanical CAD workflows. The benchmark thus highlights a significant gap between general GUI interaction competence and the ability to complete complex, long-horizon engineering design and analysis tasks, providing a challenging testbed for future research on capable CAD agents.

title: Crash Narrative-Guided Countermeasure Recommendation Using Large Language Models: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Intersection Safety
summary: Improving safety at intersections requires identifying crash mechanisms and recommending appropriate countermeasures. However, this process traditionally relies on expert judgment, making it labor-intensive, difficult to scale, and dependent on the availability of experienced traffic safety engineers. Although crash narratives contain rich description of crash mechanisms, this unstructured information remains largely underutilized in safety analyses. This study presents a crash narrative-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that translates narrative-derived crash mechanisms into site-specific countermeasure recommendations. Key mechanism attributes including traffic control, signal indication, driver fault, vehicle movement, and travel direction were extracted from crash narratives and linked to evidence-based treatments from the FHWA Proven Safety Countermeasures and the CMF Clearinghouse. The framework integrates embedding-based retrieval of historically similar intersections, association-rule mining, statistical guidance on the expected number of relevant countermeasures, and an engineering reasoning guidance that directs LLM through a domain-consistent decision process before selecting countermeasures. Evaluated on 312 fatal and serious-injury crashes across 115 intersections in Lake and Sumter Counties, Florida, using five-fold cross-validation, the framework achieved a precision of 0.82, recall of 0.85, and F1-score of 0.82, while recommending an average of 3.91 countermeasures per location with 3.14 matching, closely matching the actual average (3.86). Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of retrieval-augmented LLMs as an interpretable and scalable decision-support tool for transportation agencies for translating crash narratives into countermeasure recommendations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that uses crash narratives to automatically recommend intersection safety countermeasures, achieving high precision and recall and showing promise as a scalable decision-support tool for agencies.
AI.motivation: Traditional intersection safety diagnosis and countermeasure selection depend heavily on expert judgment, which is labor-intensive, hard to scale, and constrained by the availability and consistency of experienced engineers. Meanwhile, crash narratives contain detailed descriptions of crash mechanisms but are unstructured and underused in quantitative safety analysis and decision support. There is a need for an interpretable, data-driven way to systematically convert narrative crash descriptions into site-specific, evidence-based countermeasure recommendations.
AI.method: The study builds a crash narrative-guided RAG framework around large language models. First, it extracts key crash mechanism attributes from narratives—including traffic control type, signal indications, driver fault, vehicle movement, and travel direction. These attributes are then linked to evidence-based safety treatments from FHWA’s Proven Safety Countermeasures and the CMF Clearinghouse. The framework combines: (1) embedding-based retrieval of historically similar intersections, (2) association-rule mining to discover common patterns between crash mechanisms and treatments, (3) statistical guidance on the expected number of relevant countermeasures, and (4) an engineered reasoning protocol that constrains the LLM to follow a domain-consistent decision process before recommending countermeasures.
AI.result: Using 312 fatal and serious-injury crashes at 115 intersections in two Florida counties and five-fold cross-validation, the framework reached a precision of 0.82, recall of 0.85, and F1-score of 0.82 in recommending countermeasures. On average, it suggested 3.91 treatments per location, of which 3.14 matched actual implemented countermeasures, very close to the observed average of 3.86 implemented measures per site.
AI.conclusion: The proposed crash narrative-guided RAG framework can effectively and credibly translate unstructured crash narratives into targeted, evidence-based countermeasure recommendations. Its strong performance and interpretable, structured reasoning show that retrieval-augmented LLMs can function as scalable, practical decision-support tools for transportation agencies, potentially reducing reliance on manual expert-only processes for intersection safety diagnosis and treatment selection.
