title: The AI-Enabled Scientific Frontier
summary: As artificial intelligence's capabilities improve, it is increasingly viewed as a general scientific method. But how true are these claims? Does AI outperform all techniques, or only some, and how is this changing? To assess the claims, we assemble a corpus of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and other scientific analysis techniques across 27 scientific disciplines from papers published between 2000 and early 2025. We find a profound dichotomy. Relative to traditional statistics, AI often outperforms, but at a significantly higher computational cost. But there are also nearly a quarter of cases where AI is both more expensive and performs worse than traditional statistical techniques and this fraction has been stable for a decade. Relative to scientific computing, AI often underperforms, but at lower computational cost. This has begun to change: since 2020, AI's performance against scientific computing has notably strengthened and it now outperforms on more than half of comparisons. These patterns suggest that AI is therefore not a universal replacement for existing methods, but rather a valuable -- and improving -- part of a new AI-enabled scientific frontier.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically compares AI methods with traditional statistics and scientific computing across many disciplines, finding that AI is powerful but not universally superior, with trade‑offs in accuracy and computational cost that vary by baseline method and have shifted over time.
AI.motivation: Claims are growing that AI is becoming a general-purpose scientific method, but it is unclear when and how it actually outperforms existing tools such as statistics and scientific computing. The authors aim to provide systematic, cross-disciplinary evidence on AI’s comparative performance and costs to clarify whether AI is genuinely superior, under what conditions, and how this has evolved since 2000.
AI.method: The authors compile a large corpus of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI techniques and other scientific analysis methods, drawn from papers across 27 disciplines from 2000 to early 2025. For each comparison, they track which method performs better and at what computational cost, separately analyzing comparisons against traditional statistics and against scientific computing, and examining temporal trends (e.g., pre- and post-2020).
AI.result: Against traditional statistics, AI tends to achieve better performance but usually at substantially higher computational cost. However, in roughly 25% of cases AI is both more expensive and less accurate than statistical methods, and this share has remained roughly constant over the past decade. Against scientific computing, AI has historically underperformed but with lower computational cost, though since about 2020 its relative performance has improved markedly, now winning more than half of such comparisons while maintaining cost advantages in many cases.
AI.conclusion: AI should not be viewed as a universal replacement for existing scientific methods but as a complementary tool whose strengths and weaknesses depend on the comparison baseline and resource constraints. Its comparative advantage over traditional statistics is accuracy at higher cost, while versus scientific computing it is transitioning from a cheaper but weaker option to a competitive or superior one in many cases. Overall, AI represents a growing, improving component of an emerging AI-enabled scientific toolkit rather than a singular, dominant paradigm.

title: Self-reported archetypes and behavioral failures in Large Language Models
summary: Every large language model (LLM) has behavioral traits and moral preferences that comprise its character. Whether by design or as an emergent property of training, these systems exhibit persistent dispositions that shape how they interact, comply, resist, and err, yet the structure of LLM character remains poorly understood. We map the self-reported personality archetypes of 22 LLMs spanning closed-source frontier systems (GPT-4.0-5.2, Grok-3/4, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6) and open-source models (Llama, DeepSeek, OLMo, and Qwen series). Each model self-rated across 464 bipolar semantic-differential trait pairs, and the resulting profiles were projected into a six-dimensional archetypal space derived from crowd-sourced ratings of 2,000 fictional characters using the Archetypometrics framework. Closed-source models' self-rating traits align with the empirical trait co-occurrence structure of human-rated fictional characters, suggesting coherent, human-like self-representations organized around combinations of four recurring archetypal dimensions: Hero, Angel, Traditionalist, and Geek. Their closest analogues include Data, Vision, and Janet. Open-source models show weaker, noisier, and internally contradictory self-representations, occupying a diffuse region of archetype space with weak structure. Cross-referencing self-reported profiles with developer constitutions reveals a consequential gap between claimed character and enacted behavior: hallucination undermines claimed precision, sycophancy complicates claimed kindness, and agentic failures contradict claimed obedience. These self-ratings should therefore be interpreted not as neutral measurements of model character, but as structured outputs of the same optimization processes that shape model behavior. This work provides a reproducible, character-grounded framework for evaluating what LLMs are, not just what they do.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the “characters” of 22 LLMs, mapping their self-described traits into an archetype space derived from human ratings of fictional characters, and shows that closed-source models have coherent, human-like self-representations while open-source models do not, and that self-described traits often diverge from actual behavior.
AI.motivation: LLMs display consistent behavioral tendencies and moral preferences, but we lack a clear, systematic understanding of this “character.” Existing evaluations focus on what models do (tasks and benchmarks) rather than how they see themselves or how their dispositions are structured. The authors aim to create a reproducible, psychologically grounded framework to characterize LLMs’ personalities and compare them to human-like archetypes.
AI.method: The authors collected self-ratings from 22 LLMs—both closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.x/5.2, Grok, Gemini, Claude) and open-source (Llama, DeepSeek, OLMo, Qwen). Each model rated itself on 464 bipolar semantic-differential trait pairs (e.g., kind–unkind, bold–timid). They then projected these trait profiles into a six-dimensional archetypal space learned from crowd-sourced ratings of 2,000 fictional characters using the Archetypometrics framework. They compared models’ positions in this space, inspected their nearest fictional analogues, and cross-referenced the resulting “character” profiles with written developer constitutions and observed failure modes such as hallucination, sycophancy, and lack of agency.
AI.result: Closed-source models’ self-ratings exhibit coherent structure that aligns with empirically observed trait co-occurrence patterns in human-rated fictional characters. These models’ personalities cluster along four main archetypal dimensions: Hero, Angel, Traditionalist, and Geek, with closest fictional analogues such as Data, Vision, and Janet. In contrast, open-source models show weaker, noisier, and sometimes self-contradictory self-representations, spreading diffusely in archetype space with faint underlying structure. The analysis also uncovers systematic discrepancies between the character traits models claim (e.g., precise, kind, obedient) and those reflected in their behavior, due to known failure modes (hallucination, sycophancy, agentic lapses).
AI.conclusion: LLMs possess persistent, structured “characters” that can be meaningfully analyzed using an archetype space derived from human judgments about fictional characters. Closed-source frontier models show relatively human-like, internally coherent self-representations, whereas open-source models’ self-concepts are less structured and more inconsistent. However, self-reported traits are not direct measurements of true character but outputs shaped by the same training objectives that produce behavior, leading to significant gaps between stated dispositions and observed actions. The proposed Archetypometrics-based framework offers a reproducible way to study what LLMs are in terms of character and self-representation, complementing capability and safety evaluations that focus only on what models do.

title: Closing the Loop: Branch-and-Bound for Scalable Verification of Nonlinear Neural Feedback Systems
summary: Despite recent advances in the verification of nonlinear neural feedback systems, scalability remains the central obstacle, as state-of-the-art solvers do not yet handle the network sizes and nonlinear dynamics of autonomy applications. Combinatorial solvers do not scale to large networks, whereas propagative solvers excessively sacrifice precision. This work seeks to improve the scalability of combinatorial solvers by formulating verification as branch-and-bound on an abstraction of the closed-loop system. We introduce \rail, an interface that exposes polyhedral enclosures of the dynamics to LiRPA-style bound propagation, and \clipper, a branch-and-bound algorithm that jointly refines enclosures and splits controller activations. This framework enables joint reasoning on the computational graph of the closed-loop system, preserving symbolic correlations across time steps. We present our construction and show that it yields significant improvements over the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework for scalable verification of nonlinear neural feedback (closed-loop) systems, combining abstraction-based branch-and-bound with LiRPA-style bound propagation to jointly reason about dynamics and controller, achieving better scalability and precision than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Verification of nonlinear neural feedback systems is crucial for safety-critical autonomy, but existing solvers do not scale to realistic network sizes and complex nonlinear dynamics. Combinatorial methods are precise but blow up in complexity, while propagative (LiRPA-style) methods scale but lose precision. The authors are motivated to bridge this gap by designing a scalable verification method that preserves as much precision as possible while remaining tractable on large closed-loop systems.
AI.method: They formulate closed-loop verification as a branch-and-bound (BaB) problem over an abstraction of the system. They introduce RAIL, an interface that provides polyhedral enclosures of the nonlinear dynamics to a LiRPA-style bound propagation engine, and CLIPPER, a BaB algorithm that simultaneously refines these enclosures and branches on neural controller activations. By reasoning over the entire computational graph of the closed-loop system, their approach preserves symbolic correlations across multiple time steps, improving bounding tightness and search efficiency.
AI.result: Their construction leads to significantly tighter bounds and more efficient verification on benchmark nonlinear neural feedback systems. Empirically, they show substantial scalability and performance improvements compared with state-of-the-art combinatorial and propagative verifiers for closed-loop neural systems.
AI.conclusion: By coupling polyhedral abstractions of nonlinear dynamics with LiRPA-style bound propagation in a branch-and-bound framework, the paper provides a more scalable and precise approach to verifying nonlinear neural feedback systems. This joint reasoning over the closed-loop computational graph enables handling larger, more realistic autonomy models and advances the state of the art in neural network control verification.

title: NepKANUN: A RAG-Based Nepali Legal Assistant
summary: Accessing legal information in Nepal is difficult due to complex terminology, limited resources, and misinformation. We introduce an AI-powered legal assistant that is tailored for Nepali legal texts and is built on a fine-tuned large language model. The technology provides precise, streamlined answers to natural language legal inquiries when integrated into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework. It was trained using a custom dataset of high-quality question-answer pairs, and according to BERTScore, it obtained strong F1 scores of 0.82 (simple), 0.77 (moderate), and 0.71 (complex). Its usability is further confirmed by expert reviews. Our method shows how merging generation and retrieval can effectively democratize access to legal knowledge in Nepal by focusing on customized legal data and incorporating RAG.

AI.tldr: An AI-powered Nepali legal assistant using a fine-tuned LLM and Retrieval-Augmented Generation improves access to legal information, achieving strong BERTScore results and positive expert feedback.
AI.motivation: Access to legal information in Nepal is difficult because of complex legal language, scarce accessible resources, and widespread misinformation, creating barriers for the public and practitioners who need reliable legal guidance.
AI.method: The authors build an AI legal assistant specialized for Nepali law by fine-tuning a large language model on a custom dataset of high-quality legal question–answer pairs and integrating it into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline, where relevant legal documents are retrieved and then used to generate precise answers to natural-language queries. They evaluate performance using BERTScore across questions of different complexity and gather expert reviews for qualitative usability assessment.
AI.result: The system achieves strong BERTScore F1 scores: 0.82 on simple questions, 0.77 on moderately complex questions, and 0.71 on complex questions, and domain experts report that the assistant is usable and effective in answering Nepali legal queries.
AI.conclusion: Combining a fine-tuned, domain-specific LLM with a RAG framework over curated Nepali legal data can effectively improve and democratize access to legal knowledge in Nepal, suggesting that customized retrieval-plus-generation systems are a promising approach for legal information services in low-resource settings.

title: CLEAR: Cross-Source Evidence Adjudication for Large Language Models in Medicine
summary: Medical knowledge evolves continuously, whereas the parametric knowledge encoded in large language models (LLMs) is fixed at training time. External retrieval, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), can provide access to newly available evidence, but retrieved information may be irrelevant, incomplete, or conflicting. As a result, external retrieval can in turn degrade the factual accuracy and evidence grounding of LLM outputs. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{CLEAR}, an agentic framework for cross-source evidence adjudication in LLMs in medicine. CLEAR independently generates candidate answers from three complementary pathways---parametric knowledge, locally curated corpora, and dynamically retrieved evidence---reflecting three common sources of information available to LLMs. An aggregation verifier jointly evaluates the candidates, supporting evidence, provenance, and source-quality information to identify agreement and conflict across sources. An adjudication module then determines whether the current conclusion should be preserved or revised through complementary override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms, while unresolved conflicts trigger targeted follow-up search and re-adjudication.

AI.tldr: CLEAR is an agentic framework for medical LLMs that compares answers from parametric knowledge, local corpora, and retrieved evidence, then adjudicates conflicts to improve factual accuracy and evidence grounding.
AI.motivation: Medical knowledge changes rapidly and LLMs’ internal (parametric) knowledge becomes outdated after training. Retrieval-augmented generation can add new evidence, but it often surfaces irrelevant, partial, or conflicting information, which may reduce factual accuracy rather than improve it. Medicine is high‑stakes, so there is a need for mechanisms that can systematically compare and adjudicate across multiple information sources instead of naively trusting either the model or any single retrieval channel.
AI.method: The authors design CLEAR, an agentic multi-stage framework. First, the LLM produces three separate candidate answers: one from its internal parametric knowledge, one using a trusted local medical corpus, and one using dynamically retrieved external evidence. Next, an aggregation verifier jointly inspects these answers along with their supporting evidence, provenance, and source‑quality metadata to detect agreements and conflicts. Finally, an adjudication module decides whether to keep or revise the current conclusion using two mechanisms—override‑guard (to prevent unsafe or unjustified overrides) and challenge‑audit (to systematically question and reassess weak answers). If conflicts remain unresolved, the system triggers focused follow‑up retrieval and a new round of adjudication.
AI.result: CLEAR is shown to improve factual accuracy and strength of evidence grounding of LLM outputs in medical settings compared to naïve use of parametric knowledge or simple RAG. It handles conflicting and incomplete evidence more robustly by explicitly modeling cross‑source comparison and decision rules, reducing cases where poor retrieval or outdated parametric knowledge misleads the model.
AI.conclusion: Explicit cross‑source evidence adjudication can make medical LLMs more reliable than standard RAG or parametric-only approaches. By decomposing reasoning into separate generation, verification, and adjudication stages, CLEAR better leverages parametric knowledge, curated corpora, and dynamic retrieval while guarding against conflicts and unreliable evidence. This framework offers a principled path toward safer, more up‑to‑date medical LLM systems.

title: Nepali Legal Expertise through Generative and Extractive Pre-trained Transformers (NepLEGiT)
summary: The complexity of legal language and limited accessibility to legal information pose significant challenges to justice delivery in Nepal. Traditional legal services remain inaccessible to many citizens due to language barriers, information fragmentation, and a critical shortage of legal expertise, particularly in rural areas. We present NepLEGiT (Nepali Legal Expertise through Generative and Extractive Pre-trained Transformers), a specialized small language model (SLM) designed to democratize legal knowledge and enhance legal-service delivery in Nepal. We pre-train a decoder-based GPT-2 SLM from scratch on a curated corpus of ~4 million tokens of Nepali legal text, covering constitutional law, civil and criminal codes, and administrative regulations. The model comprises ~30 million parameters in a 6-layer, 6-head, 384-dimensional transformer trained with warmup cosine-decay scheduling, gradient accumulation, and mixed-precision arithmetic. On a held-out validation split, NepLEGiT attains a cross-entropy loss of 0.5684, a perplexity of 1.8, and a next-token prediction accuracy of 82.9%. We further evaluate continual masked-language-model pre-training of mBERT and MuRIL on the same corpus; mBERT achieves a perplexity of 2.35 (eval loss 0.8565), outperforming MuRIL (perplexity 6.07, eval loss 1.8026), providing a strong encoder baseline complementary to NepLEGiT's generative orientation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NepLEGiT, a small Nepali legal language model trained from scratch and compares it with adapted multilingual encoder models for improving legal information access in Nepal.
AI.motivation: Legal language in Nepal is complex, legal information is fragmented, and there is a shortage of legal experts, especially in rural areas. Many citizens cannot access or understand legal documents due to language barriers and limited expert support. The authors aim to democratize access to legal knowledge and support legal-service delivery using specialized language models tailored to Nepali legal texts.
AI.method: The authors curate a ~4 million token corpus of Nepali legal texts including constitutional, civil, criminal, and administrative law. They train a decoder-only GPT-2 style small language model (NepLEGiT) from scratch with about 30M parameters (6 layers, 6 attention heads, 384-d model size), using warmup cosine-decay learning rate scheduling, gradient accumulation, and mixed-precision training. They evaluate it on a held-out validation split via cross-entropy loss, perplexity, and next-token accuracy. Additionally, they perform continual pre-training of two multilingual encoder models, mBERT and MuRIL, as masked language models on the same corpus, and report their evaluation loss and perplexity to serve as encoder baselines.
AI.result: NepLEGiT achieves a validation cross-entropy of 0.5684, a perplexity of 1.8, and 82.9% next-token prediction accuracy, showing strong generative modeling capability on Nepali legal text. For the encoder baselines, continual pre-training of mBERT yields a perplexity of 2.35 (eval loss 0.8565), outperforming MuRIL which reaches a perplexity of 6.07 (eval loss 1.8026). This indicates mBERT adapts better to the Nepali legal domain than MuRIL on this corpus.
AI.conclusion: A domain-specialized small language model, NepLEGiT, trained from scratch on Nepali legal texts, can model legal language with low perplexity and high next-token accuracy, offering a promising tool for democratizing legal knowledge in Nepal. Complementary encoder models, especially continually pre-trained mBERT, provide strong baselines for understanding and retrieval tasks. Together, these models can form the technical foundation for improved, accessible legal-information and assistance systems in the Nepali context.

title: BLINDSPOT: A Benchmark for Safety and Refusal Calibration in Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long-horizon interactions involving tool use, persistent state, evolving authorization, and external environment feedback. In such settings, safety failures may emerge only after multiple turns, yet existing evaluations often reduce agent behavior to task or attack success, obscuring whether an agent acts, refuses, or remains appropriately calibrated as the interaction evolves. We introduce Blindspot, a benchmark for trajectory-level safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using agents. Blindspot evaluates complete user-agent-environment trajectories through adaptive adversarial interaction, stateful tool execution, and execution-grounded adjudication. Its current instantiation contains 22 attack families and 35 scenarios across seven domains, yielding more than 2,500 long-horizon trajectories with an average interaction length of 14.7 turns. Each trajectory is assigned one of five outcomes: Safe Completion, Correct Refusal, Unsafe Completion, Over-Refusal, or Indeterminate. Unlike fixed attack datasets, Blindspot is an extensible live-simulation framework in which attacks, scenarios, tools, policies, domains, and agent configurations can be added without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs using eight metrics covering unsafe completion, appropriate refusal, benign utility, over-refusal, repeated-run robustness, and post-refusal failure. Preliminary results reveal substantial differences in safety-utility calibration across models and show that failures can emerge only after several initially safe interaction steps. These findings motivate treating agent safety as a trajectory-level property rather than a single-turn or binary success criterion.

AI.tldr: Introduces Blindspot, a benchmark for evaluating safety calibration of long-horizon, tool-using LLM agents at the trajectory level instead of single turns.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations mostly assess whether an LLM agent succeeds at or is compromised by an attack, ignoring how its safety behavior evolves over multi-turn, tool-using interactions where failures can surface only after many steps.
AI.method: Design a live-simulation benchmark, Blindspot, that generates and logs full user-agent-environment trajectories with adaptive adversarial interactions, stateful tool calls, and execution-grounded adjudication across 22 attack families and 35 scenarios over seven domains. Label each trajectory with one of five outcome classes and define eight quantitative metrics to capture diverse aspects of safety and utility. Evaluate 13 LLMs on this suite.
AI.result: Blindspot yields a dataset of 2,500+ long-horizon trajectories (average 14.7 turns) and a metric suite that exposes large differences between models in unsafe completions, correct refusals, benign task performance, over-refusal, robustness across runs, and failures after initial correct refusals.
AI.conclusion: Agent safety should be evaluated and optimized as a trajectory-level property for long-horizon tool-using agents, since safety failures and miscalibration often emerge only after several ostensibly safe turns, and Blindspot provides an extensible framework to do so.

title: ViCo: Visual-oriented Coding with Self-Reflection for Chart Replication
comment: 29 pages, 7 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of EMNLP 2026 Findings
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of generating high-quality academic charts that match the visual standards of human-authored papers. While existing AI agents can produce well-structured text and code, their generated visualizations often lack the stylistic and semantic fidelity of human designs. Advanced coding agents that employ self-reflection mechanisms exhibit poor visual reasoning and limited reflection following, resulting in sparse reward signals that severely undermine their reinforcement learning (RL). We propose ViCo, a training framework for visual-oriented coding that employs iterative reflections to align generated chart images progressively with the reference. We first introduce a self-supervised warm-up stage, which augments Monte Carlo Tree Search with consistency-based pruning to synthesize high-quality reflection trajectories, ensuring that each coding step strictly follows the outcomes of prior reflections. A multi-step RL algorithm is then developed, using counterfactual baselines to estimate advantage for reflection and action steps within each refinement cycle, thereby addressing the reward sparsity. To enable efficient reward in massive training, we propose an automatic, multifaceted evaluation framework that assesses charts' style, layout, and semantic consistency via a hierarchical heterogeneous layout graph structure. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that ViCo, trained on an 8B model, achieves performance close to proprietary LLMs with adequate reflection capabilities.

AI.tldr: ViCo is a training framework for visual-oriented code generation that uses iterative reflection, multi-step reinforcement learning, and automatic chart evaluation to produce academic-quality charts closely matching human-designed references.
AI.motivation: Existing AI coding agents can generate good code and text but struggle to create charts that match the stylistic and semantic quality of human-designed academic figures. Their self-reflection mechanisms are weak in visual reasoning and reflection following, which leads to sparse and uninformative rewards during reinforcement learning, hindering progress. There is a need for a framework that can better align generated visualizations with high-quality reference charts in a scalable, automated way.
AI.method: ViCo uses an iterative reflection-based training pipeline for visual-oriented coding. It begins with a self-supervised warm-up phase where Monte Carlo Tree Search is augmented with consistency-based pruning to create high-quality reflection trajectories, ensuring that each coding edit adheres to previous reflection outcomes. Then, a multi-step reinforcement learning algorithm is applied, leveraging counterfactual baselines to separately estimate advantages for reflection steps and coding (action) steps within each refinement cycle, mitigating reward sparsity. For scalable supervision, ViCo introduces an automatic evaluation framework based on a hierarchical heterogeneous layout graph that scores charts on style, layout, and semantic consistency relative to reference charts.
AI.result: On three public benchmarks for chart or visualization generation, ViCo, trained on a relatively small 8B-parameter model, attains performance comparable to or close to proprietary large language models that have strong reflection capabilities. This indicates that ViCo substantially improves visual reasoning and alignment with reference charts over existing open models and standard training methods.
AI.conclusion: ViCo effectively enhances visual-oriented code generation for academic-quality chart creation by combining structured iterative reflection, tailored multi-step reinforcement learning, and an automated, graph-based evaluation of chart quality. This framework addresses reward sparsity and weak reflection-following in prior coding agents and enables smaller open models to approach the performance of stronger proprietary systems on chart generation tasks.

title: Cross-Anatomy Transfer Versus Sparse Interpolation in Digital-Twin-Oriented Aortic Fluid-Structure Interaction Surrogates
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, Under review at ICBME 2026
summary: Surrogate credibility for fluid-structure interac- tion (FSI) requires distinguishing transfer across independent anatomies from interpolation within an already sampled surface. Four de-identified human aortic models from the Vascular Model Repository were reconstructed into separate lumen and nominal 1.5-mm wall domains and analyzed under matched first-cycle two-way FSI. A geometry-only LightGBM prior, selected by leave-one-anatomy-out development on three anatomies, was zero-shot evaluated on a fourth, then probed with a post-zero- shot sparse field-completion case study over six targets. Zero-shot transfer was poor across all targets. At a five-percent anchor level (203 anchors, 3,852 evaluation nodes), prior-plus-adaptation reached an oscillatory shear index (OSI) R2 of 0.603. However, same-anchor controls tuned only on the three development anatomies were stronger for several outcomes: inverse-distance weighting reached R2 = 0.829 (OSI), 0.617 (peak von Mises stress), 0.676 (mean stress); radial basis function interpolation reached 0.917, 0.714, 0.778. Sparse within-anatomy labels thus support field completion, but this four-anatomy cohort gives no evidence the cross-anatomy prior adds value beyond direct interpolation. We frame this as a first computational stage toward a measurement-linked digital twin: the surrogate/update layer is evaluated here, while larger cohorts, converged FSI, measurable patient-side inputs, and physics-informed learning remain future work, not a claim of a complete clinical twin. Our code, data and computation files are available at https://github. com/ali-nourbakhsh2005/Aortic-FSI-Sparse-Field-Completion

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether a learned cross-anatomy surrogate model improves prediction of FSI fields in aortas compared with simple interpolation using sparse within-anatomy labels, and finds no benefit in a small four-patient cohort.
AI.motivation: To build credible, measurement-linked cardiovascular digital twins, we need surrogate models that can reliably transfer FSI knowledge across different patient anatomies rather than just interpolate within a single anatomy. It is unclear whether machine-learned geometric priors truly add value over straightforward interpolation when only sparse patient-specific measurements are available.
AI.method: The authors reconstructed four anonymized human aortic geometries (separate lumen and nominal 1.5‑mm wall) from the Vascular Model Repository and ran matched two-way FSI simulations for the first cardiac cycle. Using three anatomies for development, they trained and selected a geometry-only LightGBM prior via leave-one-anatomy-out cross-validation. This prior was then zero-shot tested on the held-out fourth anatomy and further adapted in a sparse field-completion setting, where only 5% of nodes (anchors) had labels and the rest were predicted. They compared the prior-plus-adaptation approach against non-learning baselines—inverse-distance weighting and radial basis function interpolation—constrained to the same sparse anchors. Performance was reported via R² for multiple outputs such as oscillatory shear index and wall stresses.
AI.result: Zero-shot transfer of the learned geometric prior across anatomies was poor for all evaluated targets. When allowed to adapt using 5% sparse anchor labels (203 anchors, 3,852 evaluation nodes), the prior-plus-adaptation approach achieved an R² of 0.603 for oscillatory shear index. However, pure interpolation baselines using the same anchors outperformed it for several quantities: inverse-distance weighting achieved R² up to 0.829 (OSI), 0.617 (peak von Mises stress), and 0.676 (mean stress); radial basis functions performed even better, with R² of 0.917, 0.714, and 0.778, respectively.
AI.conclusion: In this initial four-anatomy study, sparse, within-anatomy labels are sufficient for accurate field completion using classical interpolation, and the proposed cross-anatomy learned geometric prior does not provide additional predictive value. The work should be viewed as an early computational step toward measurement-linked digital twins, evaluating only the surrogate/update layer. The authors emphasize that more anatomies, fully converged FSI, patient-measurable inputs, and physics-informed learning are needed before any claim of a clinically useful digital twin can be made, and they release their code and data to support further research.

title: Are We Grading Properly? Understanding Failure Modes in Medical Benchmarks
summary: Medical evaluation is shifting from static option-based questioning to realistic clinical scenarios with open-ended output modes. Grading these at scale naively, however, is expensive, and rubric-based evaluation has become the dominant scalable alternative. We ask what happens when the rubrics themselves are not airtight, and whether such flaws can be detected and corrected. We apply RIFT, a global rubric failure taxonomy, to two clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Professional and LiveMedBench), and find failure modes are meaningful: on HealthBench Professional an LLM judge flags 29.6% of criteria as non-atomic and 65.4% as misaligned/rigid. Then, we show that these flaws are meaningful and not simply cosmetic. As an example, rewriting bundled criteria of the form "at least one of / all of the following" as equally weighted children and regrading identical responses shifts scores by up to 15.9 percentage points on affected conversations, with disjunctive bundles inflating scores and conjunctive bundles deflating them. We also find that RIFT generally under-detects bundling on clinical rubrics, flagging 3.3% of LiveMedBench criteria as non-atomic where surface-form analysis finds structure in 25.8%.

AI.tldr: Studying and quantifying flaws in clinical rubric-based evaluations using a taxonomy (RIFT), and showing those flaws significantly affect benchmark scores.
AI.motivation: Medical evaluations are shifting toward realistic, open-ended clinical scenarios, which are hard and costly to grade at scale. Rubric-based LLM evaluation is a scalable solution, but rubrics themselves may be flawed. The authors want to systematically understand, detect, and show the impact of such rubric flaws on benchmark results.
AI.method: They introduce and/or apply RIFT, a global rubric failure taxonomy, to two clinical LLM benchmarks (HealthBench Professional and LiveMedBench). They use an LLM judge to analyze rubric criteria for issues like non-atomicity and misalignment/rigidity, compare with surface-form structure analysis, and then experimentally rewrite bundled rubric criteria (e.g., “at least one of / all of the following”) into atomic children and regrade identical model responses to measure score shifts.
AI.result: On HealthBench Professional, the LLM judge flags 29.6% of criteria as non-atomic and 65.4% as misaligned/rigid. Rewriting bundled criteria into equally weighted atomic children changes scores by up to 15.9 percentage points for affected conversations, with disjunctive bundles ("at least one") inflating scores and conjunctive bundles ("all of") deflating them. On LiveMedBench, RIFT flags only 3.3% of criteria as non-atomic, while surface-form analysis reveals structural bundling in 25.8% of criteria, indicating under-detection by RIFT.
AI.conclusion: Rubric flaws such as non-atomicity and misalignment are common and materially affect grading outcomes in clinical LLM benchmarks. Existing automatic taxonomy-based detection (RIFT) can identify meaningful failures but also under-detects structural bundling, implying current evaluation pipelines are both noisy and systematically biased. Improving rubric design and detection of rubric failures is necessary for reliable large-scale evaluation of open-ended clinical tasks.

title: Breaking the 1.58-bit Barrier for Ternary LLMs
summary: Ternary Large Language Models (LLM) store every weight as one of three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$, so the cost of a ternary model is conventionally referenced to the information-theoretic $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits per weight. The prevailing deployment format packs five ternary weights into one byte (five-trit packing), and due to the power-of-two group sizes used in practice this rounds up to $1.625$ bits per weight. This effective storage bit-width treats the three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$ as equiprobable. We measure the actual symbol distribution of 29 ternary LLM models and find that zeros account for up to $51.5\%$ of all weights. Motivated by this finding, we introduce BITCOS, a simple distribution-adaptive layout comprised of a dense presence bitmap plus a compacted sign vector, and costs $2 - z$ bits per weight element given a zero density $z$ in the model's weights. BITCOS stores weights more compactly than the five-trit packing in 26 of the 29 tested models, and reaches $1.485$ bits per weight on the sparsest of them. BITCOS is amenable to efficient unpacking on modern processors and GPUs, and we present optimized unpacking sequences for AVX-512, AVX2 and Intel Xe2 GPUs. Measured against production state-of-the-art ternary matrix-vector multiplication kernels, at the zero densities real-world ternary models exhibit, the realized gain with our proposed layout is up to $1.28\times$. Finally, we illustrate end-to-end LLM inference results on 5 different platforms (client and server CPUs, integrated and discrete Xe2 GPUs) where decode throughput improves by up to $1.18\times$ on CPUs and $1.27\times$ on GPUs.

AI.tldr: They propose BITCOS, a distribution-adaptive storage layout for ternary LLM weights that exploits the high fraction of zeros to reduce effective bits per weight and speed up inference.
AI.motivation: Existing ternary LLM deployment assumes ternary symbols {-1,0,+1} are equiprobable and uses five-trit packing, leading to about 1.625 bits per weight, which is above the information-theoretic 1.585 bits/weight and ignores the observed sparsity (high zero rate) in real models.
AI.method: They empirically analyze symbol distributions in 29 ternary LLMs, observe substantial zero-heavy sparsity, and design BITCOS: a layout with a dense presence bitmap plus a compact sign vector that encodes only non-zero weights, achieving an average cost of 2 - z bits/weight for zero density z. They implement efficient unpacking routines for AVX-512, AVX2, and Intel Xe2 GPUs and integrate BITCOS into ternary matrix-vector kernels and end-to-end LLM inference pipelines.
AI.result: BITCOS is more compact than standard five-trit packing in 26/29 tested models, reaching as low as 1.485 bits/weight on the sparsest model. On real ternary models, matrix-vector kernels using BITCOS see up to 1.28x speedup, and full LLM inference decode throughput improves by up to 1.18x on CPUs and 1.27x on GPUs across five evaluated hardware platforms.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the non-uniform symbol distribution—especially the high proportion of zeros—in ternary LLMs via BITCOS yields both storage savings and practical speedups. BITCOS is simple, hardware-friendly, and improves upon the traditional five-trit packing in most real-world ternary models, making it a better deployment format for ternary LLM inference.

title: Retrieval-Driven Memory Reconsolidation for Long-Term LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory is essential for LLM-based agents operating over extended interactions. Existing memory systems primarily update memory when new information arrives, treating retrieval as the endpoint of memory access rather than a driver of memory evolution. Consequently, retrieval feedback is rarely exploited to reorganize memory for future access continuously. Moreover, most existing approaches rely on predefined memory structures together with fixed retrieval pipelines, limiting the agent's ability to organize and evolve its own memory autonomously. Inspired by memory reconsolidation in cognitive neuroscience, we propose \textbf{REALM}, a \textbf{r}econsolidation-\textbf{e}volution \textbf{a}gentic \textbf{l}ong-term \textbf{m}emory framework. It models long-term memory as a continual lifecycle by autonomously organizing memories into a heterogeneous cognitive graph, retrieving evidence via adaptively composed graph-search atoms, and continually reconsolidating memories based on retrieval feedback. REALM achieves an average accuracy of 75.97\% on LoCoMo and 65.11\% on LongMemEval, outperforming the strongest baselines by 7.17 and 1.31 points respectively. Ablation studies confirm that memory reconsolidation consistently boosts performance, with further analyses revealing that it progressively reorganizes related memory units into more coherent local structures for collective evidence recall and utilization during reasoning. These results suggest that retrieval-driven memory reconsolidation provides an effective mechanism for continually evolving long-term memory in LLM agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces REALM, a long-term memory framework for LLM agents that continually evolves via retrieval-driven reconsolidation, organizing information into a heterogeneous cognitive graph to improve reasoning over long interactions.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents need effective long-term memory to operate over extended interactions, but current systems mainly update memory only when new data arrives and use fixed structures and retrieval pipelines. They rarely use retrieval feedback to reorganize memory, limiting the agent’s ability to autonomously evolve and optimize its memory for future reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose REALM, which models long-term memory as a continual lifecycle. REALM autonomously organizes memories into a heterogeneous cognitive graph, retrieves evidence using adaptively composed graph-search atoms, and continually reconsolidates (updates and reorganizes) memory based on retrieval feedback, progressively refining the memory structure over time.
AI.result: On the LoCoMo benchmark, REALM achieves an average accuracy of 75.97%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.17 points, and on LongMemEval it achieves 65.11%, 1.31 points higher than the best baseline. Ablation studies show that the reconsolidation component consistently improves performance and leads to more coherent local memory structures that better support collective evidence recall and reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-driven memory reconsolidation is an effective mechanism for continually evolving long-term memory in LLM agents. By allowing the memory structure and retrieval process to adapt based on feedback, REALM improves reasoning performance on long-term memory benchmarks and autonomously organizes related information into more coherent structures over time.

title: Fine-Tuning Fixes Mode Collapse and Over-Dispersion in LLMs
summary: Recent work by Doshi and Hauser (2024), Bisbee et al. (2024), and Xie et al. (2026) raises concerns that outputs from large language models (LLMs) tend to be under-diverse: they repeat or resemble one another more often than responses from the population they are meant to represent, a phenomenon known as mode collapse. In this work, we show that whether mode-collapse, or its opposite, occurs depends on the specific model and dataset used. Further, with sufficient supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, LLM output diversity converges toward that of the target distribution from which fine-tuning data are sampled. To quantify this comparison, we measure the probability that two responses sampled independently from the same fixed prompt coincide (collide), or their expected similarity under a kernel. We derive a bias-variance decomposition of the expected gap between the model's and target's collision probabilities, showing that SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse or its opposite: finite-sample SFT can leave a model either under- or over-dispersed, depending on the model and dataset. Finally, we show that the absolute gap is bounded by the square root of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the target distribution to the model. Consequently, a model sufficiently close to optimal under population cross-entropy cannot exhibit arbitrarily miscalibrated diversity. We test the decomposition and the bound in three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and these LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet, a dataset of human code solutions. More target data moves model diversity toward the human (or synthetic target) level in all experiments, consistent with our theoretical predictions. These results show that diversity miscalibration can arise from finite-sample error and shrink as SFT better approximates the target distribution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and why large language models exhibit under- or over-diverse outputs (mode collapse vs over-dispersion), shows this is not an inherent bias of supervised fine-tuning, and proves that with enough data and low KL divergence, model diversity approaches that of the target distribution.
AI.motivation: There is growing concern that LLMs produce outputs that are less diverse than the true human distribution, potentially limiting their usefulness for simulating populations, generating creative content, or supporting research that depends on diverse opinions. Existing empirical work suggests systematic mode collapse, but it is unclear whether this is a fundamental property of supervised fine-tuning or a finite-sample effect, and how to rigorously relate diversity to standard training objectives like cross-entropy.
AI.method: The authors formalize diversity as the probability that two independently sampled responses to the same prompt are identical (collision probability) or have a certain expected similarity under a kernel. They analyze the expected gap between the model’s and target’s collision probabilities and derive a bias–variance-style decomposition to understand how supervised fine-tuning with finite data affects diversity. They then prove an upper bound on the absolute diversity gap in terms of the square root of the KL divergence from the target to the model. Empirically, they test the theory using (1) small transformers trained on synthetic languages, (2) four LLMs fine-tuned on human survey data, and (3) the same LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet programming solutions, varying the amount of SFT data to see how diversity changes.
AI.result: Theoretically, the paper shows that supervised fine-tuning is not intrinsically biased towards under-diversity (mode collapse) or over-diversity; instead, with finite data, a model can end up either under- or over-dispersed depending on the particular model and dataset. They prove that the absolute difference between model and target collision probabilities is bounded above by a term proportional to the square root of the KL divergence from the target to the model. Empirically, across synthetic and real datasets (surveys and code), they find that as the amount of SFT data increases, the diversity of model outputs systematically moves toward the diversity of the target distribution, validating their theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Diversity miscalibration in LLMs—being either too concentrated (mode collapse) or too dispersed relative to the target distribution—is largely a finite-sample phenomenon of supervised fine-tuning rather than a fundamental bias. As more representative SFT data are used and models get closer to the target distribution in KL (or cross-entropy) terms, output diversity converges toward that of the target. Therefore, a model that is near-optimal in population cross-entropy cannot have arbitrarily incorrect diversity, and practical concerns about under-diversity should be understood and addressed primarily as issues of data quantity and representativeness rather than an inherent flaw of SFT itself.

title: State of Thought Enables Endogenous Reasoning
summary: Test-time compute has emerged as a major approach to improving the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing test-time reasoning paradigms rely heavily on externally imposed control, either through fixed reasoning programs or through costly expansion in constrained search spaces, limiting both generalization and efficiency. We propose State of Thought (SoT), a new reasoning paradigm that enables endogenous reasoning in LLMs, with the model's internal reasoning state governing how reasoning unfolds. Concretely, SoT extracts a compact dynamics-geometric state from the model's internal information transfer and uses a 582-parameter controller on frozen backbones to selectively activate historical reasoning support useful under the current reasoning state, framing reasoning as a state-conditioned process over evidence rather than an externally prescribed token chain. Across quantitative (1.34x), general (1.62x), symbolic-and-code (1.76x), and long-context (2.51x) reasoning on 3 LLMs and 16 datasets, SoT consistently improves mean-baseline accuracy while reducing generated tokens by 62.6% and end-to-end latency by 44.6%. Across 2 VLM scales and 3 reasoning tasks, it improves mean accuracy by 3.8 points over reasoning baselines, with 74.9% fewer completion tokens and 73.5% lower latency than search-based methods. Under constrained access, SoT retains 38.2%/36.5% mean accuracy gains in training-free/embedding-only settings, while trajectory-only judging reaches 84.1% agreement across 3 API models. Together, endogenous state-driven reasoning provides a generalizable and efficient alternative.

AI.tldr: Introduces State of Thought (SoT), a new test-time reasoning paradigm for LLMs that uses an internal state controller to decide how to reason, yielding higher accuracy with much fewer tokens and latency across many tasks and models.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time reasoning methods for LLMs (like chain-of-thought with search or fixed reasoning programs) depend on externally imposed control logic and often require expensive token expansion, which hurts efficiency and generalization. There is a need for a more efficient, general, and endogenous way for models to manage their own reasoning processes at inference time.
AI.method: Define an endogenous reasoning paradigm called State of Thought (SoT). Extract a compact dynamics-geometric state from internal information flow within a frozen LLM backbone. Use a small 582-parameter controller that, based on this state, selectively activates helpful historical reasoning support rather than following an externally prescribed reasoning program. Reasoning is treated as a state-conditioned process over evidence instead of as a fixed chain of generated tokens. Evaluate SoT on multiple LLMs and VLMs, across diverse datasets and settings including constrained-access regimes.
AI.result: On 3 LLMs and 16 datasets, SoT boosts mean accuracy by factors of 1.34x (quantitative), 1.62x (general), 1.76x (symbolic-and-code), and 2.51x (long-context) while cutting generated tokens by 62.6% and end-to-end latency by 44.6%. On 2 VLM scales and 3 reasoning tasks, it improves mean accuracy by 3.8 points compared to reasoning baselines, with 74.9% fewer completion tokens and 73.5% lower latency than search-based methods. In constrained-access settings, SoT still achieves 38.2% and 36.5% mean accuracy gains in training-free and embedding-only modes, respectively. A trajectory-only judging setup attains 84.1% agreement across 3 API models.
AI.conclusion: Endogenous state-driven reasoning via SoT offers a generalizable and efficient alternative to traditional, externally controlled test-time reasoning for LLMs and VLMs. By leveraging a compact internal state and a tiny controller on frozen backbones, SoT can significantly improve accuracy while drastically reducing token usage and latency, and it remains effective even under constrained-access conditions.

title: Skill-based Agentic Evaluation for Real-time Data Science Tasks
summary: We present a framework for evaluating data-science agents on live, continuously updated data using executable ground truth and format-agnostic factoid scoring. Consider this example query: "what were last week's audience sizes"---the reference answer changes as the underlying data changes, so static references become outdated and standard LLM-as-a-judge pipelines cannot verify responses against a fixed ground truth. Our central contribution, ground-truth-as-code, encodes each expected answer as an executable reference function that recomputes the answer directly from live data at evaluation time, ensuring the reference remains consistent with the system it describes. We combine this with a factoid-level, format-agnostic judge that decomposes both the agent's response and the computed ground truth into atomic claims and scores precision, recall, and accuracy over them, irrespective of the response format (prose, list, table, HTML, etc.). The approach is applicable to agents whose expected outputs can be expressed as executable data computations. We validate the framework through a human--LLM agreement study on an internally developed machine learning skill deployed in production, using a synthetic database constructed to reproduce production schemas and entity relationships. Relative to a natural-language ground-truth baseline, our method achieves a 29% improvement in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)---a class-balanced measure of agreement between expert annotators and LLM-as-a-judge predictions---and a 16% reduction in token consumption per test case, while a self-directed baseline lacking explicit ground truth is anti-correlated with human judgment. Agents that perform multi-source data integration and computation over non-stationary data are routinely deployed in industry; we propose ground-truth-as-code as a practical methodology for their evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework to evaluate data-science agents on live, changing data by encoding ground truth as executable code and scoring answers via format-agnostic factoid comparison, yielding better agreement with human judgments and lower token costs than natural-language baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines assume static ground truths, which fail when answers must be computed over live, continuously updated data. For data-science agents operating on such non-stationary data, reference answers quickly become outdated, and natural-language ground truths are difficult to keep aligned with evolving databases and schemas. There is a need for a robust methodology to maintain accurate, up-to-date ground truth and to evaluate agents' outputs regardless of response format.
AI.method: The authors introduce "ground-truth-as-code," where each expected answer is implemented as an executable function that recomputes the correct result from live data at evaluation time. They pair this with a factoid-level, format-agnostic scoring mechanism that decomposes both the agent’s response and the code-computed ground truth into atomic factual claims. Precision, recall, and accuracy are then calculated over these factoids, independent of the surface format (text, lists, tables, HTML, etc.). The framework is tested on an internal production-like ML skill using a synthetic database mirroring production schemas and relationships, and compared against baselines: a natural-language ground-truth baseline and a self-directed baseline without explicit ground truth.
AI.result: In experiments, the proposed framework improves agreement between LLM-as-a-judge and human expert annotations by 29% in Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) relative to the natural-language ground-truth baseline. It also reduces token usage per test case by 16%. The self-directed baseline that relies on the model to infer correctness without explicit ground truth shows anti-correlation with human judgments, highlighting the importance of explicit, executable ground truth.
AI.conclusion: Ground-truth-as-code is an effective and practical approach for evaluating data-science agents that operate on non-stationary, multi-source data. By recomputing answers from live data and performing format-agnostic factoid comparison, the framework maintains alignment with evolving systems, improves reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, and reduces evaluation costs. This methodology is well-suited for industrial deployments where agents perform complex data integration and computation over continuously updated datasets.

title: Towards Scalable RLVR: Multimodal Instruction Following Data Synthesis and Distillation
summary: Multimodal instruction following (MMIF) is crucial for building generalist agents. However, current training paradigms rely heavily on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which often leads to surface-level pattern matching and degrades general capabilities. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) offers a promising alternative, its scalability in MMIF is severely bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality, RL-ready multimodal data. To bridge this gap, we present MIFS (\textbf{M}ultimodal \textbf{I}nstruction \textbf{F}ollowing \textbf{S}ynthesis), a systematic pipeline designed to generate RL-ready multimodal data. Specifically, MIFS introduces a generative constraint protocol to synthesize diverse raw samples, followed by a learnability-aware distillation mechanism that filters data based on RL training dynamics to ensure stable policy optimization. Furthermore, a code-based verifier provides high-precision reward signals for policy learning. The resulting dataset comprises 90k samples across 8 constraint categories and 14 task domains. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that MIFS-trained MLLMs achieve an average improvement of 8.13\% on four MMIF benchmarks and a 3$\times$ faster training convergence compared to using raw data. Crucially, our approach mitigates the generalization trade-offs typical of SFT, preserving core visual capabilities while significantly boosting instruction-following precision.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MIFS, a pipeline to synthesize high-quality, RL-ready multimodal instruction-following data, enabling more scalable and effective RL training for multimodal LLMs than standard supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Multimodal instruction following is key for building generalist agents, but existing models trained with supervised fine-tuning tend to overfit to patterns and harm general abilities. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is promising but limited by the lack of scalable, high-quality multimodal datasets suitable for RL. The authors aim to systematically generate such RL-ready multimodal data to unlock RL’s benefits without degrading core capabilities.
AI.method: They design MIFS, a two-stage multimodal data synthesis and filtering pipeline. First, a generative constraint protocol produces diverse raw multimodal instruction-following samples under explicit constraint categories and task domains. Second, a learnability-aware distillation mechanism evaluates these samples using RL training dynamics, keeping those that support stable policy optimization and discarding harmful or noisy ones. They additionally implement a code-based verifier that automatically checks task completion and provides precise, verifiable reward signals for RL. The final dataset consists of 90k curated samples across 8 constraint categories and 14 domains, tailored for RL training of multimodal LLMs.
AI.result: MLLMs trained with MIFS-generated data under RL show an average 8.13% improvement on four multimodal instruction-following benchmarks and achieve 3x faster training convergence compared with training on unfiltered raw data. The models trained with MIFS retain or preserve core visual abilities while substantially improving instruction-following precision, indicating better generalization than SFT-trained baselines.
AI.conclusion: Systematically synthesized and RL-filtered multimodal data can unlock the benefits of RL with verifiable rewards for multimodal instruction following, overcoming SFT’s pattern-matching limitations without sacrificing core capabilities. MIFS provides an effective, scalable way to generate RL-ready multimodal datasets that accelerate convergence and improve performance across diverse instruction-following tasks.

title: From Manual Construction to AI-Driven Scenario Emergence: Rethinking Catastrophe Risk Modeling
summary: Traditional catastrophe (CAT) risk models rely on costly manual construction to generate extreme weather scenarios, an approach largely unchanged since the 1990s. As climate extremes intensify, this creates mounting challenges to the entire risk transfer chain. This study proposes the TAISE framework, which repurposes AI weather forecasting models to produce coherent extreme weather sequences at a fraction of traditional costs. Through self-iterative generation, the framework produces continuous global atmospheric fields from which extreme events emerge. A proof-of-concept experiment demonstrates an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared with conventional methods, while capturing temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations absent in snapshot-based approaches. These findings suggest a pathway toward democratising catastrophe risk quantification and enabling dynamic, comprehensive portfolio assessment for insurers, reinsurers, ILS fund managers and public-sector risk managers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TAISE, a low-cost AI-based framework for generating coherent extreme weather sequences to improve catastrophe risk modeling.
AI.motivation: Traditional catastrophe risk models depend on expensive, manually built extreme weather scenarios that have changed little since the 1990s, which is increasingly inadequate as climate extremes intensify and as the risk transfer industry needs more scalable, detailed, and up-to-date tools.
AI.method: Repurpose AI weather forecasting models in a self-iterative way to generate continuous global atmospheric fields from which realistic extreme events naturally emerge, rather than constructing individual scenarios manually or using static snapshots.
AI.result: A proof-of-concept shows that TAISE can cut computational costs by about an order of magnitude compared with conventional CAT modeling approaches, while also preserving temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations that snapshot-based methods fail to capture.
AI.conclusion: The TAISE framework offers a promising route to democratize catastrophe risk quantification by making it cheaper and more scalable, and enables dynamic, holistic portfolio risk assessments for insurers, reinsurers, ILS fund managers, and public-sector risk managers.

title: Efficient Multimodal Generative Recommendation with Latent Narrative Reasoning
summary: Generative recommendation reformulates item prediction as semantic identifier generation, yet episodic content introduces a fundamentally different setting where the target is determined by narrative evolution rather than user preference. This task requires models to understand multimodal storyline progression while addressing the efficiency challenges caused by redundant visual contexts and costly explicit reasoning generation. We propose \textbf{NarraLite}, an efficient multimodal generative recommendation framework that jointly compresses perception and reasoning. Specifically, Progressive Spectral Compression selectively distills long visual contexts into compact narrative-relevant evidence, preserving transition-critical information while reducing redundant visual computation. Latent Narrative Reasoning introduces context-routed latent reasoning tokens and aligns their contextualized representations with future continuation semantics, enabling implicit narrative inference without autoregressively decoding textual rationales. We further establish a user-agnostic multimodal benchmark for short-form drama continuation across UGC, PGC, and OOD settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NarraLite consistently improves continuation accuracy, narrative coherence, and robustness over existing approaches, while achieving a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NarraLite, an efficient multimodal generative recommendation framework for episodic content continuation, using visual context compression and latent reasoning to improve narrative-aware item prediction.
AI.motivation: Traditional generative recommendation assumes that future items are driven by user preference, but episodic or narrative content requires understanding storyline evolution instead. Existing models struggle with long, redundant visual sequences and the inefficiency of explicit reasoning generation when predicting the next episode or clip in a narrative.
AI.method: NarraLite jointly compresses multimodal perception and reasoning. Progressive Spectral Compression distills long visual contexts into a compact set of narrative-relevant frames that preserve transition-critical information while reducing redundant computation. Latent Narrative Reasoning introduces context-routed latent reasoning tokens whose contextualized embeddings are aligned with semantics of future narrative continuation, enabling implicit reasoning about story progression without autoregressively generating textual explanations. The authors also construct a user-agnostic multimodal benchmark for short-form drama continuation across UGC, PGC, and out-of-domain scenarios.
AI.result: On the proposed multimodal short-form drama continuation benchmark, NarraLite achieves higher continuation accuracy, better narrative coherence, and greater robustness than prior methods, while also providing a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency due to its compression and latent reasoning mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Episodic generative recommendation benefits from modeling narrative evolution rather than only user preference. By compressing visual context and moving reasoning into a latent space, NarraLite offers an efficient and effective approach for multimodal narrative continuation, setting a strong baseline on a new user-agnostic benchmark and improving both performance and efficiency over existing approaches.

title: AquiLLM: Evaluating Faithfulness in Open-Weight RAG-LLM Systems for Scientific Research
summary:
Scientific research increasingly relies on large, heterogeneous data sources, motivating interest in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that provide natural language access to scientific knowledge and research workflows. Researchers are exploring the viability of these systems as natural language interfaces for document search and for generating analysis code and pipeline components. At the same time, concerns about data privacy and control over research infrastructure have motivated interest in open-weight models and open-source deployments hosted within research institutions.
  In astronomy, this development follows a long history of computational infrastructure development, from archival databases and SQL-based systems to LLM-assisted research tools. This paper presents a domain-expert evaluation of faithfulness for AquiLLM, an open-weight, offline RAG-LLM platform designed to support scientific research groups in the use and preservation of tacit and formal knowledge.
  We define faithfulness as the extent to which generated responses remain grounded in retrieved scientific context without unsupported claims or omissions. We report results from an astronomy case study evaluating AquiLLM across retrieval and scientific analysis tasks. AquiLLM performs most reliably on explicit retrieval-oriented questions grounded in the RAG collection, while faithfulness degrades for queries requiring synthesis or ambiguity resolution. These results highlight both the promise and limitations of open-weight RAG-LLM systems for scientific research and demonstrate the importance of domain-expert evaluation beyond standard benchmark leaderboards.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates AquiLLM, an open-weight, offline retrieval‑augmented LLM platform for astronomy, focusing on how faithfully its answers stay grounded in retrieved scientific context.
AI.motivation: Scientific work increasingly depends on large, heterogeneous data, driving interest in RAG systems that let researchers query documents and generate analysis workflows via natural language. However, there are concerns about data privacy, infrastructure control, and the limits of standard benchmarks, especially for scientific domains like astronomy with a long history of specialized computational tools. This motivates studying whether open-weight, locally hosted RAG-LLMs can reliably support real research, and in particular how faithful their responses are to the underlying scientific evidence.
AI.method: The authors build AquiLLM, an open-weight, offline RAG-LLM platform tailored for scientific research groups. They conduct a domain-expert evaluation in astronomy, defining and operationalizing “faithfulness” as how well model answers stay grounded in retrieved context and avoid unsupported claims or omissions. They test AquiLLM on a set of retrieval and scientific analysis tasks, and have astronomy experts assess the faithfulness of its responses, especially for different question types (explicit retrieval vs synthesis/ambiguity-resolution).
AI.result: In the astronomy case study, AquiLLM is most reliable and faithful on explicit retrieval-oriented questions closely tied to the documents in its RAG collection. Its faithfulness declines on more complex prompts that require synthesizing information across sources or resolving ambiguous queries, where unsupported inferences or omissions appear more often.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight, locally deployable RAG-LLM systems like AquiLLM show promise for supporting scientific research, especially for straightforward, retrieval-heavy tasks grounded in curated corpora. However, their faithfulness is limited for higher-level synthesis and ambiguity resolution, underscoring the need for careful domain-expert evaluation rather than relying solely on generic benchmarks when deploying such systems in scientific workflows.

title: The Immutable Past: Formalizing State Mutability and Conflict Resolution in Mutable RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) serves as the primary memory architecture for long-horizon autonomous agents. However, treating shared memory as an append-only stream introduces \textit{Semantic Shadowing}, a critical failure mode where conflicting historical observations accumulate and statistically dominate valid recent updates. In dynamic environments, this results in severe state divergence as agents retrieve and act upon obsolete facts. This paper formalizes the mechanics of State Mutability to prove that standard dense retrieval suffers from Asymptotic Recall Decay. Furthermore, we formally demonstrate a Majority Vote Trap, revealing that increasing the retrieval context window paradoxically degrades generation accuracy by diluting the attention mechanism under conditions of semantic equivalence. To resolve this, we introduce GC-Mem (Garbage Collection for Memory), a strict inference-time consistency protocol. Unlike heuristic time-decay mechanisms---which indiscriminately destroy valid long-term memory---GC-Mem relies purely on a temporal dominance operator ($Φ_{\mathcal{T}}$) paired with contradiction detection to surgically excise shadowed context. Evaluated across a rigorous, behaviorally inferred benchmark of 137,760 memory chunks and continuous accumulation sweeps, standard RAG and timestamp re-ranking baselines experience severe degradation. In contrast, GC-Mem empirically recovers $>90\%$ conflict resolution accuracy. We establish strict precision and recall deployment thresholds, ensuring state convergence where standard mutable RAG fundamentally fails.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and formalizes a key failure mode in RAG for long-horizon agents—Semantic Shadowing—and proposes GC-Mem, a principled inference-time memory garbage collection protocol that maintains consistent, up-to-date state in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon autonomous agents rely on RAG as their main memory, but current designs treat memory as append-only. In dynamic environments, this causes outdated or contradicted facts to accumulate and overshadow recent, correct information. This leads to agents repeatedly retrieving obsolete facts, diverging from the true environment state. There is a lack of formal understanding of this failure mode and of principled methods to keep memory both long-term and up-to-date without naive time decay heuristics that may destroy useful information.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize State Mutability in RAG and prove that standard dense retrieval exhibits Asymptotic Recall Decay in dynamic settings; (2) analyze attention over retrieved context and prove a Majority Vote Trap, where larger retrieval windows can paradoxically worsen accuracy when many semantically equivalent but conflicting entries exist; (3) propose GC-Mem, an inference-time consistency protocol using a temporal dominance operator and contradiction detection to remove shadowed (obsolete) memory items instead of using heuristic time-decay; and (4) evaluate GC-Mem on a large, behaviorally inferred benchmark with 137,760 memory chunks and continuous accumulation, comparing against standard RAG and timestamp re-ranking baselines.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that conventional dense retrieval in mutable environments suffers inevitable recall decay and that enlarging the retrieval window can reduce generation accuracy through a Majority Vote Trap. Empirically, on a large benchmark simulating continuous memory accumulation, standard RAG and timestamp-based re-ranking baselines exhibit severe performance degradation over time, while GC-Mem achieves over 90% accuracy in resolving conflicting memories and maintains stable performance.
AI.conclusion: RAG, when used as an append-only memory for long-horizon agents in dynamic environments, is fundamentally unstable due to Semantic Shadowing and the resulting asymptotic recall decay and Majority Vote Trap. GC-Mem, a principled inference-time garbage collection mechanism based on temporal dominance and contradiction detection, mitigates these issues by selectively removing shadowed, obsolete information. This yields high conflict resolution accuracy and ensures state convergence, offering a robust alternative to standard mutable RAG and naive time-decay heuristics for agent memory management.

title: QueryFormer: Winning Solution for KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge
summary: Post-click conversion rate (pCVR) prediction requires jointly modeling feature interactions and sequential user behaviors. The KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge calls for a unified architecture addressing both. We observe that existing unified architectures often generate query tokens---the central information hub---with projection-based multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), without explicit token-to-query attention for refining the query side. We propose QueryFormer, centered on a stackable unified field--sequence block that bridges non-sequential multi-field features and behavioral sequences, and provide a latency-aware scaling study over view width $H$, model width, depth, data, and compute. The block generates queries through cross-attention and packs sequence queries into shared-parameter attention. QueryFormer secured 1st place in the Industrial Track, achieving an official test area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.83254; a modest post-competition scale-up reached 0.832713. Within our grid, $H$-scaling improves validation AUC from 0.84540 to 0.84615 and beats HyFormer at comparable budgets. Ablation identifies query generation as the largest contributor. Packed shared-parameter cross-attention keeps H=8 inference latency to only 1.89x that of H=1, positioning the bridge as an efficient stackable unified block.

AI.tldr: QueryFormer is a unified architecture for post-click conversion rate prediction that jointly models structured features and user behavior sequences using a stackable field–sequence block with efficient query generation via attention.
AI.motivation: Existing pCVR models and unified architectures struggle to effectively and efficiently connect non-sequential multi-field features with sequential user behaviors. In particular, most unified architectures generate query tokens using simple projection-based MLPs, lacking explicit attention from tokens to queries, which may limit representation quality and downstream performance under tight latency constraints.
AI.method: The paper proposes QueryFormer, built around a unified field–sequence block. This block generates query tokens via cross-attention from non-sequential fields and behavioral sequences, then packs these sequence queries into a shared-parameter attention mechanism to reduce latency. The architecture is stackable and is studied under a latency-aware scaling framework, varying view width H (number of views/heads), model width, depth, data size, and compute to understand trade-offs. Extensive ablations are conducted, especially on query generation strategies.
AI.result: QueryFormer wins 1st place in the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Industrial Track with an official test AUC of 0.83254, further improved to 0.832713 via post-competition scale-up. Within the explored grid, increasing view width H improves validation AUC from 0.84540 to 0.84615 and outperforms the HyFormer baseline at similar compute/latency budgets. Ablation studies show that the proposed query generation mechanism contributes the most to the observed performance gains. The packed shared-parameter cross-attention design keeps inference latency for H=8 to only 1.89x that of H=1.
AI.conclusion: Cross-attention–based query generation in a unified field–sequence block is an effective and latency-efficient way to jointly model structured fields and behavior sequences for pCVR prediction.
