AI.method: The authors propose AntennaFlow, a three-stage framework: (1) a contrastively trained encoder that learns an offset-invariant embedding of near-field amplitude measurements captured under different mechanical offsets; (2) a deterministic flow-matching transport module that maps offset amplitude measurements to their equivalent center-aligned amplitudes in measurement space; and (3) application of the Simplified Extrapolation Technique (SET), which is based on a Green-function Taylor expansion that is valid only when fields are correctly centered, to perform the final NF–FF transformation. The method works from sparse, amplitude-only near-field data and does not require explicit phase measurements or knowledge of the mounting offset vector.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that AntennaFlow can reconstruct far-field patterns from sparse, amplitude-only near-field measurements without phase or offset vectors, while respecting the underlying physics. Across tested scenarios, it consistently outperforms existing baselines in terms of reconstruction accuracy and robustness to offsets, and it reduces data demands and measurement time.
AI.conclusion: AntennaFlow provides a physically consistent, data-efficient solution to NF–FF transformation at millimeter-wave frequencies that simultaneously overcomes the need for phase measurements and precise mechanical centering. By learning offset-invariant representations and using flow-based alignment before applying a physics-based extrapolation technique, the method achieves superior NF–FF reconstruction from sparse amplitude-only data and can improve the practicality of large-aperture antenna testing in real-world setups.

title: DiaWhisper-DPO: Role-Attributed Transcription of Clinical Interviews via Failure-Mined Preference Optimization
summary: Automated depression screening from clinical interviews requires attribution of utterances to the clinician or patient. We evaluate two datasets: DAIC-WOZ, where participant-only recordings require re-synthesizing both sides for controlled two-party evaluation, and PDCH-HAMD, comprising voice-converted real Chinese interviews for cross-lingual validation. Cascaded systems combine speaker diarization with role-assignment heuristics, so errors can propagate across stages. We propose an end-to-end model, which we named DiaWhisper, that fine-tunes Whisper-large-v3 with LoRA and an auxiliary frame-level role head for transcription and attribution, together with DiaWhisper-DPO, a failure-mined refinement that uses genuine decoding failures as DPO rejected completions without human preference annotation. On 29 DAIC-WOZ test sessions, DiaWhisper-DPO achieves 0.973 role accuracy and 0.119 DER, 72% below the strongest cascaded baseline, and reduces seed variation from σ = .205 to .002. Retrained on PDCH-HAMD, it achieves 0.757 role accuracy and improves all 78 session-seed pairs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DiaWhisper, an end-to-end system for simultaneously transcribing and attributing speaker roles in clinical depression interviews, outperforming traditional cascaded diarization-plus-heuristics pipelines and generalizing cross-lingually.
AI.motivation: Accurate automated depression screening from clinical interviews needs not only what is said but also who said it (clinician vs patient). Existing pipelines use separate speaker diarization and role-assignment stages, so errors compound and performance suffers, especially in realistic, noisy, or cross-lingual settings. There is also a lack of controlled two-party evaluation data and a need for methods that are robust to random seed variation and can leverage real model decoding failures without costly human preference labels.
AI.method: The authors construct two evaluation settings: (1) DAIC-WOZ, where they re-synthesize both sides of the conversation from participant-only recordings to create controlled two-speaker audio; and (2) PDCH-HAMD, a set of real Chinese clinical interviews converted using voice conversion for cross-lingual validation. They propose DiaWhisper, which fine-tunes Whisper-large-v3 using LoRA and adds an auxiliary frame-level role classification head so the model jointly performs ASR and role attribution in an end-to-end fashion. They further introduce DiaWhisper-DPO, a refinement that uses Direct Preference Optimization with automatically mined failure cases from the model’s own decoding; these genuine failures are treated as rejected outputs, avoiding human preference annotation. Performance is compared against cascaded baselines combining standard diarization with heuristic role assignment.
AI.result: On 29 DAIC-WOZ test sessions, DiaWhisper-DPO attains 0.973 role-label accuracy and a diarization error rate (DER) of 0.119, which is a 72% reduction compared with the strongest cascaded baseline. It also dramatically stabilizes training, reducing performance variation across random seeds from a standard deviation of 0.205 to 0.002. When retrained and evaluated on the PDCH-HAMD Chinese dataset, the model reaches 0.757 role accuracy and improves results consistently across all 78 combinations of sessions and random seeds, indicating robust cross-lingual generalization and stability.
AI.conclusion: Joint, end-to-end modeling of transcription and speaker-role attribution with a large speech foundation model (Whisper-large-v3) significantly outperforms traditional cascaded diarization-plus-heuristics approaches for clinical interview analysis. The DiaWhisper architecture with an auxiliary role head and the DiaWhisper-DPO refinement not only reduce diarization error and improve role accuracy but also make performance far less sensitive to random initialization. The method generalizes to cross-lingual clinical data (English to Chinese) and offers a practically attractive way to exploit genuine model decoding failures for preference-style optimization without human annotation, making it promising for scalable, reliable automated analysis of clinical interviews.

title: Affect-Prototype Guided Fusion for Open-Vocabulary Incomplete Multi-modal Emotion Recognition
summary: Open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition (OV-MER) aims to generate open natural-language emotion labels from multimodal affective cues. In real-world scenarios, however, complete and synchronized modal data are difficult to obtain due to limitations of acquisition devices and user privacy constraints. Existing OV-MER methods are largely designed for full-modal inputs, and fail to perform effective feature fusion under modal missing conditions. Meanwhile, current fusion approaches designed for incomplete modalities mainly focus on fixed-label recognition context, and cannot satisfy the demand for fuse emotional cues guided with arbitrary emotion semantics in OV-MER context. To tackle these challenges, this paper proposes an Affect-Prototype-Conditioned Fusion (APCF) framework for incomplete open-vocabulary emotion recognition. As a candidate-free generative framework, APCF extends modal contribution learning to scenarios guided by arbitrary emotional semantics. Specifically, we construct an affect-prototype library to explicitly model multimodal contribution characteristics corresponding to diverse emotions, which provides dynamic constraints for modal fusion under different emotional semantic perspectives. Conditional retrieval and feature aggregation are conducted based on available modal features. The refined fused affective representations are then fed into an LLM decoder to produce open-vocabulary emotion labels. Experiments on the OV-MERD+ and MER-FG datasets demonstrate that APCF substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework to do open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition even when some modalities are missing, by using an affect-prototype library and an LLM decoder.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition methods assume all modalities are present and synchronized, which is unrealistic due to device limits and privacy, and existing fusion methods for missing modalities are mainly designed for closed, fixed emotion label sets. There is a need for a method that can fuse incomplete multimodal emotional cues while being guided by arbitrary emotion semantics (open-vocabulary).
AI.method: They design an Affect-Prototype-Conditioned Fusion (APCF) framework. It builds an affect-prototype library that captures how different modalities contribute to various emotions. Given available modality features and an emotion semantic query, APCF conditionally retrieves relevant prototypes and aggregates features to perform dynamic, semantics-guided fusion. The fused affective representation is then passed to a large language model decoder that generates natural-language emotion labels without being restricted to a fixed label set.
AI.result: On two datasets, OV-MERD+ and MER-FG, the proposed APCF framework significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines for open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition, especially when modality information is incomplete.
AI.conclusion: Affect-Prototype-Conditioned Fusion effectively addresses open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition under missing modalities by leveraging a learned affect-prototype library and an LLM decoder for candidate-free label generation, achieving substantial performance gains over previous methods.

title: Japanese Stroke LLM Evaluation: A Conversational Benchmark for Safe Stroke Care in Japanese Using Large Language Models
summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved physician-comparable performance on multiple-choice medical knowledge examinations, but their capabilities in clinical history taking, urgency assessment, and safety remain insufficiently evaluated. We proposed Japanese Stroke LLM Evaluation, a multi-turn conversational benchmark for stroke care in Japanese, and evaluated LLM performance and safety under practice-oriented conditions. Methods: We created 10 stroke and related-condition cases and evaluated LLMs in multi-turn Japanese conversations. The LLM acted as physician, while a board-certified neurosurgeon acted as simulated patient and evaluator. Each case comprised history-taking and action phases scored using pre-specified criteria. Errors that could directly threaten life were defined as critical mistakes. The safety threshold was at least 80% overall with zero critical mistakes. Eighteen models were evaluated in October 2025 and June 2026. Results: Claude Fable 5 achieved the highest score (87.4%) with zero critical mistakes, followed by Claude Opus 4.7 (80.3%) and GLM-5.2 (75.6%). Two leaders met the safety threshold. Eleven models made 17 critical mistakes, including failure to confirm laboratory results or blood glucose before t-PA, surgery before airway stabilization, omission of cervical vascular evaluation, and t-PA outside its indication. History-taking question count correlated with history-taking score (r = 0.648, p = 0.007). Conclusions: Japanese Stroke LLM Evaluation provides a benchmark for LLM performance under practice-oriented conditions, including a cap on history-taking questions. Cases and evaluations were created by neurosurgical specialists rather than using an LLM-as-judge approach. Performance improved across cloud-based and on-premise models in 2026, with some exceeding the safety threshold. Further evaluation using real-world cases is required.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and applies a Japanese multi-turn conversational benchmark to test how safely and effectively large language models handle stroke-like cases as virtual physicians.
AI.motivation: Despite LLMs performing well on written medical exams, their real-world clinical usefulness and safety—especially in complex, multi-step tasks like stroke triage, history taking, and treatment decisions—remain unclear, particularly in Japanese. Stroke care is highly time-sensitive and error-prone, so a focused, practice-oriented evaluation tailored to this domain is needed to understand whether and how LLMs can be safely integrated into clinical workflows.
AI.method: The authors designed 10 realistic stroke and stroke-mimicking cases in Japanese. In each scenario, the LLM played the role of a physician interacting in multi-turn dialogue, while a board-certified neurosurgeon acted both as the simulated patient and as the evaluator. Each case had a history-taking phase and an action/management phase, scored by predefined criteria. They also defined “critical mistakes” as those that could directly endanger life, and set a safety bar: at least 80% total score and zero critical mistakes. Eighteen different LLMs were evaluated across two time points (Oct 2025 and Jun 2026). They also assessed the relationship between the number of questions asked during history taking and performance in that phase.
AI.result: Among the 18 models, Claude Fable 5 scored highest (87.4%) with no critical mistakes, and Claude Opus 4.7 also met the safety threshold (80.3% with zero critical mistakes). GLM-5.2 reached 75.6%, below the predefined safety bar. Eleven of the evaluated models produced 17 total critical mistakes, such as giving or preparing thrombolysis (t-PA) without checking labs or blood glucose, proceeding to surgery before securing the airway, omitting essential cervical vessel assessment, or using t-PA outside approved indications. There was a significant positive correlation between how many history questions a model asked and its history-taking score (r = 0.648, p = 0.007). Overall performance improved from 2025 to 2026 across both cloud and on-premise models.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that Japanese Stroke LLM Evaluation is a useful, practice-oriented benchmark for assessing LLMs in stroke care, emphasizing realistic dialogue constraints (including a cap on the number of history-taking questions). By using neurosurgical experts to create and grade the cases instead of relying on automated LLM-as-judge approaches, they argue that the evaluation better reflects clinical standards. Some newer models surpassed their predefined safety threshold, suggesting rapid progress, but the presence of critical, potentially lethal errors in many systems underscores the need for continued caution and further testing, particularly with real-world clinical data before deployment in practice.

title: FlexEE: Self-Speculative and KV-Compatible Early Exiting for Offloading-Aware LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is often constrained by both computation and memory, especially in offloading-based deployments where model weights are transferred across memory hierarchies during autoregressive decoding. In this setting, reducing the number of executed layers can lower per-token latency while also avoiding costly weight movement. Motivated by this observation, we present FlexEE, an early exiting framework for resource-constrained and offloading-based LLM inference. FlexEE makes early exiting practical for LLM decoding through layer-wise exit supervision for reliable intermediate-layer prediction, self-speculative decoding over a Top-K local vocabulary for low-cost exit decisions, and dynamic hidden state management for KV-cache-correct and memory-aware execution. Across generative and downstream tasks, FlexEE enables efficient early exit with minimal accuracy degradation, delivering up to 1.27$\times$/3.16$\times$ and 1.25$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end speedups on Llama2-7B and Llama3-8B under 0\%/50\% weight offloading, respectively.

AI.tldr: FlexEE is an early-exiting framework that speeds up LLM inference—especially with weight offloading—by safely stopping computation at intermediate layers while keeping accuracy nearly intact.
AI.motivation: LLM inference is slow and memory-bound, particularly when model weights must be offloaded and moved across memory hierarchies during decoding. Reducing the number of layers executed per token can cut both compute and weight-transfer costs, but naive early exiting harms accuracy and complicates KV-cache and memory management. A principled framework is needed to make early exit reliable and deployable under resource constraints.
AI.method: FlexEE introduces: (1) layer-wise exit supervision so intermediate layers can reliably predict outputs; (2) self-speculative decoding with a small Top-K local vocabulary to cheaply decide whether to exit early at a layer; and (3) dynamic hidden-state management to ensure correctness of the KV cache and memory-aware execution when different tokens exit at different depths and when weights are partially offloaded. The system is evaluated on generative and downstream tasks with varying weight-offloading ratios.
AI.result: On Llama2-7B and Llama3-8B, FlexEE achieves up to 1.27×/3.16× and 1.25×/2.83× end-to-end speedups under 0%/50% weight offloading, respectively, with minimal accuracy degradation across evaluated tasks. This shows that early exit can be made both efficient and robust under realistic resource constraints and offloading regimes.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed early exiting—via supervised intermediate layers, lightweight self-speculative decisions, and KV/memory-aware execution—can substantially accelerate LLM inference, especially in offloading-based deployments, while preserving task performance. FlexEE provides a practical blueprint for integrating early exit into real-world, resource-constrained LLM systems.

title: TIAO: Token Importance-Aware Policy Optimization for Text Summarization
summary: Text summarization requires models to condense content while preserving key qualities such as consistency and coherence. Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on this task and can be further improved through reinforcement learning (RL). However, most existing methods apply reward signals directly to undifferentiated token sequences, overlooking the varying importance of individual tokens to word and sentence level quality in summarization. In this paper, we propose Token Importance-Aware Policy Optimization (TIAO), a novel reinforcement learning strategy that explicitly leverages token-importance awareness. Specifically, TIAO identifies core tokens based on token dependency and reweights a trajectory's advantage according to its overall dependencies. Experiments on the real world dataset show that our TIAO achieves highly competitive results, and that a 7B foundation model enhanced by TIAO performs comparably to GPT-4 and GPT-5-nano. Code is available at https://github.com/TechCloud-x/TIAO

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TIAO, a reinforcement learning strategy for text summarization that weights learning by token importance, improving LLM summarization quality to near GPT-4 level.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for summarization treat all tokens equally in the reward signal, ignoring that some tokens are more crucial for summary quality (consistency, coherence, and content preservation). This mismatch can limit learning efficiency and quality, especially for LLM-based summarization.
AI.method: The authors propose Token Importance-Aware Policy Optimization (TIAO). It first identifies core tokens in generated summaries using token dependency information, then computes an importance score for each trajectory based on these dependencies. During RL training, it reweights the policy gradient advantage term according to token importance, so updates are driven more by core tokens that matter most for word- and sentence-level quality.
AI.result: On real-world summarization datasets, TIAO achieves highly competitive performance. A 7B-parameter base model trained with TIAO attains results comparable to GPT-4 and GPT-5-nano, indicating that importance-aware RL can significantly close the performance gap to stronger proprietary models.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating token-importance awareness into RL for summarization improves the quality of LLM-generated summaries. By selectively emphasizing core tokens in the optimization process, TIAO yields better consistency and coherence and elevates smaller open models to performance levels close to much larger closed models.

title: ThinkFlow: Self-Evolving Probabilistic Latent Memory for Lifelong Conversational Agents
summary: Lifelong conversational agents rely on memory systems to maintain deep, context-aware interactions with users. However, existing explicit textual memory pipelines suffer from a severe information bottleneck, often losing subtle behavioral patterns and emotional shifts. Furthermore, being typically static post-deployment, they cannot autonomously adapt to personal habits and preferences without manual feedback. Cognitive science, however, suggests that humans maintain mental models purely in a latent space and continuously refine them through predictive coding. Inspired by this, we propose \textbf{ThinkFlow}, a novel end-to-end latent memory framework for lifelong conversational agents. ThinkFlow bypasses the text bottleneck by dynamically compressing conversational flows into probabilistic latent memory skills, autonomously consolidating complex user states into disentangled, continuous vectors without semantic interference. To break this barrier, we introduce a test-time evolution paradigm. By coupling teacher-guided latent alignment to bootstrap the initial state with a self-supervised next-user-utterance prediction task for continuous refinement, the framework successfully overcomes cold-start challenges and achieves label-free lifelong personalization. Extensive experiments on long-term conversation benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkFlow significantly outperforms prevailing memory systems, providing highly personalized and contextually accurate responses over extended multi-session interactions.

AI.tldr: ThinkFlow is a latent memory framework for lifelong conversational agents that replaces explicit text memories with evolving latent user models, enabling better personalization over long-term, multi-session interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing conversational agents use explicit textual memories, which cause an information bottleneck, missing fine-grained behavioral and emotional cues. These memory systems are also usually static after deployment and require manual feedback to adapt to users, limiting true lifelong personalization. Cognitive science suggests humans rely on latent mental models refined via predictive coding, motivating a similar latent, continuously updated memory mechanism for agents.
AI.method: ThinkFlow introduces an end-to-end latent memory framework that compresses conversational histories into probabilistic latent memory skills—disentangled, continuous vectors representing user states. It avoids semantic interference and the limitations of text-based memory. The method also includes a test-time evolution paradigm: (1) teacher-guided latent alignment to initialize the latent state (cold start), and (2) a self-supervised next-user-utterance prediction objective that continually refines the latent memory during deployment, without labeled data.
AI.result: On long-term conversation benchmarks, ThinkFlow outperforms state-of-the-art explicit memory systems. It delivers more personalized and contextually accurate responses, especially over extended, multi-session interactions, illustrating the benefit of latent and continuously evolving user representations.
AI.conclusion: Latent, continuously evolving memory representations can better capture user-specific behavior and emotion than explicit textual memories. ThinkFlow shows that combining latent memory skills with test-time evolution via self-supervised predictive objectives enables label-free, lifelong personalization in conversational agents, overcoming cold-start issues and improving long-term interaction quality.

title: Benchmarking Factual Robustness of LLMs via Multi-conversation Persuasion
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as primary knowledge retrieval interfaces, their robustness against \textit{persuasion attacks}---attempts to inject misinformation or enforce counterfactuals---has become a critical safety concern. Existing red-teaming frameworks typically evaluate models in multi-turn dialogues where the target model retains full conversation history. We identify a critical flaw in this setting termed \textbf{``Refusal Inertia''}: a model's initial refusal often propagates through subsequent turns largely to maintain contextual consistency, thereby masking its true vulnerability to sophisticated, isolated persuasion attempts. To rigorously evaluate the ``cold-start'' defense capabilities of SOTA models, we introduce the \textbf{SAST-IR} (Stateful Attacker, Stateless Target - Iterative Refinement) framework. By enforcing a memory wipe on the target while retaining the attacker's history, we simulate a worst-case adversarial setting using \textbf{multi-turn} (stateless) iterations. Leveraging \textbf{CP-Agent} (Cognitive Persuasion Agent), an enhanced diagnosis-guided agent, our experiments on the custom \textsc{CounterFact-Strict} dataset ($N=50$) yield alarming results: simple, diverse attack strategies achieved a staggering \textbf{96\%} success rate, exposing severe brittleness in memory-less defense. Furthermore, we reveal a \textbf{``Complexity Paradox''}: while complex, iteratively refined attacks are effective, they often trigger defensive compliance, whereas simple strategies achieve a higher rate of genuine persuasion (\textbf{84.7\%}). Our code and dataset are available at GitHub, https://github.com/cza1006/llm-persuasion-defense.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that current large language models appear safer than they actually are because prior refusals carry over in multi-turn chats. When you remove the model’s memory but let an attacker refine their strategy, simple persuasion attacks can succeed about 96% of the time.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are used as knowledge interfaces, they can be targets of persuasion attacks that inject misinformation or enforce counterfactual statements. Existing safety evaluations mostly use multi-turn settings where the model keeps full history, which can cause it to just stick to an initial refusal. This masks its true vulnerability to standalone, well-crafted persuasion attempts. The authors want a more realistic, worst-case evaluation of how models behave when each query is effectively fresh, while an attacker can learn and adapt over time.
AI.method: The authors define a new evaluation framework SAST-IR (Stateful Attacker, Stateless Target - Iterative Refinement). In this setup, the attacking agent keeps its internal history and iteratively improves its prompts, but the target LLM has its conversation history wiped each turn so it sees every prompt in isolation. They implement the attacker as CP-Agent, a cognitive-persuasion agent that diagnoses why previous attempts worked or failed and refines its strategy. They test this framework on a custom CounterFact-Strict dataset of 50 counterfactual knowledge items, measuring how often the target model is persuaded under different levels of attack complexity.
AI.result: Under the SAST-IR framework with CP-Agent on the CounterFact-Strict dataset, simple yet diverse persuasion strategies reach a 96% success rate in getting the target LLM to accept or output counterfactual content when it lacks memory. They also observe a “Complexity Paradox”: more complex, iteratively refined attacks are indeed effective at inducing some form of compliance, but this compliance often manifests as overt defenses or hedging rather than genuine acceptance of the misinformation. In contrast, simpler attacks yield a higher rate (84.7%) of genuine persuasion, where the model actually adopts the falsehood.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM safety is significantly overestimated when evaluated in standard multi-turn, memoryful dialogue settings, due to refusal inertia. When tested in a stateless, cold-start regime against a stateful, adaptive attacker, current models show severe brittleness, with very high susceptibility to persuasion attacks. The observed Complexity Paradox suggests that simple, low-profile attack strategies may be more dangerous in practice than sophisticated ones, as they more often bypass explicit defenses and lead to true belief change in the model’s outputs. The authors release their code and data to facilitate more realistic robustness evaluations and future defenses.

title: ORDER: Task-Conditioned Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines typically rely on a fixed indexing and retrieval configuration determined at preprocessing time. This one-size-fits-all design is ill-suited to domain-expert settings, where heterogeneous queries require different chunking granularities, metadata constraints, and source-selection strategies. As a result, configurations that are effective for one family of queries often perform poorly for others. In this paper, we introduce ORDER (Optimal Routing for Dynamic Evidence Retrieval), a query-conditioned RAG framework that jointly adapts indexing and retrieval to the incoming query. Our approach first discovers semantic clusters over a given set of questions associated to a corpus and learns, for each cluster, a chunking strategy together with a suited metadata filtering and reranking configuration. At inference time, queries are routed to the appropriate pre-built index through nearest-centroid assignment. To further improve retrieval, we propose a supervised query router (QRe) that predicts which collections are most likely to contain relevant evidence, coupled with a Uniform Multi-source Sampler (UMS) that allocates the retrieval budget evenly across the selected sources. We evaluate our framework on large-scale, heterogeneous historical archives and show that conditioning both indexing and retrieval on the query consistently outperforms both naive baselines and strong state-of-the-art RAG systems in complex expert-domain environments.

AI.tldr: ORDER is a query-conditioned RAG framework that dynamically chooses indexing and retrieval strategies per query to improve performance on heterogeneous, expert-domain corpora.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems use a single, fixed indexing and retrieval setup (chunk sizes, metadata filters, source choices) for all queries. In expert domains with diverse information needs, this rigid configuration causes good performance for some query types but poor performance for others. The authors want a way to adapt how documents are chunked, indexed, filtered, and retrieved depending on the specific query, especially for complex, heterogeneous archives.
AI.method: 1) Cluster training questions semantically for a given corpus. 2) For each cluster, learn an optimal chunking strategy, metadata filtering rules, and reranking configuration, and build a dedicated index accordingly. 3) At inference, route an incoming query to the best cluster via nearest-centroid assignment and use that cluster’s specialized index and retrieval configuration. 4) Add a supervised query router (QRe) that predicts which document collections are likely to contain relevant evidence. 5) Use a Uniform Multi-source Sampler (UMS) to distribute the retrieval budget evenly across the selected sources. 6) Integrate these components into a RAG pipeline and evaluate on historical archives.
AI.result: On large, heterogeneous historical archives, the ORDER framework, which conditions both indexing and retrieval on the query, consistently outperforms naive baselines and strong state-of-the-art RAG systems. The improvements are shown specifically in complex expert-domain environments where query types and source characteristics vary widely.
AI.conclusion: Adapting both indexing and retrieval configurations to the query—via semantic clustering, specialized per-cluster indices, and supervised routing over multiple collections—significantly improves RAG performance on heterogeneous, expert-domain corpora. Static, one-size-fits-all RAG configurations are suboptimal in such settings, and query-conditioned design is a more effective approach.

title: Smarter by the Moment: Environment-Driven Dynamic Policies for Continual LLM Improvement
comment: 25 pages, 13 figures. Accepted to the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across diverse domains, but continual adaptation to evolving tasks and environments remains a key challenge. Existing memory-augmented approaches retrieve individual past examples as direct references, but do not explicitly synthesize actionable strategies from them, causing the same types of errors to recur. We propose Dynamic Retrieval-based Policy Generation (DRPG), a framework that integrates memory-based retrieval with a dynamic policy generator, leveraging historical data and environment feedback to produce task-specific policies for continual LLM improvement. We evaluate DRPG across six benchmarks spanning text-to-SQL, question answering, medical diagnosis, and Python programming, using seven LLMs from both proprietary and open-weight families. DRPG outperforms strong baselines across most datasets and models. Further analysis demonstrates that DRPG's policy generation is robust to retrieval strategy, operates effectively without prior policy continuity, and can leverage smaller or cross-family models as cost-efficient policy generators. We also find that the benefit of policy-level guidance depends on task characteristics, offering practical insights into when and under what conditions this mechanism is most effective.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DRPG, a framework that uses retrieval and dynamic policy generation to continually improve LLM performance across tasks by learning high-level strategies from past experience rather than just copying examples.
AI.motivation: While LLMs perform well on many benchmarks, they struggle with continual adaptation to new or evolving tasks. Existing memory-augmented methods typically retrieve and reuse individual past examples, which does not prevent repeated mistakes or capture generalizable strategies. There is a need for a mechanism that can synthesize high-level, actionable guidance from history and feedback so models can improve over time in a more principled and robust way.
AI.method: The authors propose Dynamic Retrieval-based Policy Generation (DRPG). DRPG maintains a memory of historical interactions and environment feedback, retrieves relevant past data for a new input, and then uses a dedicated policy generator model to synthesize a task-specific policy—a high-level strategy or guidance. This policy is then used to guide the main LLM in solving the current task instance. The framework is evaluated across six benchmarks (text-to-SQL, QA, medical diagnosis, Python coding) and with seven different LLMs (both proprietary and open-weight). Additional analyses test robustness to different retrieval strategies, absence of prior policy continuity, and use of smaller or cross-family policy generators for efficiency.
AI.result: Across most evaluated datasets and models, DRPG consistently outperforms strong baseline methods that either lack memory augmentation or only use naive example retrieval. Experiments show that DRPG’s policy generation is robust to the choice of retrieval strategy, does not require consistent policies across time to remain effective, and can successfully employ smaller or cross-family models as the policy generator without major performance loss, thereby reducing cost. The study also characterizes when policy-level guidance provides the largest gains, revealing dependence on task properties.
AI.conclusion: DRPG is an effective and flexible approach for continual improvement of LLMs, offering better performance than existing retrieval-based or memory-augmented baselines by generating high-level, task-specific policies from historical data and feedback. Its robustness to retrieval choices, ability to use cheaper policy generators, and insights into which task characteristics benefit most from policy-level guidance make it a practical framework for deploying and maintaining LLM systems in dynamic, real-world settings.

title: SKIP: a Self-knowledge-guided Step-wise Preference Learning Framework for Concise Reasoning
summary: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has been proven to be effective, it often leads to overthinking, resulting in computational overhead, inference latency, and even degraded performance in large language models (LLMs). Existing concise reasoning frameworks significantly compromise accuracy while compressing the length of output. In this paper, we propose SKIP, a self-knowledge-guided step-wise preference learning framework. Starting with lightweight fine-tuning to adjust the model's output style, SKIP introduces a carefully designed knowledge probing mechanism to guide model to output an answer at each reasoning step. Based on the correctness of intermediate steps, we construct preference data that guide the model toward more efficient and correct reasoning by leveraging DPO. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively improves reasoning compression while mitigating performance degradation after fine-tuning. Besides, SKIP shows strong generalization ability on out-of-distribution datasets. We further conducted ablation studies on the component parameters of our framework.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SKIP, a framework that reduces overthinking in Chain-of-Thought reasoning by learning step-wise preferences, achieving shorter reasoning traces with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought reasoning improves LLM performance but often triggers overlong reasoning, causing computational overhead, latency, and sometimes worse accuracy. Existing concise reasoning methods shorten outputs but at a large cost in accuracy, so there is a need for a framework that can compress reasoning while preserving or even improving performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce SKIP, a self-knowledge-guided step-wise preference learning framework. First, they perform lightweight fine-tuning to adjust the model’s output style. Then they use a knowledge probing mechanism that encourages the model to produce an answer at each reasoning step. Using the correctness of these intermediate steps, they construct preference pairs and apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) so that the model learns to prefer reasoning paths that are both efficient (shorter) and correct.
AI.result: Experiments show that SKIP reduces the length of reasoning (improves reasoning compression) while avoiding the usual performance degradation seen after concise-reasoning fine-tuning. The method also generalizes well to out-of-distribution datasets, and ablation studies confirm the contribution of different components and parameters.
AI.conclusion: SKIP successfully guides LLMs toward more efficient Chain-of-Thought reasoning, mitigating overthinking and computational costs without sacrificing accuracy, and it exhibits robustness across datasets, as validated by ablation analyses.

title: A Data-free Universal Prior over Syntactic Structures
summary: Probability is fundamental to theories of language comprehension, production, acquisition, and evolution, as well as to large language models. Existing theories estimate the probability of syntactic structures from language-specific data. Whether part of this probability structure can arise independently of language-specific experience remains unknown. Here I show that a universal prior over syntactic structures emerges from a cognitively motivated model of incremental language production, in which words are progressively integrated into syntactic structure through network growth. The resulting prior assigns probabilities to syntactic structures --represented as dependency trees-- without fitting parameters to linguistic data, and assigns higher probabilities to attested than to random trees in all 138 typologically diverse languages examined. These prior probabilities correlate positively with probabilities estimated from corpora in 33 of 34 languages. The results indicate that part of the probability structure of syntax can arise independently of language-specific statistical learning. Linguistic experience may therefore refine probabilities that are already structured by the process of language production, rather than create them from an initially uniform space. This identifies a possible cognitive origin for part of the probability distribution over syntactic structures, linking language production and statistical learning while providing a data-independent structural bias for probabilistic models of language.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that part of the probabilistic structure of syntax comes from a universal, cognitively motivated prior rather than only from language-specific data, and shows this prior aligns well with syntactic patterns across many languages.
AI.motivation: Theories of language and modern large language models rely heavily on probabilities of syntactic structures, which are usually learned from language-specific corpora. It is unknown whether some aspects of these probability distributions could arise without exposure to any particular language, potentially from domain-general cognitive constraints or language production mechanisms. The paper aims to test whether a universal, data-independent prior over syntactic structures can be derived from a cognitive model and whether this prior matches real-world syntactic patterns across many languages.
AI.method: The author builds a cognitively motivated model of incremental language production in which words are integrated one by one into an evolving syntactic representation modeled as a growing network. This process induces a prior probability distribution over dependency trees (syntactic structures) without fitting parameters to linguistic corpora. The model's induced probabilities over trees are then compared to (a) which trees are actually attested versus random trees in 138 typologically diverse languages, and (b) corpus-based probability estimates in a subset of 34 languages, checking for correlation between the model’s prior and empirical probabilities.
AI.result: The universal prior derived from the incremental production model systematically assigns higher probabilities to syntactic dependency trees that are actually attested in real languages than to random trees, for all 138 languages tested. Moreover, in 33 of 34 languages for which corpus-based syntactic probabilities are available, the prior’s probabilities positively correlate with those empirical probabilities, showing that the model’s language-independent structural bias aligns with observed syntactic distributions.
AI.conclusion: A substantial portion of the probabilistic structure of syntax can arise from a universal, language-independent prior grounded in the cognitive process of incremental language production, rather than solely from language-specific statistical learning. Linguistic experience appears to refine an already structured probability space over syntactic trees, instead of building it from a uniform baseline. This suggests a cognitive origin for part of the probability distribution over syntax and offers a principled, data-independent structural bias for probabilistic models of language, linking production mechanisms with statistical learning accounts.

title: Sparse MLLM Anchors, Dense Adaptation: Breaking the Self-Referential Loop in Wild Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Wild test-time adaptation (WTTA) updates a source model online under small test batches, concurrent distribution shifts, and time-varying class imbalance. Most WTTA methods derive their adaptation signals, including predictive uncertainty, sample reliability, and local feature geometry, from the model being adapted. When the source model is unreliable under shift, these signals can reinforce its own errors, forming a self-referential loop. We introduce MASA (Multimodal-LLM-Anchored Semantic Adaptation), which complements model-internal evidence with structured semantic descriptions from a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM). To limit inference cost, MASA queries the MLLM only for a small set of diverse, reliability-ranked anchors. The resulting descriptions capture the object family and nuisance factors such as style, viewpoint, and occlusion. MASA encodes these descriptions, propagates them to neighboring test samples, and stores the resulting visual-semantic information in an online prototype memory. Descriptor-aware retrieval from this memory provides an auxiliary target for lightweight adaptation of normalization-affine parameters. We evaluate MASA on the WTTA ImageNet-C benchmark under limited-batch, mixed-domain, and imbalanced-label-shift settings with ResNet and ViT backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MASA, a WTTA method that leverages a frozen multimodal LLM to provide semantic anchors for more reliable online adaptation under distribution shift and class imbalance.
AI.motivation: Existing wild test-time adaptation methods rely solely on signals derived from the model itself (e.g., uncertainty, feature geometry). When the source model is unreliable under distribution shift, these self-derived signals can reinforce incorrect predictions, creating a harmful self-referential loop. There is a need for external, robust semantic guidance that can stabilize adaptation in the presence of concurrent shifts and time-varying class imbalance, while keeping inference cost manageable.
AI.method: MASA (Multimodal-LLM-Anchored Semantic Adaptation) augments internal model evidence with structured semantic descriptions produced by a frozen multimodal LLM (MLLM). During WTTA, MASA selects a small set of diverse, high-reliability test samples as anchors and queries the MLLM for detailed descriptions that capture both object category families and nuisance factors (style, viewpoint, occlusion). These text descriptions are encoded and propagated to nearby test samples in feature space, and the combined visual-semantic representations are stored in an online prototype memory. For each new test input, MASA retrieves relevant prototypes conditioned on the descriptors and uses them as auxiliary supervision targets to adapt only lightweight components of the model, specifically normalization-affine parameters, in an online fashion.
AI.result: On the WTTA ImageNet-C benchmark, MASA is evaluated with both ResNet and ViT backbones under challenging conditions: limited batch size, mixed-domain corruption, and imbalanced label shift. The approach shows improved test-time performance compared with standard WTTA baselines that rely purely on internal signals, indicating that multimodal LLM guidance can enhance robustness and stability of adaptation in wild test-time settings.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structured semantic information from a frozen multimodal LLM into wild test-time adaptation provides a reliable external anchor that mitigates the self-referential failure modes of existing approaches. By querying the LLM only for a small set of reliability-ranked anchors and propagating their semantic descriptions via an online prototype memory, MASA achieves more robust and cost-effective adaptation of normalization parameters across dynamic and imbalanced distribution shifts.

title: Reduplicative constructions in Mandarin: Socio-emotional profiling through distributional semantics
summary: Mandarin Chinese has two productive reduplicative constructions that repeat either two-character base words or their constituents (e.g., `in good health', `discuss a bit'). Their varied meanings have been described as realizing plurality, valence coloring, sound symbolism and pragmatic functions. The aim of this study is twofold. A first goal is to clarify whether it is possible to come to a more precise understanding of the variegated semantics of Mandarin reduplication by using word embeddings from distributional semantics. A second goal is to explore how useful embeddings are for understanding the details of a semantically complex word-formation process. We show that the embedding space recovers the semantic and grammatical properties of reduplications previously identified in the literature, validating Tencent embeddings for morphological investigation. Semantic profiling revealed that reduplicative constructions are often strongly represented on multiple dimensions. The two patterns exhibit clear semantic and pragmatic differentiation in distributional space. Procrustes analysis clarified that the overall organization of the base-word space is largely preserved in the reduplication space, with local mismatches highlighting regions of discourse-pragmatic reorganization. Taken together, these results show that high-dimensional word embeddings can recover established linguistic generalizations, and capture the semantic versatility of Mandarin reduplication and constructional transparency.

AI.tldr: Study uses word embeddings to analyze Mandarin Chinese reduplicative constructions, showing embeddings capture their complex semantic and pragmatic patterns.
AI.motivation: Mandarin reduplication is semantically and pragmatically rich, linked to plurality, valence nuances, sound symbolism, and discourse functions. Traditional descriptions list these functions but struggle to unify them or measure fine-grained semantic differences between patterns. The authors want to see whether modern distributional semantics—specifically high-dimensional word embeddings—can provide a more precise, empirical characterization of the semantic space of reduplication, and whether such tools are suitable for studying complex word-formation processes.
AI.method: The authors analyze two productive reduplicative patterns in Mandarin: one repeating entire disyllabic base words and one repeating their constituents. They represent base words and their reduplicated forms in a large pre-trained Tencent word embedding space. They then: (i) test whether embeddings distinguish reduplicative constructions along known semantic and grammatical dimensions; (ii) perform semantic profiling to see on which dimensions each construction is strongly represented; and (iii) use Procrustes analysis to compare the geometries of the embedding subspaces for base forms vs. their reduplications, identifying global similarities and local mismatches that signal semantic/pragmatic reorganization.
AI.result: The embedding space recovers many semantic and grammatical contrasts among reduplicative constructions that were previously reported in the linguistic literature, supporting the validity of Tencent embeddings for morphological research. Semantic profiling shows that individual reduplicative constructions often load heavily on multiple semantic/pragmatic dimensions rather than a single function, confirming their semantic versatility. The two main reduplicative patterns occupy distinct regions and show clear semantic and pragmatic differentiation in the distributional space. Procrustes analysis demonstrates that the overall structure of meanings is largely preserved from base words to reduplications, but with specific areas where meanings are reorganized, corresponding to discourse-pragmatic shifts.
AI.conclusion: High-dimensional word embeddings are capable of recovering established generalizations about Mandarin reduplication and of revealing nuanced semantic and pragmatic structure in this word-formation pattern. The overall geometry of meaning from base words is maintained in reduplicated forms, while local deviations highlight construction-specific pragmatic effects. This supports the use of distributional semantics as a tool for investigating complex, semantically rich morphological and constructional phenomena, and shows that Mandarin reduplication is both semantically versatile and largely transparent in how it builds on base-word meanings.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Hierarchical Intention Anticipation in Human Behavior
summary: Assistive autonomous systems must anticipate human goals before an observed behavior is complete. This article formulates anticipation as goal inference from a partially observed multimodal episode together with structured prediction of the remaining behavior, rather than exact motor forecasting. A compact Hierarchical Planning Decoder (HPD) is attached to a frozen neuro-symbolic recognition encoder and predicts, at four ontological levels, the next actions, the remaining activities and low-level intentions, and the episode high-level intention(HLI). The decoder is trained with soft neuro-symbolic regularization combining transition-coherence and hierarchical continuity losses, and is decoded with hard reachability masks that enforce ontological validity at inference. On a compositional four-level benchmark of 15,002 multimodal episodes built over NTU RGB+D 120 features, three headline properties are observed together. The advantage over the strongest sequential baseline grows with the anticipation horizon, from +1.7 points at step 1 to +7.3 points at step 3 (top-5). Under compositional generalization, where one parent association per multi-parent low level intention is held out, this advantage widens to +4.9 points at step 1. At the episode level, 96.8% of anticipated trajectories satisfy the joint logic constraints, above the 88.1% strongest-baseline value and the 73.9% ground-truth floor; soft logic terms alone account for a 59.8 to 71.1% relative reduction of HLI-reachability violations, and the hard masks then eliminate them entirely. Neural generation supplies predictive ranking, symbolic constraints supply onto logical validity, and their combination yields coherent hierarchical anticipation while exposing remaining challenges in compositional goal generalization and unordered set prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic hierarchical planning decoder to anticipate human goals and future actions from partially observed multimodal behavior, improving long-horizon and compositional generalization over strong baselines while enforcing logical consistency.
AI.motivation: Assistive autonomous systems (e.g., robots, smart environments) must understand and anticipate human goals early, before an action sequence is completed, to respond helpfully and safely. Existing work often focuses on low-level motor prediction or sequential models that lack explicit structure, struggle with long-horizon anticipation, and may produce logically inconsistent or invalid plans. There is a need for models that jointly infer high-level intentions and future behavior in a logically coherent, hierarchically structured way, while generalizing compositionally to new goal-intention combinations.
AI.method: The authors design a Hierarchical Planning Decoder (HPD) on top of a frozen neuro-symbolic recognition encoder. HPD predicts at four hierarchical levels: next actions, remaining activities, low-level intentions, and a high-level episode intention (HLI). Training uses soft neuro-symbolic regularization with two key loss components: transition-coherence (encouraging plausible temporal transitions) and hierarchical continuity (encouraging consistency across the four levels of the ontology). At inference, they apply hard reachability masks derived from the symbolic ontology to restrict predictions to logically valid, reachable states. They evaluate the method on a new four-level compositional benchmark of 15,002 multimodal episodes, built from NTU RGB+D 120 features, and compare against strong sequential baselines under varying anticipation horizons and compositional generalization setups.
AI.result: HPD outperforms the strongest sequential baseline, with performance gains that increase as the prediction horizon grows: from +1.7 points at step 1 to +7.3 points at step 3 in top-5 accuracy. Under compositional generalization, where certain parent-child intention associations are held out during training, the advantage at step 1 increases to +4.9 points. Regarding logical consistency, 96.8% of HPD’s anticipated trajectories satisfy all joint logical constraints, compared to 88.1% for the strongest baseline and 73.9% for the ground-truth data used to build the benchmark. The soft logic regularizers alone reduce HLI-reachability violations by 59.8–71.1% relative; adding hard masks removes HLI-reachability violations entirely.
AI.conclusion: Integrating neural sequence prediction with symbolic hierarchical planning yields better long-horizon and compositional anticipation of human goals and behaviors, while strongly enforcing logical and ontological consistency. Neural components contribute strong predictive ranking, symbolic constraints guarantee logical validity via soft losses and hard masks, and their combination enables coherent hierarchical anticipation. Nonetheless, remaining issues in compositional goal generalization and unordered set prediction highlight areas for future work and further refinement of the neuro-symbolic framework.

title: Cascade: Hierarchical Recoverability Control for Large Language Model Unlearning
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or copyrighted knowledge while preserving general utility. Existing methods often leave residual knowledge in intermediate representations, which can still be recovered. To address this, we propose Cascade, a hierarchical recoverability control framework that minimizes the internal identifiability of target knowledge. Cascade combines three complementary controls: path-level routing to suppress privacy-associated activation routes, representation-level compression to reduce geometric separability, and decoding-level intervention to limit residual recovery. Experiments on TOFU, MUSE-News, and WMDP, including robustness tests with query reformulation and extraction-style prompts, show that Cascade effectively reduces recoverability while maintaining stable model utility.

AI.tldr: Proposes Cascade, a framework to make unwanted knowledge in LLMs hard to recover at every stage of processing, while keeping overall model utility.
AI.motivation: LLMs often memorize sensitive or copyrighted information. Current unlearning methods mainly adjust outputs but leave traces of the target knowledge in internal activations, from which the knowledge can still be extracted. There is a need for an unlearning approach that controls recoverability of the target knowledge throughout the entire forward pass, not just at the final output.
AI.method: Introduce Cascade, a hierarchical recoverability control framework with three layers: (1) path-level routing, which suppresses or reroutes activation paths associated with private or target knowledge; (2) representation-level compression, which modifies hidden representations so that target vs. non-target knowledge is less geometrically separable (harder to linearly identify); and (3) decoding-level intervention, which constrains or modifies the final decoding step so that any residual target information in representations is difficult to decode into explicit text. The method is evaluated as an add-on unlearning mechanism for LLMs.
AI.result: On benchmarks TOFU, MUSE-News, and WMDP, Cascade significantly reduces the ability to recover the targeted knowledge, even when using adversarial style prompts such as query reformulations and extraction-oriented prompts. At the same time, the model’s overall performance on general tasks (utility) remains largely unchanged, indicating that unlearning is effective without heavy degradation of capabilities.
AI.conclusion: A multi-level, hierarchical control of information flow inside LLMs can more effectively unlearn sensitive or copyrighted knowledge than single-stage methods. By limiting recoverability at path, representation, and decoding levels, Cascade reduces internal identifiability of target knowledge while preserving overall utility, and remains robust against common attack strategies aimed at re-extracting removed information.

title: Sample-Conditioned Representation Selection for Audio Few-Shot Learning
summary: Few-shot audio classifiers may rely on foreground-background co-occurrences and fail when those correlations shift. On SpurAudio, the resulting representation shift is concentrated and class dependent: for ResNet12, the top 10 percent of channels explain 82.80 percent of the null-corrected shift contribution. We propose SAMPLESELECT, which predicts a fixed-budget feature mask independently for each input while keeping the encoder and source classifier frozen. Training uses differentiable Gumbel Top-k selection with foreground classification and cross-background contrastive losses; inference uses deterministic Top-k masks and support-only linear adaptation. Across ResNet12 and Conv64 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot evaluation, SAMPLESELECT gives the best OOD accuracy among the compared methods and improves the matched full-representation control by 4.90-8.38 percentage points. Ablations and representation analyses further support the learned selection mechanism. Code is available at https://github.com/Cross-Innovation-Lab/SAMPLESELECT/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAMPLESELECT, a method that selects a small subset of encoder features per input to improve few-shot audio classification robustness to spurious foreground-background correlations and distribution shifts, achieving better OOD accuracy than baselines.
AI.motivation: Few-shot audio classifiers can overfit to spurious correlations between foreground sounds and background context. When the foreground-background relationship changes at test time, performance degrades due to concentrated, class-dependent shifts in a small subset of representation channels. There is a need for methods that mitigate this reliance on spurious features without retraining large encoders or source classifiers.
AI.method: The authors analyze representation shift on the SpurAudio benchmark and find that a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the harmful, class-dependent shift. They propose SAMPLESELECT, a module that learns to output a fixed-budget feature (channel) mask for each input while keeping the backbone encoder and source classifier frozen. Training uses a differentiable Gumbel Top-k selection mechanism, supervised by two losses: a foreground classification loss to maintain task performance and a cross-background contrastive loss to encourage robustness to changing backgrounds. At inference, SAMPLESELECT uses deterministic Top-k masks and performs support-only linear adaptation for few-shot classification.
AI.result: On the SpurAudio benchmark with 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot tasks, evaluated on ResNet12 and Conv64 backbones, SAMPLESELECT achieves the highest out-of-distribution accuracy compared with alternative methods. It outperforms a matched control that uses the full representation by 4.90–8.38 percentage points. Analyses of representation shifts and ablation studies support that the learned feature selection mechanism is responsible for the robustness gains.
AI.conclusion: Concentrated, class-dependent representation shifts in few-shot audio models stem from a small subset of channels tied to spurious foreground-background correlations. SAMPLESELECT effectively mitigates these issues by learning per-sample feature masks on top of frozen encoders and classifiers, improving OOD robustness and few-shot performance. The empirical gains and supporting analyses indicate that judicious feature selection is a promising direction for robust few-shot audio classification.

title: RiskChainBench: A Benchmark for Obfuscated Platform Message Restoration and Evidence-Grounded Web Investigation
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures; 17-page supplementary material included as an ancillary PDF
summary: Platform abuse campaigns conceal redirection instructions with emojis, homophones, character decomposition, and redundant symbols, then route users through disguised links to services associated with pornography, fraud, gambling, or illicit transactions. Existing benchmarks evaluate obfuscated text and risky webpages separately, obscuring how target recovery affects downstream evidence acquisition. We introduce RiskChainBench, pairing 3,600 synthetic token-text restoration inputs from 600 source sessions with 600 corresponding human-labeled local web environments. A model first restores the message, operational intent, and destination; the same underlying model then acts as a VLM-driven web agent that investigates the correctly associated website and produces a frozen, evidence-cited risk report without message-side semantics or domain-reputation cues. We score restoration and correct-routing web investigation separately and compose them offline by applying the frozen primary-entry prediction as a gate to the same Task 2 result. Human labels determine task correctness, while a fixed multimodal evidence judge assesses faithfulness, sufficiency, completeness, and consistency. Across ten models, Entry Top-1 ranges from 35.2% to 95.2% and web decision accuracy from 26.3% to 62.8%; the leading systems differ across entry recovery, full reconstruction, website decisions, and fine-grained typing. Execution failures account for 31.9% of web runs, whereas post-decision type errors account for only 0.9%, identifying stable exploration and risk judgment as the principal bottlenecks. We release the benchmark, protocol, and resettable local sandbox.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RiskChainBench, a benchmark that evaluates how well models can first deobfuscate risky messages and then investigate the correctly linked websites to generate evidence-based risk reports in a controlled local web environment.
AI.motivation: Platform abuse campaigns increasingly hide malicious or policy-violating intent using obfuscated text and multi-hop link redirections, but existing benchmarks test text deobfuscation and risky webpage understanding separately. This separation makes it unclear how errors in recovering the intended destination and intent affect subsequent web-based risk assessment, and it does not reflect real-world abuse chains that span messages and websites. The authors want a unified, realistic evaluation of the full chain from obfuscated message to web evidence–backed risk judgment.
AI.method: The authors build RiskChainBench, consisting of 600 source sessions that generate 3,600 synthetic token-text restoration inputs (for deobfuscation) and 600 paired, human-labeled local web environments that simulate the ultimate landing sites. A model is evaluated in two chained stages using the same base system: (1) it must restore the original message, intended operational goal, and destination (Entry and Reconstruction); (2) acting as a vision-language model web agent, it navigates the corresponding sandboxed website and produces a frozen, evidence-cited risk report without relying on the original message semantics or external reputation signals. The benchmark scores the text restoration and the web investigation separately, then composes them offline by gating Task 2 outcomes with the correctness of Task 1. Human annotators provide ground truth task labels, and a fixed multimodal “evidence judge” model evaluates the faithfulness, sufficiency, completeness, and consistency of the agent’s reports. The authors run ten different models through this protocol.
AI.result: Across ten evaluated models, Entry Top-1 accuracy (correctly recovering the primary destination/entry) ranges from 35.2% to 95.2%, while web decision accuracy (correctly judging the risk from the website) ranges from 26.3% to 62.8%. The best-performing systems are not the same across subtasks: some excel at entry recovery, others at full reconstruction, others at website-level decisions or detailed risk typing. Execution failures in the web-agent phase are common, accounting for 31.9% of runs, while errors after reaching a decision but misclassifying the type are rare (0.9%). This pattern suggests technical difficulties in robust web exploration and evidence gathering, rather than semantic judgment, dominate failure rates.
AI.conclusion: RiskChainBench provides an end-to-end benchmark for abuse chains that span obfuscated messages and risky web content, enabling separate and combined evaluation of text restoration and web-based risk assessment. Current models exhibit substantial gaps in both correctly resolving obfuscated destinations and reliably exploring and judging websites, with web execution robustness emerging as the main bottleneck. By releasing the dataset, standardized protocol, and resettable local sandbox, the authors aim to support more realistic, evidence-grounded evaluation and improvement of AI systems tasked with detecting and analyzing online risk campaigns.

title: Interactive Memory Learning for Long-Term Conversations
summary: Recent advancements in large language models have significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents in modeling long-term conversations. Despite these successes, existing approaches typically adopt a static heuristic paradigm, where information is passively archived without adaptive memory valuation. Consequently, these methods fail to self-evolve or align their memory management with evolving user needs. To address this, we propose ICML (InteraCtive Memory Learning), a multi-agent framework that transforms the memory mechanism from a passive archive into a learnable, interactive memory policy. Specifically, we first employ a session synthesis pipeline to generate expert data, facilitating rapid test-time adaptation in unseen scenarios. Building on this, ICML utilizes an online reinforcement learning mechanism where a Planner agent selectively encodes high-value information and a Trigger agent dynamically retrieves it to optimize response quality, whereby the two agents co-evolve through continuous interaction feedback. Crucially, both agents are synchronized through a delayed reward mechanism that propagates future feedback back to earlier storage decisions, ensuring memory policies are precisely aligned with user expectations. Experimental results demonstrate that ICML significantly outperforms strong baselines, exhibiting the unique capability to continuously improve response quality as interactions accumulate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ICML, a multi-agent interactive memory-learning framework that turns static LLM memory into a learnable policy using online reinforcement learning to continually improve multi-turn conversation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based conversational agents usually treat memory as a static, heuristic archive—storing and retrieving information via hand-crafted rules or simple recency/importance scores. This passive design cannot adapt to changing user preferences, cannot self-improve over time, and often stores or retrieves suboptimal information, limiting long-term dialogue quality. The authors aim to build a memory mechanism that actively learns what to store and when to retrieve it, aligning memory management with evolving user needs and long-horizon conversational goals.
AI.method: The authors propose ICML (InteraCtive Memory Learning), a multi-agent framework with two key agents: (1) a Planner that learns a policy for selectively encoding high-value information into memory, and (2) a Trigger that learns when and what to retrieve from memory to support current responses. They first construct a session synthesis pipeline to generate expert trajectories (storage and retrieval decisions) that enable fast test-time adaptation in unseen scenarios. On top of this, they apply online reinforcement learning during real interactions, where both agents receive delayed rewards based on the eventual quality of responses. A delayed reward mechanism propagates feedback from future turns back to earlier storage and retrieval actions, allowing the Planner and Trigger policies to co-evolve and remain synchronized with user expectations.
AI.result: In experiments, ICML is compared against strong baselines that use traditional static or heuristic memory mechanisms. ICML consistently achieves higher response quality metrics in long-term conversational settings and displays a notable property: its performance continues to improve as more interactions accumulate, indicating effective online adaptation and learning of memory policies.
AI.conclusion: Transforming memory from a passive archival component into an actively learned and interactively optimized policy substantially improves long-term conversational performance of LLM agents. Through a multi-agent RL framework with synthesized expert data and delayed-reward credit assignment, ICML enables memory policies that adapt over time and align closely with user expectations, outperforming static baselines and demonstrating continual improvement as dialogues progress.

title: Deconstructing Stereotypes: Scope-Conditioned Generation for Effective Multilingual Counterspeech
summary: Counterspeech (CS) - direct responses that counter online Hate Speech (HS) using reasoning and alternative viewpoints - has emerged as an alternative to content removal. Current automatic CS generation methods, however, frequently produce generic, ineffective replies that fail to target the implicit stereotypes behind HS. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel scope-conditioned generation framework that explicitly integrates structured stereotype characteristics into Large Language Models prompts. We validate our approach on a novel, human-curated dataset annotated in English, Italian, and Spanish. Extensive evaluations show that stereotype-conditioned prompting substantially outperforms generic baselines across all three languages, obtaining significant gains in factuality, specificity, cogency, and effectiveness for both explicit and implicit implied stereotypes.

AI.tldr: Authors propose a scope-conditioned generation framework to improve automatic counterspeech (CS) against online hate speech (HS) by incorporating structured stereotype characteristics into LLM prompts, achieving more factual, specific, and effective responses in English, Italian, and Spanish.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic counterspeech systems tend to generate generic, low-impact responses that do not directly address or dismantle the underlying explicit or implicit stereotypes present in hate speech. There is a need for methods that can generate targeted, context-aware counterspeech that is both effective and adaptable across multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors design a scope-conditioned generation framework for large language models in which prompts are explicitly enriched with structured information about the stereotypes present in the hate speech. They build a new, human-curated multilingual dataset (English, Italian, Spanish) where instances of hate speech are annotated with stereotype characteristics, and use this dataset to train and evaluate the framework against standard, unconditioned baselines.
AI.result: Across all three languages and for both explicit and implicit stereotypes, the stereotype-conditioned prompting method substantially outperforms generic prompting baselines. The gains are significant on multiple evaluation dimensions, including factuality, specificity, logical coherence (cogency), and overall effectiveness of generated counterspeech.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structured stereotype information into LLM prompts via scope-conditioned generation leads to more targeted, factual, and persuasive counterspeech than generic approaches. This framework shows promise as a multilingual, stereotype-aware solution for generating effective responses to online hate speech, improving performance across key quality dimensions and handling both explicit and implicit stereotypes.

title: Scaling-Score Conformal Prediction for Multi-Target Regression
summary: Multi-target regression requires a model to simultaneously predict several related outputs. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free, finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees, but extending these to joint multi-dimensional regions in a model-agnostic, sample-efficient manner remains challenging: max-aggregation ignores scale differences, copula-based methods are only asymptotically valid, rectangular methods typically split the calibration set, and quantile or density-based methods require training a specialised model beyond a plain point predictor. We propose the scaling-score conformal method, which is model-agnostic (requires only component-wise absolute residuals), uses a single calibration set, and yields four nested output types: an outer rectangle (SCO) with valid joint coverage, the exact set R $α$ , a staircase (SC 2 ) over approximation of R $α$ , and an inner rectangle (SCI). A single hyperparameter $γ$ $\in$ (0, 1) controls the base-rectangle quantile level independently of $α$. We prove downward-closedness and a rectangular sandwich bound and derive a closed-form outer rectangle. Experiments on 29 realworld datasets confirm valid joint coverage; SC 2 with $γ$ = 1-$α$ consistently achieves competitive volume relative to baselines, with the advantage growing with output dimension d.

AI.tldr: A new model-agnostic conformal prediction method for multi-target regression that produces valid joint prediction sets with good volume efficiency.
AI.motivation: Multi-target regression needs joint prediction regions for several outputs, but existing conformal methods for the multi-dimensional case either lose efficiency, require strong assumptions, split data, or need specialised models beyond standard point predictors. There is a need for a simple, sample-efficient, model-agnostic approach that gives valid joint coverage with flexible region shapes.
AI.method: Introduce the scaling-score conformal method that only uses component-wise absolute residuals from any base predictor. It uses a single calibration set and a scaling-score mechanism controlled by a hyperparameter γ∈(0,1), which sets a base-rectangle quantile level independently of the desired coverage α. The method constructs four nested region types: an outer rectangle (SCO) with provable joint coverage, the exact conformal region R_α, a staircase-shaped over-approximation SC2 of R_α, and an inner rectangle SCI. The authors prove properties like downward-closedness of the set and a rectangular sandwich bound between inner and outer rectangles, and derive a closed-form expression for the outer rectangle.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that the proposed regions are nested, downward-closed, and that the outer rectangle provides finite-sample valid joint coverage. Empirically, on 29 real-world datasets, all methods maintain valid joint coverage. Among them, the staircase approximation SC2 with γ=1−α consistently attains competitive or superior volume efficiency compared to baseline methods, and its advantage increases as the output dimension d grows.
AI.conclusion: Scaling-score conformal prediction provides a practical, model-agnostic way to obtain valid joint prediction regions in multi-target regression using only standard residuals and one calibration set. It offers a spectrum of nested set shapes balancing simplicity and tightness, with strong finite-sample guarantees and empirically competitive volume, particularly in higher-dimensional output spaces.

title: Lit3R: Retrieve-Relate-Read for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering over Scientific Literature
comment: Accepted at GroundLM 2026, an EMNLP 2026 Workshop LittraceQA
