summary: We describe tus-nlp's Lit3R (Retrieve-Relate-Read) system for LitTraceQA, a shared task for literature-grounded question answering that requires systems to retrieve relevant papers, identify supporting evidence, and generate answers. Lit3R combines off-the-shelf retrieval, reranking, and large language model (LLM) components without task-specific training. The retriever iteratively combines BM25-based sparse and dense retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and LLM-based verification, and complements retrieval based on the question with paper-to-paper expansion. The reader first identifies supporting evidence within individual papers and then synthesizes evidence across papers to produce the final answer and evidence trace. On the official test set, our system ranked 4th on the leaderboard. Our code is available at https://github.com/tus-ist-nlp/littraceqa.

AI.tldr: Lit3R is a Retrieve-Relate-Read pipeline for literature-grounded QA that uses standard retrieval, reranking, and LLM components without task-specific training, achieving 4th place on the LitTraceQA leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Literature-grounded QA requires not only answering questions but also finding and citing supporting evidence across scientific papers. Existing systems often need task-specific training or struggle to both retrieve and justify answers effectively. The authors aim to build a strong, training-free pipeline that can robustly retrieve relevant papers, identify evidence, and produce answers plus evidence traces for the LitTraceQA shared task.
AI.method: Lit3R is a multi-stage pipeline. For retrieval, it iteratively combines BM25 sparse retrieval, dense retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and LLM-based verification, and augments question-based retrieval with paper-to-paper expansion to discover additional relevant articles. For reading, an LLM first extracts supporting evidence spans within each paper, then synthesizes these pieces of evidence across multiple papers to generate the final answer along with an explicit evidence trace. The system relies on off-the-shelf models and prompts, without fine-tuning for the specific task.
AI.result: On the official LitTraceQA test set, the Lit3R system achieved 4th place on the leaderboard, indicating competitive performance against other participating systems in terms of answer quality and evidence grounding.
AI.conclusion: A carefully designed, modular Retrieve-Relate-Read pipeline using off-the-shelf retrievers, rerankers, and LLMs—without task-specific training—can perform competitively on literature-grounded QA tasks like LitTraceQA. Iterative hybrid retrieval, LLM-based verification, and cross-paper evidence synthesis are effective design choices, and the released codebase can serve as a baseline or building block for future work.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning-Based Genetic Biomarkers Dataset for Multiple-Stage Hepatocellular Carcinoma Prediction
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, published at the 18th International Conference Series on Developments in eSystems Engineering
summary: Liver cancer is a complex disease responsible for a high number of deaths across the globe each year, making automated solutions for liver cancer classification urgent. The most common form of liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for over 90% of liver cancer cases. There is a distinct lack of publicly available HCC datasets utilizing genomic data, which is necessary for training artificial intelligence (AI) models for automated HCC classification. This study proposes constructing a multi-stage HCC dataset using XGBoost and Semi-Supervised learning on three separate datasets of genomic biomarkers, utilizing their existing labels in the Semi-Supervised learning process to label the proposed dataset. The proposed dataset consists of 770 patient samples in total, categorized into five classes that represent normal tissue alongside different stages of HCC. Each sample in the dataset consists of 11,150 different gene expression levels. The XGBoost model demonstrated a final classification accuracy of 96.5% during the Semi-Supervised learning process.

AI.tldr: They build and label a multi-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) genomic dataset using semi-supervised learning with XGBoost, achieving 96.5% accuracy.
AI.motivation: There is a high global mortality rate from liver cancer, especially hepatocellular carcinoma, but a notable lack of publicly available genomic datasets that cover different HCC stages for training AI classification models. This data gap limits progress in automated HCC diagnosis and staging.
AI.method: They aggregate three separate genomic biomarker datasets and apply a semi-supervised learning framework built around XGBoost. Existing labels in the source datasets guide the semi-supervised labeling of a new, unified multi-stage HCC dataset. Each sample includes 11,150 gene expression features, and XGBoost is used iteratively to assign labels and evaluate classification performance.
AI.result: They construct a new dataset of 770 patient samples divided into five classes (normal tissue plus four HCC stages), each represented by 11,150 gene expression levels. During the semi-supervised labeling process, the XGBoost classifier attains a final accuracy of 96.5%.
AI.conclusion: A high-dimensional, multi-stage HCC genomic dataset can be reliably assembled and labeled via semi-supervised learning with XGBoost, potentially enabling more effective training of AI models for automated liver cancer classification and staging. The reported accuracy suggests the approach is promising for generating useful labeled resources when curated datasets are scarce.

title: HUMAID-NER: A Disaster Tweet Dataset for Joint Named Entity Recognition and Event Classification via Uncertainty-Weighted Multitask Learning
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Published in The Asian Bulletin of Big Data Management, Vol. 6, No. 1, pp. 138-152, 2026
summary: Rapid extraction of structured information from social media is important for humanitarian response, yet existing disaster tweet resources mainly provide document-level category labels without span-level entity annotations. We introduce HUMAID-NER, the first named entity recognition dataset built on the HumAID benchmark, containing 60,000 English disaster tweets annotated in BIO format across ten operationally motivated entity types and yielding approximately 175,000 labelled entity spans. Annotations are generated through a reproducible three-stage hybrid pipeline combining a spaCy transformer model, disaster-domain EntityRuler patterns, and structured regular expressions with priority-based overlap resolution. We also propose a joint multitask learning framework that performs disaster-specific named entity recognition and humanitarian event classification using a shared RoBERTa-large encoder. To reduce task conflict during joint training, the model uses homoscedastic uncertainty weighting with learnable task parameters and a two-stage training schedule that freezes the lower 18 of 24 encoder layers in the second stage. On the HUMAID-NER validation set, the proposed system achieves NER span micro-F1 of 0.841 and classification macro-F1 of 0.761 simultaneously. A real-time web dashboard demonstrates end-to-end deployment. The dataset, models, and pipeline code are released to support reproducibility and future crisis informatics research.

AI.tldr: Introduces HUMAID-NER, a large NER dataset and multitask model for extracting structured disaster-related information from tweets, enabling simultaneous entity recognition and humanitarian event classification for crisis response.
AI.motivation: Humanitarian responders need fine-grained, structured information (who, what, where, needs, damage, etc.) from social media during disasters, but existing datasets mostly provide only coarse document-level labels and lack span-level entity annotations tailored to operational needs. This limits the development of NER models that can support real-time situational awareness and decision-making in crises.
AI.method: The authors build HUMAID-NER by annotating 60,000 English disaster tweets from the HumAID benchmark with BIO-format labels for ten operational entity types, resulting in ~175k entity spans. Annotations are created via a three-stage hybrid automatic pipeline that combines: (1) a spaCy transformer-based NER model; (2) disaster-specific pattern rules via EntityRuler; and (3) structured regular expressions, with a priority-based scheme to resolve overlapping spans. They then propose a joint multitask framework that uses a shared RoBERTa-large encoder to perform both disaster-specific NER and humanitarian event classification. To handle negative transfer between tasks, they apply homoscedastic uncertainty-based loss weighting with learnable task-specific parameters and a two-stage training schedule where, in the second stage, the lower 18 of 24 encoder layers are frozen.
AI.result: On the HUMAID-NER validation set, their multitask RoBERTa-large model achieves a span-level NER micro-F1 of 0.841 and a humanitarian event classification macro-F1 of 0.761 simultaneously. They also operationalize the system in a real-time web dashboard and release the dataset, models, and code.
AI.conclusion: HUMAID-NER fills a key gap in crisis informatics by providing the first large-scale, disaster-focused NER dataset on HumAID, along with a strong multitask baseline model that jointly handles entity extraction and event classification. The hybrid annotation pipeline is reproducible, and the publicly released resources support further research and deployment of systems for real-time, structured analysis of disaster-related tweets to aid humanitarian response.

title: Symbolic Separation: Grounding Deep Agents in Knowledge Graphs for Trustworthy Operational Data Analytics
summary: Generative AI promises natural language access to the massive numerical telemetry of data centers and Industry 4.0 installations, yet text-to-query and tool-using agents stay unreliable: even frontier models answer little more than half of real-world database questions, and far fewer of the multi-step, operational ones, because the LLM must compose how heterogeneous sources relate and hallucinates the relations, not just the fields. We propose symbolic separation: a deep agent reasons freely but may act on data only through an ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graph with deterministic pre-execution validation. Unlike a tool API's interface contract, this domain-semantic contract turns a complex question into one validated graph traversal instead of LLM-inferred joins. Instantiated as the Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst and evaluated on 49.9 TB of superconputer telemetry against a rigid workflow and a non-symbolic ablation, it raises end-to-end task success from 43% to 86%, prevents silent data-integrity errors that no syntactic check catches, and cuts token cost by 2.4x, letting a smaller on-premise model outperform a larger one.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a neurosymbolic agent that constrains LLM access to data via an ontology-backed virtual knowledge graph, dramatically improving reliability and cost for complex telemetry analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-SQL and tool-using LLM agents are unreliable for real-world, multi-step, operational queries over heterogeneous telemetry. They often hallucinate relationships between data sources, not just field names, leading to wrong joins, low task success, and undetectable data-integrity errors in data center and Industry 4.0 environments.
AI.method: The authors propose "symbolic separation": an LLM-based deep agent that can reason in natural language but can only interact with data through an ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graph (VKG). The VKG enforces a domain-semantic contract and performs deterministic pre-execution validation of queries. Complex questions are mapped to validated graph traversals rather than LLM-inferred joins. This is instantiated in a system called the Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst and compared against a non-symbolic baseline.
AI.result: On 49.9 TB of supercomputer telemetry and under a strict workflow, the Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst doubles end-to-end task success from 43% to 86%, eliminates silent data-integrity errors that bypass syntactic checks, and reduces token costs by a factor of 2.4. It also allows a smaller on-premise model to outperform a larger one under these constraints.
AI.conclusion: Confining LLM data access to an ontology-constrained virtual knowledge graph with deterministic validation significantly boosts reliability, correctness, and efficiency for complex telemetry analytics. Neurosymbolic integration is a practical path to making generative AI agents trustworthy and cost-effective in real industrial and data-center monitoring settings.

title: Target-Language Generation in Multilingual Models: Activation Steering and Optimal Control
summary: Ensuring that multilingual language models generate coherent text in a specific target language is a major issue in multilingual language modeling. We develop an optimal control method for target-language text generation as well as a framework for evaluating the quality of generated text in terms of language adherence, linguistic coherence, and semantic coherence. We find that the proposed method performs at least as well as the prominent difference-in-means activation steering method for the majority of models tested, with substantially less hyperparameter tuning required.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an optimal-control-based method to steer multilingual language models so they generate text in a desired target language, and introduces an evaluation framework for language adherence, linguistic coherence, and semantic coherence, finding the method competitive with activation steering while needing less tuning.
AI.motivation: Multilingual language models often drift away from the desired target language or mix languages, harming usability and reliability. Existing steering methods (e.g., activation steering via difference-in-means) can help but tend to require substantial, brittle hyperparameter tuning and lack a comprehensive evaluation of how well generated text stays in the target language while remaining coherent and semantically faithful. The paper aims to provide a more principled control approach and a better evaluation framework for target-language generation quality.
AI.method: The authors formulate target-language text generation as an optimal control problem on the hidden representations or outputs of multilingual language models, designing a control signal that nudges generation toward the desired language while preserving meaning and fluency. They also construct an evaluation framework that separately measures (1) language adherence (sticking to the target language), (2) linguistic coherence (grammaticality and fluency in that language), and (3) semantic coherence (consistency of meaning with prompts or source content). They compare their method empirically to a difference-in-means activation steering baseline across multiple models, examining performance and tuning requirements.
AI.result: Across most tested multilingual models, the optimal-control steering method matches or outperforms the difference-in-means activation steering approach on language adherence, linguistic coherence, and semantic coherence. Importantly, it achieves these results with substantially fewer hyperparameter sweeps and with more stable behavior across settings, indicating a more robust control mechanism for enforcing target-language generation.
AI.conclusion: Optimal-control-based steering is a competitive and often superior alternative to standard activation steering for enforcing target-language generation in multilingual language models. Combined with a structured evaluation framework, it offers a more principled and less tuning-intensive way to ensure that generated text remains in the desired language, is linguistically well-formed, and stays semantically coherent with the intended content.

title: Shared-Prefix KV Reuse Across Standard LoRA Adapters: Quality and Serving Tradeoffs
summary: A common small-model deployment runs one shared backbone with several LoRA specialists that answer over the same context. Serving them naively re-prefills that shared context once per specialist. We study a narrow, practical question: for already-trained standard LoRA adapters -- not adapters retrained for cache compatibility -- how much task quality is preserved if the backbone's prefill KV cache is computed once and reused across specialists, and what does that buy in serving cost? On a Qwen3-1.7B backbone with two adapters (extractive QA on HotpotQA, arithmetic reasoning on GSM8K), we sweep the boundary at which the specialist takes over from the reused base cache and measure paired quality differences and serving cost. Full-prefix reuse had the lowest prefill cost and a small quality difference on held-out GSM8K (Delta = -4.6 EM at a 160-token budget; -3.0 at 320 tokens; -0.8 under a second training seed -- all favoring native, only the first excluding zero, and the magnitude not consistent). Partial recomputation provided no demonstrated advantage. Neither quality equivalence nor a general boundary-selection rule is established. We also report a closed-form ridge KV translator that did not beat direct reuse, and specialist-dependence contrasts whose intervals all include zero. The measured serving benefit is warm-cache time-to-first-token, which grows with context (~16x at 8K); two-branch peak memory was only 12% lower and, on inspection, the prefix was never physically shared across branches -- this implementation reuses KV values but copies their storage, so shared-cache memory savings are not achieved.

AI.tldr: Study of reusing a backbone KV cache across multiple LoRA specialists to cut serving cost, measuring task quality and system tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: In multi-task small-model deployments, several LoRA adapters share a backbone but are usually served naively, recomputing the same prefill KV cache per adapter, which is wasteful. The authors want to know whether already-trained, off-the-shelf LoRA adapters can safely share a single prefill KV cache without losing much task performance, and what practical serving cost savings this yields.
AI.method: Use a Qwen3-1.7B backbone with two existing LoRA adapters (HotpotQA extractive QA, GSM8K arithmetic reasoning). Sweep the token position at which computation switches from the backbone’s native prefill KV cache to adapter-specific computation. Compare full-prefix reuse vs partial recomputation, measure exact-match performance changes on held-out GSM8K and serving metrics like warm-cache time-to-first-token and memory. Also derive and test a closed-form ridge-regression KV translator to map backbone KV to adapter KV space.
AI.result: Full-prefix KV reuse produced the lowest prefill cost and only small, statistically weak quality drops in GSM8K EM scores (e.g., -4.6 EM at 160 tokens, -3.0 at 320, -0.8 for another seed, with inconsistent magnitudes and intervals mostly overlapping zero). Partial recomputation didn’t show clear benefits over full reuse. The proposed ridge KV translator failed to outperform direct KV reuse. Serving-wise, warm-cache time-to-first-token improved substantially with context length (up to ~16x at 8K tokens). However, peak memory for two branches dropped by only ~12% because the implementation reused KV values logically but copied the underlying storage, preventing real shared-cache memory savings. Specialist-dependent contrasts were inconclusive, with confidence intervals including zero.
AI.conclusion: Directly reusing a backbone’s prefill KV cache across standard, already-trained LoRA specialists appears to preserve most task quality in this setup while significantly reducing prefill latency, though not memory, under the tested implementation. No universal rule emerges for where to switch from base to adapter computation, and partial recomputation or learned KV translation does not clearly help. The study is exploratory and does not establish strict quality equivalence guarantees or a generalizable boundary-selection strategy, but indicates that simple full-prefix reuse is a promising and practical latency optimization worth further engineering, especially if true physical KV sharing can be implemented.

title: Nameless Tokenization: A Lossless Tokenizer-Level Defense Against Control-Token Forgery in Open-Weight LLMs
summary: Open-weight language models publish the strings their chat templates use to mark turns, roles and tool results, which the tokenizer maps back to the reserved identifiers the model obeys. Anyone who controls text in a prompt can therefore write a turn boundary indistinguishable from one the serving stack wrote. We audit 256 deployed chat tokenizers. All are forgeable, and the flag usually recommended as a fix leaves 56.6% forgeable because it misses the tool and reasoning markers agent systems rely on. We propose nameless tokenization, which leaves the control entries with a reserved identifier and no surface string, so the content encoder cannot emit one and message content reaches the model unaltered. Across five tokenizer families it reproduces the standard token stream exactly on attack-free data and lifts accuracy on a probe of delimiter-bearing text from 8.5% to 59.9%, where sanitizers lose it. Separating a delimiter's appearance from its identifier shows the identifier matters little against a bare task instruction, but carries most of a forged tool result and most of any forged turn once the system message tells the model to treat user content as data.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that existing open-weight chat language model tokenizers are vulnerable to prompt forgery via control-token imitation, and proposes “nameless tokenization” to prevent users from forging control tokens while preserving normal behavior and improving robustness to delimiter-bearing text.
AI.motivation: Open-weight LMs expose the literal strings corresponding to their internal control tokens (turn boundaries, roles, tools), making it possible for anyone who can write into the prompt to forge these markers and impersonate the serving stack. Existing mitigations based on a recommended tokenizer flag are incomplete, especially for tool and reasoning markers used in agent systems. The authors aim to systematically audit these vulnerabilities and design a tokenizer-level fix that prevents control-token forgery without hurting normal model performance.
AI.method: The authors audit 256 deployed chat tokenizers to test whether an attacker can forge control tokens by inserting their surface strings into prompts. They evaluate the effectiveness of the commonly recommended “safety flag” and show it still leaves many tokenizers forgeable, especially around tool/reasoning markers. They then introduce “nameless tokenization,” where reserved control identifiers have no corresponding surface string, so text encoding cannot produce them. They test this approach across five tokenizer families, checking that it reproduces standard token streams on benign data and measuring model accuracy on a probe task with delimiter-bearing text, comparing against existing sanitization-based defenses.
AI.result: All 256 audited chat tokenizers are shown to be forgeable. The widely recommended safety flag still leaves 56.6% of tokenizers vulnerable because it does not cover tool and reasoning markers. Nameless tokenization exactly matches standard token streams on non-adversarial inputs, increases accuracy on delimiter-bearing probe data from 8.5% to 59.9%, and outperforms sanitizer-based defenses that often distort inputs. Experiments separating visual delimiters from their internal identifiers show that identifiers contribute little for plain task instructions but carry most of the influence for forged tool outputs and forged turns when the system message instructs the model to treat user content as data.
AI.conclusion: Tokenizer-level vulnerabilities in open-weight chat models allow users to forge system-level control tokens, and existing recommended mitigations are insufficient, particularly for tools and reasoning markers used by agentic systems. Nameless tokenization—removing surface forms for reserved control identifiers—prevents content encoders from emitting control tokens while preserving normal behavior and substantially improving robustness on delimiter-bearing inputs. The semantics of internal identifiers are critical mainly for forged tool results and turns in data-oriented settings, so securing these identifiers meaningfully hardens systems against prompt forgery without sacrificing performance.

title: FirmCORe: A Benchmark for Structured Reasoning about Inter-Firm Collaboration Opportunities
summary: Comprehensive structured data on inter-firm relationships is often scarce or inaccessible because many relationships are privately negotiated, selectively disclosed, and fragmented across proprietary databases. This scarcity hinders the discovery of collaboration opportunities, particularly for startups and small and medium-sized enterprises. Firm profiles are readily available, but collaboration potential cannot be inferred from business similarity alone, since similar firms may be competitors, whereas dissimilar firms may offer complementary products, technologies, channels, capabilities, or capital. We present FirmCORe (Inter-Firm Collaboration Opportunity Reasoning), a human-annotated benchmark for pairwise reasoning over weakly structured firm profiles, comprising 2,805 labeled firm pairs. Given two firm profiles, a model must determine whether the available evidence supports a collaboration opportunity and, for positive pairs, jointly predict its strength, primary collaboration type, and role direction. FirmCORe also provides parallel Chinese- and English-language evaluation sets containing identical instances and gold labels, enabling controlled analysis of input-language sensitivity. Experiments with representative locally deployed and hosted large language models (LLMs) show that the strongest model achieves a macro-F1 score of 74.51 for opportunity detection but only 61.57% exact match across all four output fields. Language effects vary across models, and high cross-language agreement can mask errors shared across languages. These results indicate that current LLMs are substantially more reliable at detecting broad collaboration opportunities than at identifying their specific types and role directions.

AI.tldr: Introduces FirmCORe, a human-annotated benchmark for reasoning about inter-firm collaboration opportunities from weakly structured firm profiles, with bilingual (EN/ZH) evaluation and LLM baselines.
AI.motivation: Structured data on inter-firm relationships is scarce, fragmented, and often proprietary, which makes it difficult—especially for startups and SMEs—to systematically discover collaboration opportunities. Existing public data mostly consists of firm profiles, from which collaboration potential cannot be inferred by simple similarity, because competitors may look similar while good collaborators may look dissimilar yet complementary. There is a need for a benchmark that captures nuanced, pairwise reasoning about collaboration opportunities directly from realistic firm descriptions, and that also allows analysis of language effects on such reasoning.
AI.method: The authors construct FirmCORe, a human-annotated dataset of 2,805 firm pairs, each built from weakly structured firm profiles. Annotators label whether a collaboration opportunity exists between each pair and, when it does, also label three additional aspects: (1) the strength of the opportunity, (2) the primary collaboration type, and (3) the role direction between the firms. They create parallel Chinese and English evaluation sets with identical underlying instances and gold labels. They then evaluate several representative LLMs (both locally deployed and hosted) on the four-part prediction task and compare performance across languages and models, analyzing macro-F1 for opportunity detection and exact-match accuracy over the full output structure.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM achieves a macro-F1 score of 74.51 on the binary opportunity-detection task, but only 61.57% exact-match accuracy when jointly predicting all four required output fields (existence, strength, type, role direction). Performance and language sensitivity vary notably across models. In some cases, high agreement between Chinese and English predictions masks systematic errors that are common to both languages, indicating that cross-language consistency does not necessarily imply correctness.
AI.conclusion: FirmCORe demonstrates that current LLMs are relatively strong at recognizing broad inter-firm collaboration opportunities from weakly structured profiles but substantially weaker at precisely characterizing these opportunities in terms of type and directional roles. The benchmark provides a challenging and realistic testbed for multi-aspect, pairwise reasoning about business relationships and for studying language effects. It highlights the need for improved modeling of fine-grained collaboration attributes and more robust evaluation beyond coarse opportunity detection and cross-language agreement.

title: Autoformalizing Argumentative Material Inferences
summary: Natural language arguments are compelling before they are formally explicit. A premise supports a claim through defeasible warrants, background commitments, and exception conditions that the text leaves implicit. However, formal verification requires the opposite. Making such arguments machine-checkable requires constructing the missing commitments, not only translating given sentences into logic. Construction, however, carries a risk that translation does not: a system free to add premises can make any claim provable, and a formally valid proof may assert the claim outright, prove it without the original premise, or establish more than the claim itself. We address this problem by formulating autoformalization for argumentative material inference as guard completion, in which non-monotonic material support is turned into monotonic formal inference relative to an explicitly constructed guard set. A completion is accepted only when its proof both passes the theorem prover and survives contrastive tests of premise dependence and claim selectivity. We implement this formulation in GUARD, a neuro-symbolic framework in which LLMs construct and formalize candidate guards, Isabelle/HOL verifies the resulting theories and returns step-level feedback for iterative refinement, and the system abstains when no faithful completion can be reached. Our empirical results on Debatepedia and ARCT using different LLMs demonstrate that GUARD yields significant improvements in verified-faithful (+35.3, +32.9 points) and substantial reductions in leakage (-25.9, -21.9 points) over the state-of-the-art LLM-driven theorem proving approach. Moreover, we show that the symbolic soft critique and the explicit assumption layer account for most of these gains, with the soft critique also improving the initial validity of the elicited context and reducing the number of iterations required for successful verification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GUARD, a neuro-symbolic framework that turns informal natural language arguments into machine-checkable formal proofs by adding explicit “guard” assumptions, while enforcing faithfulness via theorem proving and contrastive tests.
AI.motivation: Natural language arguments rely on many implicit premises and defeasible warrants, which are crucial for human persuasion but problematic for formal verification. Existing autoformalization approaches mostly translate explicit text into logic and let systems add premises freely, which can make any claim provable and lead to unfaithful proofs that do not really depend on the original premises or are too strong. There is a need for a method that can construct missing assumptions while ensuring that the resulting formal proof is both sound and faithful to the original argumentative support.
AI.method: The authors recast autoformalization of argumentative inference as “guard completion”: transforming defeasible, non-monotonic material support into monotonic formal inference by explicitly constructing a set of guard assumptions. A candidate completion is only accepted if (1) its proof is verified by a theorem prover and (2) it passes contrastive tests for premise dependence (the claim fails without the stated premise) and claim selectivity (the proof does not establish stronger or unrelated claims). They implement this in GUARD, a neuro-symbolic system where large language models propose and formalize candidate guards, Isabelle/HOL checks and provides step-level feedback for iterative refinement, and the system abstains when no faithful completion is possible. They also incorporate a symbolic “soft critique” mechanism and an explicit assumption layer to guide and constrain the LLM’s proposals.
AI.result: On the Debatepedia and ARCT datasets and across multiple LLM backends, GUARD substantially outperforms previous LLM-based theorem proving approaches. It improves the rate of verified-faithful inferences by +35.3 and +32.9 points, and reduces reasoning leakage—cases where the proof goes beyond or around the intended argument—by -25.9 and -21.9 points. Ablation results indicate that most of these gains come from the symbolic soft critique and the explicit assumption (guard) layer, which also enhance the initial quality of elicited context and lower the number of refinement iterations required.
AI.conclusion: Formulating autoformalization of argumentation as guard completion and implementing it in the GUARD framework yields more faithful, verifiable mappings from natural language arguments to formal proofs. By tightly coupling LLM-based assumption construction with interactive theorem proving, contrastive dependence/selectivity tests, and an explicit assumption layer, the approach controls the risk of arbitrary premise addition and reduces leakage. This demonstrates a practical path toward reliable, machine-checkable reasoning over informal argumentative text and highlights the benefits of symbolic soft critique in neuro-symbolic systems.

title: MOCC-R1: Reinforcing Reasoning-Response Consistency for Multimodal Counselor Response Generation
summary: Multimodal counselor response generation (MCRG) aims to generate an appropriate counselor response from multimodal dialogue histories. Progress is limited by two gaps: first, existing datasets rarely capture sustained, human-recorded counseling interactions conducted by qualified counselors; Second, existing methods do not explicitly optimize consistency between counseling reasoning and the generated response, potentially undermining the reliability of MCRG systems. Thus, we introduce MOCC, a multimodal counseling conversation corpus containing over 200 hours of interactions involving 154 credential-verified counselors. Based on MOCC, we propose MOCC-R1, a two-stage framework for optimizing reasoning-response consistency. Cold-start supervised fine-tuning trains the model to generate a structured trajectory consisting of client-state understanding, a response intent that links a counseling principle to a planned action, and the final response. Reinforcement learning (RL) then rewards grounded plan coherence and plan execution, encouraging the inferred state and plan to be supported by the dialogue context and the response to realize that plan. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed MOCC-R1.

AI.tldr: They propose a new multimodal counseling dataset (MOCC) and a reasoning-aligned response generation framework (MOCC-R1) that uses supervised fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning to ensure counselor responses are consistent with explicit counseling reasoning steps.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal counselor response generation is hampered by two main issues: lack of large, high-quality, real counseling datasets with qualified counselors; and models that generate responses without explicitly ensuring that the underlying counseling reasoning is consistent with what is said, which can harm reliability and safety in mental health contexts.
AI.method: 1) Build MOCC, a multimodal counseling conversation corpus with 200+ hours of interactions from 154 credential-verified counselors. 2) Propose MOCC-R1, a two-stage framework: (a) Cold-start supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to output a structured reasoning trajectory composed of client-state understanding, a response intent connecting a counseling principle to an action plan, and the final response. (b) Apply reinforcement learning with rewards for plan coherence with dialogue context and successful execution of that plan in the final response, thus aligning reasoning and response.
AI.result: Experiments (presumably on MOCC and possibly other benchmarks) show that MOCC-R1 improves multimodal counselor response generation, particularly in terms of coherence between inferred client state, counseling plan, and actual response, validating both the dataset and the training framework.
AI.conclusion: Providing a high-quality multimodal counseling corpus and explicitly modeling and optimizing the reasoning-to-response trajectory via supervised training plus RL leads to more reliable and coherent counselor responses, addressing key gaps in existing multimodal counseling systems.

title: The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment
summary: Large Language Models are now common in student assessment, but we know little about how student demographics affect their use. Sometimes, considering student demographics may be necessary -- for example, to improve readability for users with lower educational levels. However, it also risks being a cause of discrimination, e.g., when assigning lower scores to students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. We set up controlled prompts to test 1) explicit demographic effects, where we mention demographic details directly, and 2) implicit effects, where we use conversation history as a demographic signal. We test these settings in three tasks: Automated Essay Scoring, Formative Feedback, and Metalinguistic Question Answering. We test six state-of-the-art LLMs on these tasks. In both explicit and implicit cases, the models pick up on demographic cues and can change their scoring, feedback, and answers accordingly. We find that LLMs frequently adjust the readability of feedback to education levels when these are explicitly mentioned. On the other hand, implicit conditions produce unpredictable biases, such as in question answering, where responses from lower-education levels receive lower sentiment scores. Our results provide clear evidence of demographic sensitivity in LLMs for educational assessment tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how large language models (LLMs) used in student assessment are sensitive to student demographic information, both when it is explicitly provided and when it is only implicitly signaled through conversation history.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become prevalent in educational assessment, there is a need to understand whether and how they behave differently based on student demographics, which can be beneficial for personalization (e.g., readability adaptation) but also harmful through discrimination (e.g., lower scores for disadvantaged groups).
AI.method: The authors design controlled prompting experiments to separately test explicit demographic effects (directly stating demographic details) and implicit effects (encoding demographics via conversation history). They evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on three tasks: Automated Essay Scoring, Formative Feedback, and Metalinguistic Question Answering, and analyze how outputs change with demographic cues.
AI.result: Across all three tasks and multiple LLMs, the models systematically react to demographic cues, altering scores, feedback, and answers. Explicitly stated education levels reliably trigger changes in feedback readability, while implicitly encoded demographic information leads to more erratic biases, including less positive sentiment in responses associated with lower education levels.
AI.conclusion: LLMs used for educational assessment are demonstrably sensitive to demographic information, both explicit and implicit. While some adaptations (like readability adjustment) can be desirable, there are also unpredictable and potentially discriminatory biases, underscoring the need for careful evaluation, monitoring, and mitigation before deploying such systems in real-world assessment settings.

title: End-to-End Latency-Minimizing and Load-Balanced Request Scheduling for Edge LLM Inference in Agentic AI Services
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered agentic AI services increasingly demand low-latency inference, motivating the deployment of LLMs across distributed edge servers. However, heterogeneous communication and computing capabilities, together with dynamically evolving inference states, make the edge server selection for each incoming request time-varying and tightly coupled across slots. In this paper, we investigate an online request scheduling framework for edge LLM inference that jointly minimizes long-term average end-to-end latency and regulates workload distribution across heterogeneous edge servers. Two main challenges arise in this context. First, conventional latency models cannot accurately capture the fine-grained dynamics of multi-stage LLM execution. Second, the latency consequence of a scheduling decision is observed only after request completion, making immediate decision evaluation difficult. To address these challenges, we develop a cross-slot inference model that captures transmission, prefill, iteration-level decoding, and key-value (KV) cache evolution for each diverse request, and characterize server workload through a KV cache memory-time consumption metric. We propose the LYREO approach that transforms the long-term load-balancing constraint via Lyapunov optimization and employs reward redistribution with sequencebased return prediction to convert delayed outcomes into timely learning signals for earlier decisions. Simulations under various configurations demonstrate that LYREO consistently achieves lower latency and more balanced load distribution than representative learning-based and heuristic baseline schemes.

AI.tldr: They design an online scheduler for LLM inference on heterogeneous edge servers to minimize long-term latency while balancing load, using a detailed cross-slot inference model and a Lyapunov-based learning approach (LYREO) with reward redistribution to handle delayed feedback.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agentic AI needs low-latency responses, prompting deployment across distributed edge servers. However, heterogeneous compute/communication resources and evolving inference states make it hard to decide, online, which edge server should handle each request. Existing latency models are too coarse for multi-stage LLM pipelines, and the effect of scheduling decisions is only known after requests finish, complicating learning and optimization. There is a need for an online scheduling method that explicitly models LLM execution details and can learn effectively from delayed performance signals while also ensuring long-term load balancing.
AI.method: They build a cross-slot inference model that explicitly captures transmission, prefill, step-wise decoding, and key-value cache evolution per request, and represent server workload via a KV cache memory-time consumption metric. On top of this, they propose LYREO, which uses Lyapunov optimization to convert the long-term load-balancing requirement into an online control objective, and combines it with a learning method based on reward redistribution and sequence-based return prediction so that delayed latency outcomes are converted into more immediate learning signals associated with earlier scheduling decisions.
AI.result: Simulation experiments across different setups show that LYREO yields lower end-to-end latency and achieves more balanced workload distribution compared with both learning-based baselines and heuristic scheduling methods.
AI.conclusion: A detailed, multi-stage inference model plus a Lyapunov-guided, reward-redistribution-based online scheduler (LYREO) can effectively manage heterogeneous edge LLM inference, reducing latency and achieving better load balancing than prior approaches in simulations.

title: PaperDoctor: Evidence-Grounded and Actionable Feedback for Scientific Papers in Progress
summary: Autoresearch agents are reshaping the research ecosystem, but they can also let flawed claims enter the literature at scale. Human advisors catch such issues in drafts through careful, traceable feedback, yet advisor-style assessment requires extensive manual effort and does not scale. To shift automated paper assessment from a judge to a diagnostician, we introduce PaperDoctor, an agent framework for pre-submission feedback with three key innovations. First, a holistic hierarchical framework evaluates writing, layout, references, code, theory, prior work, and experiments through three layers: L1 surface screening, L2 typed verifiers that route each claim to the appropriate evidence, and L3 reproducers that rerun experiments by priority. Second, each finding contains an observation, a pointer to specific evidence such as a sentence, equation, or code line, and a revision suggestion, making critiques auditable and actionable. Third, PaperDoctor selectively rebuilds and reruns experiments based on claim importance and compute budget, surfacing reproducibility gaps and quantitative limitations that are invisible from the manuscript alone. We evaluate PaperDoctor on 30 in-progress papers, yielding 70.6% agreement and all positive holistic scores, and on 40 manuscripts across machine learning, natural science, and social science, covering human- and AI-authored papers with code. Overall, PaperDoctor produces more auditable feedback than human and other agentic reviewers, pairs critiques with concrete suggestions by design, and complements dimensions often overlooked by human reviewers. We also develop an interactive interface that lets authors browse findings grounded in their paper. PaperDoctor reframes automated paper assessment as diagnosis rather than verdict, taking a concrete step toward AI advisors for more rigorous AI-assisted scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: PaperDoctor is an AI agent framework that provides detailed, auditable, and partially reproducibility-aware pre-submission feedback on research papers, acting more like a diagnostic advisor than a yes/no reviewer.
AI.motivation: Autoresearch and AI-powered writing tools can flood the literature with polished but potentially flawed papers. Human advisors provide high-quality, traceable feedback but their effort does not scale to the volume of AI-assisted research. The authors want to automate this advisor-style, diagnostic feedback process so that automated assessment focuses on identifying, evidencing, and fixing problems rather than issuing black-box accept/reject judgments.
AI.method: The authors design PaperDoctor, a multi-layer agent framework for paper diagnosis. It uses a holistic hierarchical pipeline with three layers: (L1) surface screening of writing, layout, references, and basic issues; (L2) typed verifiers that route individual claims to appropriate sources of evidence (text, equations, code, prior work, experiments); and (L3) reproducers that selectively rebuild and rerun experiments according to claim importance and available compute. Each finding produced by the system must include (1) a concrete observation, (2) a pointer to specific evidence like a sentence or code line, and (3) a revision suggestion. They also implement an interactive interface to browse these grounded findings.
AI.result: Applied to 30 in-progress papers, PaperDoctor achieves 70.6% agreement with comparison baselines and receives positive holistic assessments. On an additional 40 manuscripts spanning machine learning, natural sciences, and social sciences, including both human- and AI-authored papers with code, PaperDoctor yields feedback that is more auditable than that from human and other agentic reviewers and systematically couples critiques with concrete revision suggestions. It identifies reproducibility and quantitative issues that are hard to see from the manuscript alone.
AI.conclusion: PaperDoctor demonstrates that automated paper assessment can be reframed from issuing verdicts to providing structured diagnosis. By combining hierarchical claim checking, evidence-grounded critiques, and selective experiment reruns, it serves as an AI advisor that improves rigor and reproducibility in AI-assisted scientific discovery. The system complements human reviewers by covering dimensions they often miss and offering an interactive interface that makes the feedback actionable for authors.

title: Extracting ontology-compliant knowledge from scientific text describing irradiated materials using large language models
summary: The quest for new materials increasingly relies on predictive models and comprehensive simulations that span scales from atomic to macroscopic levels. However, essential data necessary for these models and simulations are often embedded in scientific literature as unstructured text, limiting reusability and posing challenges for researchers seeking to leverage existing knowledge effectively. While extracting structured data from unstructured text using large language models is gaining popularity, traditional methods typically generate key-value pairs data with straightforward schemas. In contrast, we introduce eolas, a modular pipeline that uses large language models to automatically transform scientific documents into knowledge graphs aligned with a specified ontology. We demonstrate eolas effectiveness in extracting useful information for scientists studying materials designed to endure the extreme temperatures and radiation levels found in fusion reactors. While a human expert might spend between thirty to ninety minutes extracting relevant data from an article, eolas can generate high-quality knowledge graphs in just a few minutes. These are presented in a tabular format with faceted navigation for easy human validation. Additionally, we introduce the first benchmark dataset designed to assess large language models capabilities in constructing knowledge graphs within the domain of irradiated materials. The analysis of 168 experiments using our dataset, various large language models and prompting techniques provides key insights that we summarize into practical guidelines for effectively extracting knowledge graphs aligned with an input ontology.

AI.tldr: The paper presents eolas, a pipeline that converts scientific materials-science papers into ontology-aligned knowledge graphs using large language models, and introduces a benchmark dataset plus practical guidelines for this task.
AI.motivation: Materials discovery and design increasingly depend on multiscale simulations and predictive models, which require high-quality structured data. Much of this data is locked in unstructured scientific text, making reuse and large-scale analysis difficult and time-consuming. Existing LLM-based extraction approaches mostly yield flat key–value data that do not capture rich relationships or ontologies, limiting their usefulness for complex scientific domains such as irradiated materials for fusion reactors.
AI.method: The authors develop eolas, a modular pipeline that uses large language models to transform full scientific documents into knowledge graphs conforming to a specified ontology. The system processes papers, extracts entities and relations relevant to irradiated materials, and organizes them into ontology-aligned graphs. The output is rendered in tabular form with faceted navigation for efficient human validation. In addition, they build the first benchmark dataset for evaluating LLM-based knowledge graph construction in the irradiated materials domain and systematically test different LLMs and prompting strategies on 168 experiments.
AI.result: eolas is able to automatically generate high-quality knowledge graphs from materials-science articles in a few minutes, compared to the 30–90 minutes needed by human experts to manually extract comparable information. The authors’ benchmark over 168 experiments reveals performance differences among LLMs and prompt designs, and surfaces patterns about what works best for ontology-aligned knowledge graph extraction in this domain.
AI.conclusion: A dedicated LLM-based pipeline can transform unstructured scientific literature into rich, ontology-aligned knowledge graphs efficiently and at scale, significantly reducing expert effort. The introduced benchmark and experimental analysis provide foundational evidence and actionable guidelines for future work on automated knowledge graph construction in materials science and similar scientific domains, especially for irradiated materials for fusion reactors.

title: Can LLMs Follow the Pulse of a Crisis? Evaluating Crisis Sentiment in Bangladesh's July Uprising
summary: Crisis sentiment analysis is especially challenging for low-resource languages such as Bangla, where language, context, and public reaction shift rapidly. We introduce UNRESTSENT200K, a Bangla crisis sentiment dataset with approximately 200K Facebook and YouTube comments from the July-August 2024 Bangladesh uprising. The dataset covers five event-aligned phases, from early escalation and internet blackout to regime transition and a later flood crisis. Each comment is linked to its parent post, enabling evaluation with and without discourse context. All comments are annotated through a fully human process involving 14 native Bangla-speaking annotators and senior validation, achieving substantial agreement (kappa = 0.73, alpha = 0.71) and 94.2% blind-audit agreement. We benchmark fine-tuned encoders, prompted LLMs, and LoRA-tuned LLMs. Results show that parent-post context consistently improves performance, while temporal shift across phases causes large performance drops. Strong LLMs perform well, but still struggle with sarcasm, implicit political references, and phase-dependent meaning. UNRESTSENT200K provides a benchmark for studying context-aware and temporally robust sentiment analysis in low-resource crisis discourse. UNRESTSENT200K is available at https://sami0055.github.io/UNRESTSENT200K/

AI.tldr: The paper presents UNRESTSENT200K, a large, human-annotated Bangla crisis sentiment dataset built from social media comments during the 2024 Bangladesh uprising, and uses it to benchmark context-aware and temporally robust sentiment models.
AI.motivation: Sentiment analysis during crises is difficult in low-resource languages like Bangla, where language use and public sentiment change quickly across time and events, and there is a lack of large, high-quality labeled datasets—especially with discourse context and temporal structure—to train and evaluate robust models.
AI.method: The authors collect roughly 200K Facebook and YouTube comments related to the July–August 2024 Bangladesh uprising, segment them into five temporally and event-aligned phases, and link each comment to its parent post. Fourteen native Bangla annotators, with senior-level validation, perform fully manual sentiment labeling, achieving high inter-annotator agreement. Using this dataset, the authors benchmark several model families: fine-tuned encoder models, prompted large language models, and LoRA-tuned LLMs, and they compare models with and without access to parent-post context and across different temporal phases.
AI.result: Including parent-post context consistently boosts sentiment classification performance across model types. However, performance drops substantially when models are evaluated across different temporal phases, highlighting sensitivity to temporal shift in language and sentiment. Strong LLMs achieve relatively good accuracy overall but still show notable weaknesses in handling sarcasm, implicit political references, and meanings that change depending on the phase of the crisis.
AI.conclusion: UNRESTSENT200K offers a new large-scale benchmark for Bangla crisis sentiment analysis with explicit discourse context and temporal structure. The findings underline the importance of leveraging context from parent posts and modeling temporal shifts to achieve robust sentiment analysis, and they show that even advanced LLMs face challenges with nuanced, evolving crisis discourse in a low-resource language.

title: Intrinsic Motivation in Reinforcement Learning: A Research Agenda for Adaptive Self-Organisation
summary: Biological cells can be viewed as individual, interacting agents whose collective dynamics give rise to adaptive behaviour at multiple levels of organisation, from individual cells through tissues to whole multicellular organisms. In this perspective and tutorial article we discuss whether intrinsic rewards in artificial neural systems can support adaptation, functional specialisation and higher-level self-organisation without a shared external objective. We review empowerment, curiosity, learning progress, information gain, unsupervised skill discovery, mutual information estimation and the use of world models for intrinsic reward computation. Particular attention is given to failure modes showing when such objectives do not produce sustained exploration or increasingly complex behaviour. We argue that more capable systems may require complementary objectives, communication, memory, learning at multiple temporal scales and environmental constraints. Based on this perspective, we outline three experimental directions. These include a resource-constrained environment in which otherwise stable behavioural attractors become unsustainable, allowing us to test whether environmental constraints can mitigate characteristic failure modes of intrinsic objectives. The network of recurrent agents with per-agent intrinsic rewards, and a hierarchical world-model agent in which exploratory motor competence develops before goal-directed behaviour. These experiments are intended to test whether intrinsic learning can lead to adaptive organisation at progressively higher levels.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys and critiques intrinsic motivation signals in artificial agents, arguing that, like cells in organisms, agents may self-organise adaptively without an explicit shared external task, but only if intrinsic rewards are combined with richer structures (communication, hierarchy, constraints).
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how intrinsic rewards (empowerment, curiosity, learning progress, etc.) can drive open-ended, self-organising adaptation in multi-agent / multi-level systems, analogous to how biological cells collectively yield organism-level behaviour, especially when there is no single external reward function.
AI.method: Conceptual and tutorial analysis of existing intrinsic motivation methods (empowerment, curiosity, information gain, unsupervised skill discovery, MI estimation, world models), with a focus on known failure modes. The authors then propose three concrete experimental setups to test intrinsic-reward-driven self-organisation: (1) agents in resource-constrained environments with destabilised behavioural attractors, (2) networks of recurrent agents each with their own intrinsic rewards, and (3) a hierarchical world-model agent where exploratory competence precedes goal-directedness.
AI.result: As a perspective/tutorial, it does not present empirical results. Instead, it: (a) synthesises a taxonomy of intrinsic reward approaches and their limitations; (b) identifies characteristic failure modes (e.g., lack of sustained exploration, trivialisation, or behavioural collapse); and (c) specifies experimental designs that could reveal conditions under which intrinsic rewards do or do not lead to higher-level adaptive organisation.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic reward signals alone are usually insufficient for robust, open-endedly complex behaviour. To get adaptive organisation across levels (agents, collectives, hierarchies), systems likely need combinations of intrinsic objectives, communication among agents, memory, multi-timescale learning, and environmental constraints. The proposed experiments aim to test whether appropriately structured intrinsic learning can yield progressively higher-level self-organisation, analogous in spirit to biological cell collectives.

title: Diagnosing the Fact-Grounding Gap in Multi-Hop Question Answering
summary: Multi-hop question answering requires combining information from multiple documents to answer complex questions. These systems have grown increasingly capable, yet when they fail, the error is typically attributed to not finding the right documents. Whether this holds at the level of individual reasoning steps remains largely unexamined. We investigate this across three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks and find that failures decompose into two distinct modes: retrieval failures, where the needed passage was not retrieved, and extraction failures, where the passage was retrieved but the needed fact could not be extracted - a phenomenon we term the fact-grounding gap. Extraction failures account for nearly half of all per-hop deficiencies and are invisible to standard retrieval metrics. They remain unresolved by every retrieval intervention we test, establishing a ceiling for retrieval-only improvements. The gap's severity varies across benchmarks and question types, but extraction failures appear on every dataset we measure. Our findings reveal that retrieval failures and extraction failures are fundamentally different bottlenecks requiring different solutions - a distinction absent from current evaluation practice.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why multi-hop question answering models fail and finds that many errors are due not to missing documents, but to an inability to extract the needed fact from already retrieved passages.
AI.motivation: While multi-hop QA has improved, most blame failures on poor document retrieval, assuming that once the right document is found, models can extract the answer. This assumption had not been rigorously tested at the level of individual reasoning hops.
AI.method: The authors study three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks and, at each reasoning hop, categorize errors into retrieval failures (relevant passage not retrieved) and extraction failures (passage retrieved but needed fact not extracted). They quantify how often each occurs, evaluate how visible they are to standard retrieval metrics, and test several retrieval-focused interventions to see whether they reduce errors.
AI.result: They discover a consistent split between two error modes: retrieval failures and extraction failures. Extraction failures constitute nearly half of all per-hop deficiencies, are not captured by standard retrieval metrics, and persist despite multiple retrieval-focused interventions. The severity of this fact-grounding gap varies across benchmarks and question types, but is present in all datasets analyzed.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval failures and extraction failures are fundamentally distinct bottlenecks in multi-hop QA, and improving retrieval alone cannot eliminate many of the observed errors. Therefore, evaluation protocols and model designs must explicitly address extraction and fact grounding, not just retrieval quality.

title: From Transient Prompts to Persistent Control: Scientific Poster Generation via Recursive Semantic-Geometric Contracts
summary: Scientific poster generation distills a multimodal paper into a single-page visual artifact, forcing strict trade-offs between informational coverage and readability under a fixed spatial budget. Existing methods pass plans as transient prompts and validate individual stages in isolation. This strategy causes requirements to drift across content and layout modules, and previous checks to be silently invalidated. We introduce PosterVisor, a control framework that shifts poster generation from transient prompts to persistent control. An Orchestrator grounds rubrics in the paper and visual assets, compiling them into a Semantic-Geometric Contract (SGC) that binds claims and sources to required visuals, budgets, and spatial commitments. Only fully instantiated records become executable assertions; other usable requirements remain soft guidance. Recursive Contract Enforcement (RCE) dynamically triggers checks across stages as evidence emerges. Crucially, during repairs, RCE rechecks affected checkpoint states, preventing repair-induced regressions from propagating silently. We instantiate PosterVisor in HTML/CSS and editable PPTX generators. On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, PosterVisor-PPT improves observed mean poster-grounded QA accuracy over PosterGen (64.47% vs. 58.53%) and is preferred by human judges in 72.5% of non-tied pairwise comparisons (95% CI, 61.6-83.4%). A secondary 30-paper study also yields higher VLM Overall and PaperQuiz means. These results support rubric-compiled contracts and stage-conditioned enforcement for controllable poster synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PosterVisor, a control framework for generating scientific posters from papers using persistent semantic-geometric contracts and recursive enforcement, improving accuracy and human preference over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific poster generation methods rely on transient prompts and validate stages in isolation, leading to requirement drift between content and layout modules and invalidation of earlier checks during later stages or repairs. There is a need for a more reliable, controllable process that maintains consistency between high-level rubrics, content selection, and spatial layout under strict space constraints.
AI.method: The authors introduce PosterVisor, a control framework where an Orchestrator grounds rubrics in the source paper and visual assets and compiles them into a Semantic-Geometric Contract (SGC). The SGC explicitly binds claims and sources to required visuals, budget allocations, and spatial commitments. Only fully instantiated records are turned into hard executable assertions, while partial ones act as soft guidance. The framework uses Recursive Contract Enforcement (RCE) to dynamically trigger checks throughout the generation pipeline as new evidence appears, and to recheck affected checkpoints during repairs so that fixes in one module do not silently break others. PosterVisor is instantiated in two generators: HTML/CSS-based and editable PPTX-based posters.
AI.result: On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, the PPTX instantiation of PosterVisor achieves higher poster-grounded QA accuracy than PosterGen (64.47% vs. 58.53%). Human evaluators prefer PosterVisor posters in 72.5% of non-tied pairwise comparisons, with a 95% confidence interval of 61.6–83.4%. A secondary study with 30 papers also shows higher scores on VLM Overall and PaperQuiz metrics, indicating better quality and faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Rubric-compiled Semantic-Geometric Contracts combined with stage-conditioned Recursive Contract Enforcement enable more controllable, reliable scientific poster synthesis than prompt-based baselines. Persisting requirements as contracts and revalidating them across stages reduces requirement drift and repair-induced regressions, leading to improved factual grounding and user preference in generated posters.

title: EviScope: Paired Counterfactual Evidence Diagnostics for Faithful and Efficient Grounded Language Models
comment: Accepted as an archival short paper in GroundLM Findings at EMNLP 2026; to appear in the GroundLM 2026 workshop proceedings in the ACL Anthology
summary: Grounded language-model systems are often evaluated by final answer accuracy, yet a correct answer can be unsupported, drawn from the wrong source, or produced when evidence is insufficient or contradictory. We introduce EviScope, a paired counterfactual benchmark that holds the question fixed while adding, removing, distracting, or contradicting its evidence. EviScope-v1.1 contains 40 four-condition quartets with repaired counterfactual claims and span-level support labels for automatic evaluation. Across 960 gold-blind generations from Qwen2.5-7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, paired metrics expose model-dependent grounding behavior that answer accuracy hides. On two local open models, an explicit evidence-action gate underperforms vanilla RAG on QCS: 0.15 vs. 0.50 for Qwen and 0.10 vs. 0.375 for Llama. Gemini reaches 0.944 joint success under both prompts, yet still answers 5% of conflict cases after contradiction insertion. EviScope therefore distinguishes unsupported answering, conflict blindness, and wrong non-answer actions rather than scoring answers alone.

AI.tldr: Introduce EviScope, a benchmark to evaluate whether LLM answers are properly grounded in evidence, not just accurate.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of grounded language models focus mainly on final answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish whether a correct answer is genuinely supported by provided evidence, taken from the right source, or produced in the presence of missing or contradictory evidence. There is a need for a benchmark that diagnoses how models use and react to evidence changes, such as when evidence is added, removed, distracted, or contradicted.
AI.method: The authors design EviScope, a paired counterfactual benchmark that keeps questions fixed but systematically perturbs the associated evidence (adding, removing, distracting, or contradicting it). EviScope-v1.1 comprises 40 quartets (four-condition sets) with repaired counterfactual claims and span-level support labels, enabling automatic evaluation of grounding. They evaluate LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemini 3.5 Flash) across 960 gold-blind generations and compute paired metrics to reveal grounding behaviors. They also compare vanilla RAG to an explicit evidence-action gate on two local open models.
AI.result: Paired metrics from EviScope reveal significant differences in grounding behavior not captured by answer accuracy alone. On Qwen and Llama, an explicit evidence-action gate performs worse than vanilla RAG on the QCS metric (0.15 vs. 0.50 for Qwen, 0.10 vs. 0.375 for Llama). Gemini 3.5 Flash performs very well (0.944 joint success under both prompts), but still inappropriately answers about 5% of cases after contradiction insertion, indicating residual conflict blindness.
AI.conclusion: EviScope successfully differentiates between several types of grounding failures, such as unsupported answering, conflict blindness, and incorrect non-answer behaviors, going beyond simple answer correctness. This demonstrates the importance and utility of more nuanced grounding benchmarks for evaluating grounded language-model systems.

title: Self-Emergence Agent Architecture:Behavior-Inertia HMM, Reflexive Metacognition,and Social-Contrastive Self-Modeling
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents exhibit strong language-generation and problem-solving capabilities, yet suffer from three structural limitations: personality drift, non-evolutionary reflection, and the absence of a self-other boundary. Existing generative-agent simulations rely on static memory and fixed prompts, maintaining neither behavioral inertia nor endogenous self-evolution. We propose the Self-Emergence Agent Architecture (SEAA), which integrates three components: (i) a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that encodes long-term behavioral and cognitive inertia as an editable state-transition matrix; (ii) a Reflexion-style verbal metacognition loop whose output updates the HMM parameters themselves, rather than merely being stored as text; and (iii) a multi-agent social environment in which initially identical agents continuously compare their behavior with others'. The three components form a closed loop: social action $\to$ feedback $\to$ self-reflection $\to$ inertia update $\to$ differentiated action. We state three falsifiable hypotheses and provide a reproducible experimental protocol with operational metrics. A language-model-free prototype shows the loop spontaneously breaks symmetry: initially identical agents consolidate distinct, stable personalities whereas matched controls do not. Experiments with a hosted LLM surface these differences as distinct first-person self-narratives, and a five-agent deliberation spontaneously develops social structure---a consensus hub and a unanimously rejected outlier---absent in the control. Following an epistemologically agnostic stance inspired by Zhuangzi, SEAA studies only observable behavioral emergence and makes no claim about subjective qualia. This work contributes a unified framework, a concrete architecture with pseudocode, mechanistic evidence, and a microscope-style sandbox for studying artificial-self emergence.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Self-Emergence Agent Architecture (SEAA) where agents develop stable, distinct personalities via a closed loop of social interaction, self-reflection, and adaptive behavioral inertia.
AI.motivation: Large language model agents are powerful but exhibit structural limitations: their personalities drift, their reflections do not truly update underlying behavior, and they lack a clear self-other boundary. Existing generative agents use static memory and fixed prompts, so they do not self-evolve in a principled, mechanistic way. The paper aims to provide an architecture where artificial agents can exhibit stable, differentiated, and evolving selves, enabling rigorous study of artificial self-emergence.
AI.method: Introduce SEAA with three integrated components: (i) a Hidden Markov Model encoding long-term behavioral and cognitive inertia as an editable state transition matrix; (ii) a Reflexion-style verbal metacognition loop whose output is used to update the HMM parameters directly; and (iii) a multi-agent social environment where initially identical agents continually compare their behavior to others. These elements form a closed feedback loop: social action leads to feedback, which triggers self-reflection, which then updates inertia parameters in the HMM, yielding differentiated future behavior. The authors also specify falsifiable hypotheses, an experimental protocol, and implement both a language-model-free prototype and an LLM-based prototype.
AI.result: In the language-model-free prototype, the closed loop spontaneously breaks symmetry: agents that start with identical conditions diverge into distinct, stable personalities, whereas control agents without the full loop do not show such differentiation. In LLM-based experiments, these underlying differences manifest as distinct first-person self-narratives. In a five-agent deliberation setting, agents self-organize into a social structure featuring a central consensus-forming agent and an outlier that is unanimously rejected; this structure is absent in the control condition.
AI.conclusion: SEAA provides a mechanistic and testable framework for studying how artificial agents can develop emergent, stable, and differentiated selves purely from observable behavior, without making claims about inner experience or qualia. The work offers a specific architecture with pseudocode, experimental evidence of emergent personality and social structure, and a sandbox environment for systematically probing artificial self-emergence.

title: An Empirical Study of Counterfactual Self-Explanations in LLMs
summary: Large language models can easily generate explanations for their own outputs, but such self-explanations are not necessarily faithful to the model's behavior. We study this issue through counterfactual self-explanations, where a model minimally edits an input so that its own prediction changes. Across sentiment analysis and natural language inference, we evaluate ten instruction-tuned models from the LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 families, measuring faithfulness, minimality, and alignment with human-annotated rationales. Our results show that model scale is the strongest determinant of explanation quality: larger models are substantially more likely to generate counterfactuals that flip their own predictions and target decision-relevant evidence. In contrast, the rationale-guided condition produces edit-minimal counterfactuals that are also more human-aligned. However, it does not consistently improve faithfulness. Overall, counterfactual self-explanations can provide useful behavioral evidence about model decisions, but their reliability depends strongly on model capacity and should be empirically validated rather than assumed.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how faithfully large language models can generate counterfactual self-explanations for their own predictions, showing that explanation reliability heavily depends on model size and must be empirically checked.
AI.motivation: LLMs can produce fluent explanations for their outputs, but these explanations may not actually reflect the true internal decision process. This gap between plausibility and faithfulness is a core problem for interpretability and safe deployment. The paper focuses on counterfactual self-explanations—minimal input edits that change the model’s prediction—as a potentially more behavioral and faithful explanation method, and aims to rigorously test how reliable these are across modern instruction-tuned models.
AI.method: The authors construct counterfactual self-explanations by prompting instruction-tuned LLaMA‑3 and Qwen‑2.5 models (ten variants in total) to minimally edit input texts so that the model’s own prediction flips (e.g., sentiment from positive to negative). They study sentiment analysis and natural language inference tasks. Explanations are evaluated along three axes: (1) faithfulness—does the edited input actually change the model’s prediction as intended; (2) minimality—are the edits as small as possible; and (3) human alignment—do the edits focus on spans humans annotate as decision-relevant rationales. They also compare a rationale-guided condition, where models are given human rationales as guidance when generating counterfactuals.
AI.result: Larger models produce substantially higher-quality counterfactual self-explanations: they more reliably flip their own predictions and more often edit text that corresponds to human-identified decision-relevant evidence. Rationale-guided prompting encourages more minimal edits that better align with human rationales, but does not reliably boost faithfulness (i.e., the degree to which the model’s own prediction actually flips due to the edits). Overall explanation quality varies strongly with model scale and prompting condition.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual self-explanations can be a useful, behavior-grounded way to probe how LLMs make decisions, but they are far from uniformly reliable. Model capacity (scale) is a key determinant of explanation quality, and even rationale-guided setups do not guarantee faithfulness. Therefore, practitioners should not assume such explanations are trustworthy by default; instead, they must empirically validate the faithfulness and quality of counterfactual self-explanations for any given model and setting.

title: FlashVector: Agent for Hierarchical Model Serving Stack Optimization
