summary: Model serving is one of the largest cost drivers in production recommender systems. Maximizing its throughput requires navigating a deeply layered hierarchy: GPU kernels, the ML framework computation graph, the model server, and on-demand feature processing -- each demanding specialized domain expertise. Such cross-layer expertise is inherently difficult to acquire, and does not scale with a workload that continuously grows and evolves, leaving significant cost efficiency gains unrealized. While recent AI agents have demonstrated human expert level efficiency in standalone GPU kernel optimization, automated tuning and optimization for the rest of the serving stack remain largely unexplored. We present FlashVector, an agentic system that optimizes performance across all layers of the model serving stack. The key contribution is an extensible framework to generalize the single kernel optimization agent paradigm to heterogeneous technical stacks, and to deliver performance improvements holistically. After deployment in Unity's Vector advertising platform, FlashVector achieved up to 2x throughput increase and up to 1.98x latency speedup on model server, and up to 1.6x throughput increase on feature store. These optimizations were discovered not only at the GPU kernel and computation graph levels, but also across the other components of the model serving stack, such as the model server (NVIDIA Triton's C++ codebase) and the on-demand feature transformation service (Python codebase), demonstrating the extensibility of the framework to more complex system architectures.

AI.tldr: FlashVector is an agent-based system that automatically optimizes recommender-system model serving performance across all layers (GPU kernels, computation graph, model server, and feature processing), yielding up to ~2x throughput and latency improvements in production.
AI.motivation: Production recommender systems spend a large fraction of cost on model serving. Achieving high throughput requires coordinated optimization across multiple layers—GPU kernels, ML framework graphs, model server implementations, and feature pipelines. Each layer traditionally demands its own specialized expertise, and recent work has focused mainly on single-kernel GPU optimization, leaving the rest of the serving stack under-optimized. There is a need for a unified, automated approach that can find cross-layer performance gains without requiring scarce human experts for every component.
AI.method: The authors design FlashVector, an agentic framework that extends the single-kernel optimization-agent paradigm to the entire heterogeneous serving stack. The system employs agents capable of inspecting, tuning, and modifying different layers: GPU kernels, computation graphs, model server code (e.g., NVIDIA Triton in C++), and feature transformation services (Python). The framework is extensible so new components and optimization strategies can be plugged in, enabling holistic performance search rather than isolated micro-optimizations.
AI.result: Deployed on Unity's Vector advertising platform, FlashVector delivered up to 2x throughput increase and up to 1.98x latency speedup at the model server layer, and up to 1.6x throughput increase on the feature store. The system automatically discovered optimizations not only in GPU kernels and computation graphs but also in higher-level components like the C++ model server and Python-based on-demand feature transformation service.
AI.conclusion: An agentic, extensible optimization framework can successfully generalize from single-kernel GPU tuning to full-stack model serving optimization, achieving substantial real-world performance gains. FlashVector demonstrates that automated agents can effectively optimize heterogeneous, multi-language serving architectures and unlock significant cost and efficiency improvements that are difficult for human experts to realize manually.

title: Psychological Effects of Cultural Upheavals from Millions of Song Lyrics Over 100 Years
summary: Cultural upheavals impact many aspects of social life, and many studies have investigated their impact on language patterns. However, few investigations have isolated the impact of upheavals on individuals at scale in popular media. The current work evaluated millions of song lyrics spanning more than a century in search of within-artist and between-artist signals of distress from the Vietnam War, the terrorist attacks of 9/11, and COVID-19. Compared to a five-year baseline, rates of self-references - a marker of psychological distancing - were significantly reduced after the Vietnam War and September 11th. Cognitive processing terms were elevated post-upheaval vs. pre-upheaval, which indicated artists' increased attempts to make meaning from such massive disruptions. Content patterns corroborated these findings as artists wrote more about "life and freedom" (societal conditions) and less about "courtship and nightlife" (interpersonal connection) following the upheavals. Cultural upheavals modify individual and collective verbal behavior, demonstrating their far-reaching impact on society.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes over a century of song lyrics to detect how major cultural upheavals (Vietnam War, 9/11, COVID-19) change artists’ language, revealing shifts in self-focus, thinking-related words, and thematic content.
AI.motivation: Prior research shows that large social disruptions affect language, but most work looks at broad societal patterns or aggregate media content, not how upheavals show up in the language of individual creators at scale. The authors aim to fill this gap by examining popular music lyrics over time to see how specific historical upheavals alter artists’ verbal expression, both within the same artist and across different artists.
AI.method: The authors compiled millions of song lyrics from over 100 years. They used computational linguistic analysis to quantify changes in language before versus after three major upheavals: the Vietnam War, the 9/11 attacks, and the COVID-19 pandemic. They compared a five-year pre-event baseline with post-event periods, focusing on self-references (e.g., I, me), cognitive processing terms (e.g., think, know, understand), and thematic categories such as references to societal conditions (“life and freedom”) versus interpersonal topics (“courtship and nightlife”). They examined both within-artist changes over time and between-artist patterns.
AI.result: After the Vietnam War and 9/11, song lyrics showed significantly reduced self-references, interpreted as less self-focus or psychological distancing. Cognitive processing terms increased after upheavals relative to the pre-upheaval baseline, suggesting intensified attempts to make sense of the events. Topic/content analysis showed that artists shifted to writing more about societal conditions (e.g., life, freedom) and less about interpersonal themes like romance and nightlife following the upheavals. These patterns appeared at scale across the lyric corpus.
AI.conclusion: Major cultural upheavals systematically reshape the language used in popular music. They lead artists, both individually and collectively, to distance from the self, increase meaning-making and reflective language, and pivot from interpersonal to societal themes. These linguistic shifts highlight how historical crises penetrate creative expression and provide a window into psychological and cultural responses to large-scale disruption.

title: Never Stop Thinking: Continuous-Time Language Agents
summary: Voice agents built on LLMs follow a rigid listen-think-speak loop that inserts seconds of dead air before every reply. We show that continuous-time cognition (thinking while listening and thinking while speaking) emerges from an unmodified text model under a lightweight interrupt-and-resume orchestrator, cutting live-pipeline latency by 19% overall and by half in the regime the mechanism targets. To measure whether continuous-time thinking improves what agents accomplish, we introduce ReactiveBench: 120 interactive scenarios scored against pre-registered binary requirements, plus a verifiable streaming track scored by exact correctness. ReactiveBench exposes a pitfall with broad consequences: LLM judges reward visible reasoning; a large judged "advantage" of continuous-time thinking reverses sign under an independent judge, and judge-trained models objectively complete fewer requirements when they think. A five-stage training study then locates the right signal at three levels. Its source: verifiable objectives turn thinking from harmful to helpful. Its structure: whatever a uniform reward omits, optimization trades away; brevity everywhere erodes multi-hop tool chaining. Its optimizer: preference optimization can only trade conflicting sub-goals against each other, while on-policy RL over a type-shaped reward improves every correctness axis at once, raising streaming completion from 48% to 73+/-5% across seeds and replicating at larger scale and on a second model. Orchestration makes continuous-time interaction possible; a verifiable signal, correctly sourced, shaped, and optimized, makes it good.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a simple orchestration layer that lets LLM-based voice agents think while listening and speaking, reducing latency, and a new benchmark (ReactiveBench) to evaluate whether such “continuous-time thinking” actually improves task completion. It finds that naive use of visible chain-of-thought and judge models can be misleading and even harmful, and shows that using verifiable objectives with carefully shaped, on-policy RL rewards significantly boosts correctness and streaming task completion.
AI.motivation: Current LLM voice agents operate in a strict listen-then-think-then-speak loop, leading to noticeable delays and poor user experience. There is growing interest in having models think continuously (in parallel with listening/speaking), but it is unclear (1) how to implement this efficiently without changing the base model, and (2) whether continuous-time thinking genuinely improves what agents accomplish rather than just changing their style. Moreover, many evaluation setups rely on LLM judges that may be biased toward verbose, visible reasoning, potentially mis-estimating actual task success. The authors are motivated to (a) reduce interaction latency for voice agents, (b) rigorously measure the impact of continuous-time thinking, and (c) understand and correct misaligned training signals that can make additional ‘thinking’ harmful instead of beneficial.
AI.method: 1) Propose a lightweight interrupt-and-resume orchestration scheme on top of an unmodified text LLM that supports overlapping listening, thinking, and speaking, enabling continuous-time cognition in voice agents. 2) Build ReactiveBench, a benchmark of 120 interactive scenarios with pre-registered binary success criteria, plus a streaming evaluation track with verifiable, exact-correctness scoring, to test agents’ actual task completion under different thinking modes. 3) Empirically compare standard listen-think-speak agents vs. continuous-time agents, and analyze discrepancies between LLM-judge-based evaluations and ground-truth, verifiable metrics. 4) Conduct a five-stage training study that varies the source of the learning signal (LLM judges vs. verifiable objectives), the structure of the reward (uniform vs. type-shaped, brevity penalties, etc.), and the optimization algorithm (preference optimization vs. on-policy RL) to see which combinations turn continuous-time thinking from harmful into beneficial. 5) Measure performance changes, especially streaming completion rates and multi-hop tool use, across seeds, scales, and a second model to test robustness and replicability.
AI.result: 1) The interrupt-and-resume orchestrator successfully enables continuous-time thinking on top of standard text LLMs, reducing end-to-end “live pipeline” latency by 19% overall, and by about 50% in the specific interaction regime it targets. 2) ReactiveBench reveals that LLM judge-based evaluations substantially overestimate the benefits of continuous-time thinking: judges strongly reward visible reasoning, leading to a large apparent advantage that disappears or reverses when evaluated by an independent judge or by verifiable success criteria. 3) Models trained to please such judges complete fewer objective requirements when they think more, demonstrating that naive encouragement of chain-of-thought can be harmful. 4) The training study finds that using verifiable, task-grounded objectives flips the effect of thinking from harmful to helpful. Uniform rewards cause optimization to sacrifice behaviors that are not explicitly rewarded, such as longer multi-hop tool chains, due to brevity pressure. 5) Preference optimization alone cannot increase all correctness dimensions simultaneously because it can only trade off conflicting sub-goals, whereas on-policy RL with type-shaped, verifiable rewards improves all correctness axes at once. 6) With this RL setup, streaming task completion rises from 48% to about 73±5% across random seeds, and these gains replicate at larger model scales and on a second base model.
AI.conclusion: Continuous-time cognition in LLM-based voice agents can be realized without modifying the underlying model, via a simple interrupt-and-resume orchestrator that also reduces interaction latency. However, merely adding more ‘thinking’ and optimizing against LLM judges or unstructured rewards can degrade real task performance, because such signals overvalue visible reasoning and brevity while neglecting multi-step correctness. Properly harnessing continuous-time thinking requires verifiable, task-grounded objectives, carefully structured rewards that explicitly encode the needed behaviors, and on-policy RL to optimize them. When these elements are aligned, continuous-time interaction not only becomes practical but also reliably improves objective task completion across models and scales.

title: AraMIP: Extending MIPVU Towards Metaphor Identification in Arabic
comment: Accepted at the Fourth Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference (ArabicNLP 2026), co-located with EMNLP 2026
summary: Metaphor research has gained increasing attention due to its relevance to linguistic creativity, language use, cognitive processes, and related areas. While many efforts have been devoted to metaphor identification and annotation in English and other languages, Arabic remains under-resourced in this area. In this work, we propose the Arabic Metaphor Identification Procedure (AraMIP), a novel guideline for Arabic metaphor annotation. AraMIP builds on the widely used Metaphor Identification Procedure Vrije Universiteit (MIPVU) framework, incorporating adaptations that accounts for the language-specific properties of Arabic. We distinguish three major types of Arabic figurative language: Isti'ara (metaphor), kinaya (metonymy/indirect expression), and tashbih (simile), and annotate a pilot dataset of 300 sentences (5277 words). Our analysis reveals key challenges specific to Arabic, including morphological complexity, inconsistencies in dictionary sense ordering, and the absence of standardized contextual materials for annotators. This work contributes a first step toward standardized Arabic figurative instances and facilitates the development of larger annotated resources, thereby supporting future research on figurative language in Arabic.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AraMIP, a metaphor identification and annotation guideline tailored for Arabic, adapted from MIPVU, and validates it on a small pilot corpus.
AI.motivation: Metaphor and other figurative language are central to linguistic creativity, language use, and cognition, and there has been substantial work on identifying and annotating metaphors in English and some other languages. However, Arabic lacks standardized procedures and annotated resources for figurative language, limiting research and computational modeling for this language. The authors aim to fill this resource and methodology gap.
AI.method: The authors design AraMIP, an Arabic Metaphor Identification Procedure inspired by and adapted from the MIPVU framework. They adjust the procedure to capture Arabic-specific figurative phenomena and structural properties. The method explicitly distinguishes three core types of figurative language in Arabic—isti'ara (metaphor), kinaya (metonymy/indirect expression), and tashbih (simile). They then apply AraMIP to annotate a pilot dataset of 300 sentences (5277 words), using dictionaries and contextual analysis, and examine the challenges encountered during annotation.
AI.result: Using AraMIP, the authors successfully annotate figurative instances in a 300-sentence Arabic corpus, demonstrating the feasibility of their guideline. Their analysis identifies several practical and linguistic challenges: Arabic’s rich morphology complicates sense identification; dictionary sense ordering is inconsistent, which affects decisions about basic vs. contextual meanings; and there is a lack of standardized contextual materials and reference tools for annotators. The pilot annotations provide initial evidence that AraMIP can operate as a structured guideline while highlighting areas where supporting resources are needed.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AraMIP is a viable, Arabic-specific adaptation of MIPVU for metaphor and figurative language annotation. It provides the first systematic step toward standardized identification of Arabic figurative instances across three major categories (metaphor, metonymy/indirect expression, simile). By documenting language-specific challenges, the work lays groundwork for creating larger annotated corpora and improving tools and resources that will support future computational and theoretical research on figurative language in Arabic.

title: World Model Science: Self-Organized Criticality, Weak Chaos, and Metastable Belief Dynamics in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents must maintain task state across extended sequences of observations, actions, tool calls, and intermediate beliefs. We study these trajectories through three dynamical views: self-organized criticality, weak chaos, and metastable belief dynamics. Our framework aligns agent-implied states with benchmark-grounded states and measures stress accumulation, error avalanches, temporal dependence, local--global mismatch, bounded divergence, belief-basin transitions, and finite-size scaling under explicit null models. Across 22 experiments spanning controlled puzzles, tool use, embodied tasks, multi-hop retrieval, general-assistant reasoning, and Game of Life, we find that locally valid actions can persist after global state fidelity fails, stress can trigger abrupt collapse, error sequences exhibit long memory, dependency depth changes the propagation regime, and larger horizons support larger avalanches. At the same time, divergence remains bounded, belief states show metastable rather than fully chaotic behavior, and stronger claims of universal power laws, critical points, or shared intervention optima are not supported. These results suggest a science of agent world models based on trajectory-level dynamical diagnostics rather than terminal reward alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamical-systems framework to analyze long-horizon LLM agents by examining their full trajectories rather than just final performance, revealing structured but bounded forms of instability and error cascades in their world models.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents must keep track of complex, evolving task states over many steps, yet most evaluations focus on final reward or accuracy and ignore how internal beliefs and errors evolve over time. There is a need for a principled way to study the dynamics of these agents’ world models, including when and how they fail, how errors propagate, and whether their behavior resembles known phenomena like criticality or chaos.
AI.method: The authors analyze agent trajectories through three lenses from dynamical systems and statistical physics: self-organized criticality, weak chaos, and metastable belief dynamics. They align the states implied by the agent (its internal beliefs and chosen actions) with ground-truth benchmark states, then define and measure quantities such as stress accumulation, error avalanches, temporal dependence, local–global mismatch, bounded divergence, belief-basin transitions, and finite-size scaling. They compare results against explicit null models and apply this framework to 22 experiments covering puzzles, tool use, embodied tasks, multi-hop retrieval, general reasoning, and cellular automata (Game of Life).
AI.result: Across diverse tasks, trajectories show that agents can continue taking locally reasonable actions even after their global understanding of the task state has broken down. Stress can accumulate and then cause abrupt collapses in performance, while sequences of errors show long temporal memory. The way errors propagate depends on the depth of interdependence in the task, and longer horizons allow larger error avalanches. However, divergence between agent beliefs and ground truth stays bounded, belief dynamics are metastable rather than fully chaotic, and empirical evidence does not robustly support strong claims of universal power laws, true critical points, or shared optimal interventions across settings.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon LLM agent behavior is best understood through trajectory-level dynamical diagnostics rather than only terminal rewards or static benchmarks. The agents exhibit structured, metastable belief dynamics with bounded divergence and task-dependent error cascades, challenging simple narratives of full chaos or universal criticality. This suggests the need for a “science of agent world models” grounded in dynamical analysis to better characterize, predict, and improve long-horizon agent performance.

title: ECHO: Early-layer Collaborative Hierarchical Orchestration with Bonus Logits in Speculative Decoding
summary: While draft-model-free speculative decoding offers a promising path to efficient LLM inference, it is frequently constrained by stale draft candidates and the high computational cost of the verification. To address these challenges, we propose ECHO, a hierarchical dual-loop framework that exploits the functional asymmetry between LLM layers. Leveraging the high discriminative efficiency of early layers and the authoritative distribution of final layers, ECHO bifurcates inference into a high-frequency inner loop and a low-frequency outer loop. Within the inner loop, early-layer bonus logits drive rapid, multi-step draft-tree exploration at a minimal cost. Simultaneously, the outer loop performs authoritative full-model verification through a state-reuse mechanism. Crucially, the outer loop also utilizes final-layer bonus logits to correct existing paths and supplement the tree with high-confidence candidates for subsequent cycles. Experimental results across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that ECHO significantly boosts mean accepted tokens and achieves a 2.4$\times$ to 2.9$\times$ speedup, outperforming existing state-of-the-art baselines with negligible engineering overhead and no extra deployment parameters, albeit with a one-shot fine-tuning dependency for optimal acceleration. The code is available at https://github.com/whucs21Mzy/ECHO.

AI.tldr: ECHO is a hierarchical dual-loop speculative decoding framework that uses early-layer logits for cheap draft exploration and final-layer logits for authoritative verification, significantly speeding up LLM inference with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Draft-model-free speculative decoding can accelerate LLM inference but suffers from stale draft candidates and expensive verification, limiting its practical efficiency. There is a need to better exploit the internal structure of LLMs—especially the differing roles of early vs. late layers—to improve speculative decoding without adding deployment complexity or extra models.
AI.method: The authors introduce ECHO, a hierarchical dual-loop framework that separates inference into: (1) a high-frequency inner loop that uses early-layer bonus logits to conduct rapid, multi-step draft-tree exploration at low cost; and (2) a low-frequency outer loop that performs full-model verification with a state-reuse mechanism. The outer loop also uses final-layer bonus logits both to correct previously explored paths and to enrich the draft tree with high-confidence candidates for future inner-loop steps. A one-shot fine-tuning step is used to maximize acceleration while keeping engineering overhead low and avoiding extra deployment parameters.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, ECHO increases the mean number of accepted tokens per verification and attains a 2.4×–2.9× inference speedup over state-of-the-art speculative decoding baselines. These gains are achieved with negligible engineering overhead, no additional deployment-time parameters, and only a one-shot fine-tuning requirement.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging the functional asymmetry between early and late LLM layers in a dual-loop speculative decoding framework, ECHO substantially improves the efficiency of LLM inference. It overcomes limitations of stale drafts and costly verification, delivering significant speedups without added deployment complexity, and shows that hierarchical, layer-aware speculative decoding is a practical and effective direction for accelerating LLMs.

title: Transformer-Based Token Fusion and Dynamic Graph Planning for Audio-Visual Navigation
comment: Main paper (6 pages). Accepted for publication by IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 2026 (IEEE SMC 2026)
summary: Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to localize and navigate toward a continuously vocalizing target relying solely on visual observations and acoustic cues. Currently, systems lack the ability to adaptively correct and replan when faced with incomplete or misleading visual perception. Furthermore, relying on physical collisions to compensate for missing visual information results in inefficient and unsafe navigation, whereas existing methods are overly dependent on passive visual perception. To address these issues, we propose the Transformer-based Token Fusion and Dynamic Graph Planning (TDGP) model, which incorporates high-level perception layers and leverages the Transformer model to fuse multimodal cues for precise local planning. Next, a low-level planning layer is designed that uses physical collision penalties to remove edges that collide with the map in real time and apply corresponding penalties, forcing the agent to automatically re-plan to compensate for the lack of visual information. Experiments show that our TDGP model outperforms baseline models on the Replica and Matterport3D (MP3D) datasets, and that the model's sound enhancement strategy significantly improves generalization in unheard acoustic scenarios.

AI.tldr: They propose TDGP, a transformer-based audio-visual navigation model that fuses multimodal cues and dynamically updates a planning graph with collision-based penalties, achieving superior performance and better generalization on Replica and MP3D benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-visual navigation agents struggle when visual observations are incomplete or misleading, and often rely on unsafe, inefficient physical collisions to make up for missing information. Current methods are also too dependent on passive visual perception and cannot adaptively correct or replan their paths. There is a need for a navigation framework that can robustly fuse audio-visual cues and proactively replan when visual information is unreliable, without relying on excessive collisions.
AI.method: They introduce TDGP (Transformer-based Token Fusion and Dynamic Graph Planning), which has two main components. A high-level perception layer uses a Transformer to fuse visual and acoustic tokens into a rich multimodal representation for local planning. A low-level planning layer maintains a dynamic navigation graph: when the agent experiences collisions, the corresponding graph edges are penalized or removed in real time, forcing route replanning to avoid unsafe or occluded regions and implicitly compensate for missing visual information. Additionally, they apply a sound enhancement strategy to improve robustness to novel acoustic conditions.
AI.result: On the Replica and Matterport3D (MP3D) datasets, TDGP outperforms baseline audio-visual navigation methods, indicating better navigation efficiency and target localization. The sound enhancement strategy further improves the model's generalization in previously unheard acoustic environments, leading to stronger robustness across different sound conditions.
AI.conclusion: TDGP demonstrates that transformer-based multimodal token fusion combined with dynamic graph planning can significantly improve robustness and efficiency in audio-visual navigation. By leveraging collision feedback to update the navigation graph and replan paths, the agent can compensate for incomplete or misleading visual input without relying on unsafe collision behaviors. The proposed sound enhancement techniques further extend the model's applicability to diverse, unseen acoustic scenarios.

title: Persistent Recurrent Memory Between Transformer Layers - Improves Language Model Generalization
summary: We introduce a simple architectural modification to decoder-only transformers: a persistent recurrent state that observes hidden representations via cross-attention, updates itself through a GRU, and modulates subsequent processing via gated addition. Inserted between the lower and upper halves of a 6-layer transformer, this module adds only 3.7\% additional parameters while reducing evaluation loss from $2.438 \pm 0.004$ to $1.743 \pm 0.018$, corresponding to a 28.5\% reduction on held-out language modeling data. The improvement is statistically significant across 5 random seeds ($p < 0.01$) and corresponds to reduced overfitting (generalization gap 0.12 vs 0.26). Through controlled ablations, we demonstrate that the improvement stems entirely from the persistent memory topology, not from auxiliary self-prediction objectives. A model with identical topology but no auxiliary loss performs equivalently, while a random auxiliary loss provides no benefit. Representation probing reveals that the persistent state encodes narrative position (52\% vs 33\% chance level)---information that standard attention maintains less efficiently. Our results suggest that bridging transformer layers with a lightweight recurrent memory is a simple, effective approach to improving generalization in small-scale language models.

AI.tldr: They add a small recurrent memory module to the middle of a decoder-only transformer, greatly improving language modeling performance with minimal extra parameters.
AI.motivation: Standard decoder-only transformers lack a persistent memory across timesteps beyond the attention context, which can limit their ability to track long-range narrative structure, especially in small models prone to overfitting. The authors want a simple way to enhance generalization and representational capacity without large parameter increases or complex training tricks.
AI.method: They insert a persistent recurrent state module between the lower and upper halves of a 6-layer decoder-only transformer. This state: (1) reads current hidden representations via cross-attention, (2) updates via a GRU, and (3) feeds back into later layers via gated addition. They compare models with and without this module, run multiple random seeds, assess evaluation loss and generalization gap, perform ablations on auxiliary self-prediction losses, and probe what information the persistent state encodes (e.g., narrative position).
AI.result: With only 3.7% more parameters, the modified model’s evaluation loss drops from 2.438±0.004 to 1.743±0.018, a 28.5% reduction on held-out language modeling data, and the generalization gap shrinks from 0.26 to 0.12. The gains are statistically significant over 5 seeds (p<0.01). Ablations show that these gains are due solely to the persistent memory architecture; adding or randomizing auxiliary losses does not help. Probing finds the persistent state captures narrative position substantially better than standard attention (52% vs 33% chance level).
AI.conclusion: A lightweight recurrent memory that bridges transformer layers can substantially improve generalization and narrative-structure representation in small decoder-only language models with minimal parameter overhead. The benefits come from the architectural memory topology itself, not from auxiliary training objectives, suggesting a simple, practical direction for enhancing transformer-based LMs.

title: Talking Head Synthesis with Facial Landmark Guidance via 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: Main paper (6 pages). Accepted for publication by IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 2026 (IEEE SMC 2026)
summary: Audio-driven digital human generation plays an important role in virtual communication, immersive interaction, and media production. With the development of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), recent talking-head systems have obtained more faithful 3D facial geometry and appearance modeling. A remaining difficulty is that speech features mainly describe temporal acoustic patterns rather than explicit facial layouts. As a result, directly driving 3D facial deformation with audio may produce inaccurate mouth motion, weak expression details, and local artifacts. To address this issue, we propose a facial-keypoint-guided spatial enhancement module. The predicted landmarks provide structural cues for selecting and enriching spatial points around expression-sensitive facial regions. We further introduce a global landmark compensation mechanism, where the full set of keypoints is encoded into a conditioning vector to refine 3DGS attributes. This compensation supplies whole-face structural information to the underlying shape representation. Experiments under self-driven and cross-driven settings show that the proposed method improves visual quality, facial realism, and lip synchronization.

AI.tldr: The paper improves audio-driven 3D talking-head generation by adding facial-keypoint guidance to 3D Gaussian Splatting, yielding better visual realism and lip-sync.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-driven digital humans using NeRF/3DGS capture 3D geometry and appearance well but struggle because audio describes temporal acoustics rather than explicit facial layouts, leading to inaccurate mouth motion, weak expressions, and artifacts. The authors want to bridge the gap between audio features and precise, realistic facial deformations.
AI.method: They introduce a facial-keypoint-guided spatial enhancement module: predicted 2D/3D facial landmarks are used as structural cues to select and enrich spatial points around expression-sensitive facial regions in the 3DGS representation. In addition, they propose a global landmark compensation mechanism that encodes the full set of facial keypoints into a conditioning vector that refines the attributes of all Gaussians, injecting whole-face structural information into the shape representation. The system is evaluated under self-driven (same identity) and cross-driven (audio from a different identity) settings.
AI.result: Compared with baselines that directly drive 3D facial deformation from audio, their method produces more accurate mouth movement, richer expression details, and fewer local artifacts. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate improved visual quality, facial realism, and lip synchronization in both self-driven and cross-driven scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating facial landmarks as explicit structural guidance into audio-driven 3DGS-based talking-head synthesis effectively bridges the gap between audio features and facial geometry. The proposed spatial enhancement and global landmark compensation mechanisms lead to more realistic, temporally coherent, and better lip-synchronized digital humans, suggesting that keypoint-guided conditioning is a promising direction for future talking-head generation systems.

title: Towards Illusions Awareness in Cyber-Physical System's Design
summary: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) operate through a continuous sense-compute-act loop within an open context environment, making it impossible to anticipate all the situations the system will face. To cope with this openness, stakeholders rely on assumptions, formalized into design models. However, these assumptions may no longer hold once the system is confronted with runtime reality, resulting in a discrepancy between expected and observed behaviour known in literature as the reality gap. Existing approaches mainly focus on reducing or overcoming it by making simulations more faithful to reality, with no unified methodology to structure and exploit invalidated assumptions that give rise to this gap as reusable design knowledge. We refer to the persistent reliance on invalidated assumptions -and the resulting false confidence in the design model's operational validity -as design illusions, and argue that they need to be made explicit, structured, and exploited as knowledge to support better design decisions. We propose a conceptual pipeline for illusions-awareness that identifies, classifies, characterizes, and leverages illusions to transform them into actionable design knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the notion of “design illusions” in Cyber-Physical Systems—continued belief in assumptions that runtime reality has invalidated—and proposes a conceptual pipeline to detect, structure, and reuse these illusions as design knowledge.
AI.motivation: Cyber-Physical Systems operate in open, unpredictable environments, so design-time assumptions often fail at runtime, creating a reality gap between expected and actual behavior. Current work mainly seeks to shrink this gap via better simulations, but lacks a systematic way to capture and reuse the invalidated assumptions themselves as knowledge. This leaves designers with hidden risks and missed learning opportunities when assumptions break down.
AI.method: The authors define and conceptualize “design illusions” as persistent reliance on invalidated assumptions and then propose an illusions-awareness pipeline. This conceptual pipeline includes steps to identify where assumptions fail at runtime, classify and characterize the resulting illusions, and structure them so they can be reused as design knowledge in future CPS design iterations.
AI.result: The main result is a conceptual framework rather than an implemented tool: a unified methodology (pipeline) for turning invalidated assumptions—design illusions—into explicit, organized, and reusable design knowledge, thereby helping stakeholders reason better about CPS behavior under real-world conditions.
AI.conclusion: By making design illusions explicit and systematically processing them, designers can better understand and manage the reality gap in CPS. This illusions-awareness pipeline supports more informed design decisions, reduces false confidence in models, and encourages the reuse of lessons learned from failed assumptions in future CPS development.

title: JustFit: 200K-Token LLM Serving on a 24 GiB Laptop with Just-in-Time State Management
summary: Capable open-weight models make local coding and reasoning attractive, but their context and execution state strain laptop memory. We present JustFit, an MLX-based inference runtime that combines KVExec for compressed KV execution, PhaseSwap for component residency, and StateTrans for state-preserving serving transitions. These mechanisms fuse reconstruction and coordinate just-in-time materialization and release, independently of model-weight quantization. In full-execution capacity tests on a 24 GiB M4 Pro MacBook running Qwen3.8-27B MXFP4, three independent runs complete 196,608 input and 16,384 output tokens, increasing completed single-request context from the mlx-vlm baseline's 30,720 positions to 212,992 (6.93x); a separate two-request run retains 229,376 positions in aggregate. In separate performance tests, a 32K-input, 64-output probe reaches 19.11 tokens/s, and a repeated 32K+6K workload has a median peak process footprint of 16,374 MiB. The integrated runtime answers 29 of 30 AIME 2026 problems correctly, showing how compact state and lifetime-aware execution expand local serving capacity while supporting extended generated reasoning.

AI.tldr: JustFit is an MLX-based runtime that enables large open-weight LLMs to run locally with much larger effective context and stable performance by compressing and virtualizing KV/state rather than relying only on weight quantization.
AI.motivation: Running strong open-weight LLMs locally is constrained by laptop GPU/Unified memory, especially for long-context reasoning and multi-step chains where KV cache and execution state dominate memory. Existing approaches mainly quantize weights but do little for runtime state, limiting usable context length and concurrent requests. The authors want to push the effective context and serving capacity of local models (on machines like a 24 GiB MacBook) while preserving high reasoning quality.
AI.method: They build JustFit, an inference runtime on top of Apple’s MLX with three main mechanisms: (1) KVExec, which executes with compressed KV representations, reducing memory pressure from the attention cache; (2) PhaseSwap, which manages which model components are resident in memory at each execution phase, swapping parts in and out to respect memory limits; and (3) StateTrans, which coordinates state-preserving transitions between different serving configurations or phases, enabling just-in-time reconstruction and release of state. These are integrated so that reconstruction and materialization of state are coordinated and independent of model weight quantization schemes.
AI.result: On a 24 GiB M4 Pro MacBook running Qwen3.8-27B with MXFP4 quantization, they achieve three full runs of 196,608 input tokens plus 16,384 output tokens in a single request, expanding max completed context from an mlx-vlm baseline of 30,720 to 212,992 positions (6.93x). In a two-request setting, they retain 229,376 positions in total. Performance benchmarks show 19.11 tokens/s on a 32K-input, 64-output probe, and a repeated 32K+6K workload has a median peak memory footprint of about 16.4 GiB. On the AIME 2026 benchmark, the runtime answers 29/30 problems correctly, confirming that these memory optimizations still support strong long-form reasoning.
AI.conclusion: By aggressively managing KV and execution state via KVExec, PhaseSwap, and StateTrans instead of relying solely on model-weight quantization, JustFit substantially increases the usable context window and serving capacity of large open-weight models on constrained local hardware, maintains good throughput and modest memory footprint, and preserves high reasoning quality on challenging math benchmarks.

title: Zero-shot narrative detection in social messaging
summary: This study investigates the zero-shot ability of large language models (LLMs) to identify and classify hidden narratives in social messages. Our research hypothesis is that LLMs' extensive contextual knowledge allows them to interpret messages on a deeper, pragmatic level, going beyond basic sentiment or topic analysis. Experiments on the Dipromats and SemEval datasets show that providing models with human-written narrative descriptions significantly improves performance, without the need of training examples. In contrast, automatically generated descriptions or the use of few examples (few-shot) often degrade accuracy due to subtle shifts in framing. The study also finds that ensemble methods, particularly majority voting, enhance robustness and that larger models perform best while also being less sensitive to prompt variations. The findings validate that LLMs can effectively detect strategic narratives in a zero-shot setting, and when combined with simple ensembling and human-written descriptions, they can rival supervised systems, offering a scalable solution for narrative detection, specially when there is no training data for the vast majority of domains.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language models can detect hidden strategic narratives in social messages without task-specific training, showing that zero-shot prompting with human-written narrative descriptions plus simple ensembling can approach supervised performance.
AI.motivation: Most narrative detection systems require supervised training data, which is hard to obtain across the many domains and topics where strategic narratives appear. The authors want to know whether modern LLMs, with their broad world knowledge and pragmatic understanding, can detect such narratives in a zero-shot way, enabling scalable analysis when labeled data are scarce or absent.
AI.method: The authors use LLMs in zero-shot mode to classify messages from the Dipromats and SemEval datasets according to underlying narratives. They compare prompts that include human-written narrative descriptions against prompts with automatically generated descriptions, and against few-shot prompts using a small set of labeled examples. They systematically vary prompts to assess sensitivity to framing and model size, and evaluate ensemble strategies such as majority voting across multiple runs or models to measure robustness and performance gains.
AI.result: Including human-written narrative descriptions in the prompt markedly improves zero-shot narrative detection performance, enabling LLMs to achieve accuracy close to that of supervised systems. Automatically generated descriptions or few-shot examples often reduce performance, likely due to subtle framing shifts that mislead the model. Larger LLMs outperform smaller ones and show less sensitivity to prompt variations. Ensemble methods, especially majority voting, further enhance robustness and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can reliably detect strategic narratives in social messages in a zero-shot setting when guided by carefully crafted, human-written narrative descriptions. Simple ensemble methods and larger models make the approach more robust and accurate. This combination can rival supervised systems while avoiding the need for domain-specific training data, making it a scalable solution for narrative detection in diverse and low-resource domains.

title: LimiX-2: A Contextual Mechanism Network Towards General Structured-Data Intelligence
summary: We introduce LimiX-2, a new model in the LimiX family, developed through model and data scaling guided by our previously established scaling laws. LimiX-2 adopts the Contextual Mechanism Networks (CMNs) paradigm and is pretrained with Context-Conditional Masked Modeling (CCMM). CMNs shifts the organizing principle of in-context learning from target-centric prediction to mechanism-oriented joint modeling. Rather than centering the network on the $p(y \mid x, D_{\mathrm{context}})$ objective of conventional tabular PFNs, it is designed around learning $p(x, y \mid D_{\mathrm{context}})$, a context-dependent representation of the joint structure underlying data generation. Pretraining uses synthetic datasets generated by structural causal models (SCMs) spanning diverse graph structures, functional mechanisms, and observation processes. Evaluations on TabArena, TALENT, and BCCO show that LimiX-2 outperforms current dataset-specific models and tabular foundation models. Beyond predictive performance, the CMN paradigm also promotes causal awareness in LimiX-2: its feature attention encodes direct causal relationships, enabling accurate causal skeleton recovery.

AI.tldr: LimiX-2 is a new tabular foundation model based on Contextual Mechanism Networks and trained with synthetic causal data, achieving state-of-the-art prediction and showing causal awareness.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular foundation models focus on predicting labels given inputs and context, but they often fail to capture the underlying data-generating mechanisms or causal structure. The authors previously derived scaling laws for this model family and now aim to exploit those insights to build a stronger, more causally aware model for tabular learning that generalizes across many datasets.
AI.method: They design LimiX-2 under the Contextual Mechanism Networks (CMNs) paradigm, which models the joint distribution p(x,y | D_context) instead of the usual conditional p(y | x, D_context). The model is pretrained by Context-Conditional Masked Modeling (CCMM) on large synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models (SCMs) with diverse graph structures, mechanisms, and observation processes, so it learns generic data-generating patterns. After pretraining, they evaluate the model on standard tabular benchmarks.
AI.result: On the TabArena, TALENT, and BCCO benchmarks, LimiX-2 surpasses existing dataset-specific models and prior tabular foundation models in predictive performance. Analyses of its internal attention patterns show that the model’s feature attention aligns with direct causal relations in the underlying SCMs, allowing accurate recovery of the causal skeleton.
AI.conclusion: By organizing learning around mechanism-oriented joint modeling and pretraining on diverse synthetic SCM-generated data, LimiX-2 establishes a new state of the art for tabular prediction while also demonstrating emergent causal awareness. The Contextual Mechanism Networks paradigm appears promising as a foundation for models that are both accurate and structurally interpretable in terms of underlying causal mechanisms.

title: Towards Detecting AI-Assisted Responses in Online Surveys
summary: The use of LLMs to complete online surveys impacts the validity of survey-based research, but detecting such usage remains underexplored. We introduce an initial benchmark dataset, namely ASURRE, for AI-assisted survey participation to capture usage strategies ranging from full generation and revision to persona-grounded agentic completion. Controlled by these strategies, LLM-assisted survey responses are generated using multiple LLMs on three real-world surveys in different disciplines, paired with genuine human responses. Our evaluation of existing machine-generated text (MGT) detectors shows that naive AI usage is readily detectable, whereas persona-grounded agents that mimic entire respondents push detector performance toward chance. We further show that agentic completion cannot fully replicate respondent-level behaviour and leaves distinctive behavioural traces. While individual cues can be circumvented by targeted prompting, a simple few-shot, training-free aggregator over these cues improves mean AUROC by +0.14 over the best existing detector across agentic settings. Our project is available at https://github.com/mike-qz-wang/ASURRE.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to detect survey responses written with help from large language models (LLMs) and introduces a benchmark dataset (ASURRE) plus a simple cue-based detector that outperforms existing tools, especially when LLMs act as persona-driven agents.
AI.motivation: More people may use LLMs to fill in online surveys, which threatens the validity of survey-based research. However, detecting when survey answers are LLM-assisted, especially in sophisticated ways, is not well understood or benchmarked, creating a need for systematic datasets and evaluations.
AI.method: The authors construct ASURRE, a benchmark dataset of AI-assisted survey responses generated under different usage strategies (full generation, revision, and persona-grounded agentic completion) across three real-world surveys in different disciplines, paired with genuine human responses. They test multiple existing machine-generated text detectors on these data, analyse their performance across usage strategies, and study behavioural traces that distinguish persona-grounded agentic LLM responses from human respondents. They then propose a simple, training-free, few-shot aggregator that combines multiple behavioural cues to detect agentic LLM completions and compare its AUROC against existing detectors.
AI.result: Existing detectors easily catch naive, fully LLM-generated survey answers, but their performance drops to near chance when facing persona-grounded LLM agents that mimic whole respondents. The authors find that agentic completion still leaves distinctive behavioural traces that can be exploited. A lightweight, few-shot cue aggregator that combines these traces improves mean AUROC by 0.14 over the best baseline detector across agentic settings.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted responses pose a serious challenge for survey validity, especially when LLMs are used in sophisticated, persona-driven ways that evade current MGT detectors. Nonetheless, such uses leave detectable behavioural patterns, and even simple, training-free aggregations of multiple cues can substantially improve detection. ASURRE provides an initial benchmark to systematically study and improve detection of AI-assisted survey participation.

title: Verifiable Social Reasoning for LLM Assistants
comment: First two authors contributed equally and the order between them was chosen randomly
summary: LLM assistants are widely used for daily social advice, yet evaluating their social reasoning in such consultation settings remains challenging since (i) it requires setups where the assistant learns about social situations from subjective user narratives, and (ii) social properties, such as others' intentions, typically lack verifiable ground truth. To address these challenges, we introduce Fuse, a multi-agent simulation framework for studying user-mediated social reasoning. In Fuse, a target agent with a hidden motive interacts with other agents including one representing the user, who then consults the evaluated assistant to infer the target's motive, providing verifiable ground truth by construction. Simulation faithfulness is validated through a human study with 24k annotations. We apply Fuse to 12 LLMs and demonstrate its analytical utility by systematically isolating key factors, showing that (i) user mediation compounds the inherent difficulty of social reasoning; (ii) LLMs exhibit systematic sensitivity to biased user framing; (iii) models can require more details than humans need to reach a correct prediction; and (iv) longer conversations do not always improve performance despite providing opportunities for clarifying questions. We open-source Fuse and a dataset with 21k examples.

AI.tldr: Fuse is a multi-agent simulation framework that evaluates LLMs’ social reasoning in user-consultation settings by providing synthetic but verifiable ground truth about agents’ hidden motives.
AI.motivation: Evaluating social reasoning of LLM assistants in realistic advice-seeking scenarios is hard because the assistant must interpret subjective user narratives and because key social properties (e.g., others’ intentions) usually lack objective, verifiable labels. Existing benchmarks often bypass these issues by using simplified tasks or externally annotated ground truths that do not reflect interactive consultation. The paper aims to build a controlled yet realistic environment where an assistant reasons about social situations mediated by a user, while also allowing precise measurement and analysis of performance.
AI.method: The authors design Fuse, a multi-agent simulation where a target agent is assigned a hidden motive and interacts with other agents, including a special agent that represents the user. The user-agent observes or participates in the interaction, then consults the evaluated LLM assistant to infer the target agent’s hidden motive. Because the motive is specified in the simulation, it serves as ground truth. The framework generates conversations and user narratives, then queries LLMs under different configurations (e.g., with or without user mediation, with various framings and detail levels, with different conversation lengths). The realism and faithfulness of the simulations are validated via a large human study with 24k annotations. The authors then evaluate 12 different LLMs on the Fuse-generated tasks and analyze their behavior across the controlled factors.
AI.result: The experiments reveal several consistent patterns: (i) When the LLM must reason through user-mediated narratives instead of direct access to the underlying interaction, performance in inferring the target’s hidden motive drops, indicating that user mediation adds difficulty. (ii) LLMs are systematically influenced by biased user framings and can be steered toward incorrect inferences. (iii) Compared to humans, LLMs often require more contextual details to reach correct social inferences, suggesting less efficient use of sparse or ambiguous cues. (iv) Extending the length of conversations does not reliably improve LLM performance, even though more turns give opportunities for clarification questions; in some cases, longer interactions may introduce noise or confusion. The authors also release a dataset of 21k examples produced via Fuse.
AI.conclusion: Fuse provides a controlled, user-mediated evaluation framework for social reasoning that overcomes the lack of ground truth in natural social interactions by embedding hidden motives within multi-agent simulations. The human validation suggests the simulated setups are sufficiently faithful for meaningful analysis. Using Fuse, the paper shows that current LLMs struggle with user-mediated social reasoning, are vulnerable to biased framing, and do not always benefit from more conversational context, highlighting important gaps between human and model social inference. The open-sourced framework and dataset are intended as a testbed for developing and benchmarking more robust, socially competent LLM assistants.

title: Vroom-Vroom at SHROOM-Visions: A Multi-Judge Committee for Detecting Hallucinated Spans in Vision-Language Outputs
comment: Accepted to UncertaiNLP 2026 @ EMNLP. SHROOM-Visions 2026 shared task system description
summary: This paper describes our submission to the SHROOM-Visions shared task on detecting and classifying hallucinated character spans in vision-language model outputs across four languages. We employ several fine-tuned vision-language models as independent annotators and combine their span predictions through character-level majority voting, and additionally explore activation probes. The approach ranks first in three of four languages and places on the podium in every language and metric. Our analysis indicates that disagreement among diverse models tracks disagreement among human annotators.

AI.tldr: They build an ensemble of fine-tuned vision-language models to detect and classify hallucinated text spans in model outputs, using majority voting and activation probes, achieving top performance in a multilingual shared task.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in vision-language models can cause them to describe content that is not present in the image, which is problematic for reliability. The SHROOM-Visions shared task focuses on detecting and categorizing such hallucinated spans across multiple languages, requiring robust automatic methods.
AI.method: Use several fine-tuned vision-language models as independent annotators that each predict hallucinated character spans. Combine their outputs via character-level majority voting to obtain final span predictions. Additionally, experiment with activation probes to better understand or enhance hallucination detection.
AI.result: The ensemble approach achieves first place in three of the four task languages and finishes on the podium (top ranks) for every language and evaluation metric in the shared task leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: An ensemble of diverse vision-language models with character-level majority voting is highly effective for detecting and classifying hallucinated spans in multilingual settings, and model disagreement patterns seem to mirror human annotator disagreement, suggesting that model diversity is a useful signal for uncertainty and ambiguity in hallucination detection.

title: ScienceBuddy: Recursive-in-Recursive Self-Improvement for Interactive Scientific Agents
summary: We introduce and release ScienceBuddy, an interactive scientific research workspace that brings continually improving scientific agents into researchers' everyday workflows. ScienceBuddy supports researchers in carrying out scientific tasks while transforming their requests, feedback, and execution evidence into tasks and evaluation rubrics for continual learning. At its core is recursive-in-recursive self-improvement, a paradigm that couples harness evolution with model reinforcement learning: the inner recursion improves the harness with the model fixed, while the outer recursion trains the model under the improved harness. Harness evolution shapes training experience, and model learning creates new opportunities for harness adaptation. We present case studies of researcher interaction, harness refinement, and model learning, with the benchmark cases spanning four scientific task families. By releasing ScienceBuddy as a research product, we make this paradigm available to the scientific community and take a step toward discovery intelligence: scientific AI that advances through sustained collaboration with researchers and evolves alongside the research it supports. Website: http://science-buddy.io

AI.tldr: The paper presents ScienceBuddy, an interactive AI research workspace that continuously improves itself by learning from researchers’ real workflows.
AI.motivation: To move beyond static scientific AI benchmarks and build an AI assistant that can genuinely co-evolve with researchers, learning from real scientific tasks, feedback, and outcomes instead of only from offline datasets or fixed evaluations.
AI.method: They design ScienceBuddy as an interactive system that turns researchers’ requests, feedback, and execution traces into structured tasks and evaluation rubrics. The technical core is a ‘recursive-in-recursive’ self-improvement paradigm: an inner recursion evolves the task harness—tools, prompts, evaluation criteria—while holding the model fixed; an outer recursion then uses the improved harness to train and adapt the underlying model via reinforcement learning. This cycle is iterated so that better harnesses improve model training, and better models in turn enable more sophisticated harness evolution.
AI.result: Through case studies on four families of scientific tasks, they show that (1) researchers can effectively work within ScienceBuddy on real tasks, (2) the harnesses become more refined and better aligned with user needs over time, and (3) the underlying model’s performance improves as it is trained under these evolving harnesses. The benchmark-style cases illustrate measurable gains tied to this co-evolutionary process.
AI.conclusion: ScienceBuddy operationalizes a new paradigm—recursive-in-recursive self-improvement—for building scientific AI that continuously learns from and with researchers. By releasing it as a research product, the authors aim to provide the community with a platform for “discovery intelligence,” where AI systems and human scientists jointly and iteratively advance scientific research.

title: Where Should a Document Live: Context, Representations, or Parameters?
summary: To answer questions outside of their pre-training data, large language models (LLMs) need access to new information, which can be presented in the context window as documents, encoded into the model's parameters, or injected as latent representations. However, each of these methods comes with different efficiency, cost, and performance trade-offs, with no single winner. We present a controlled comparison of representation-based (KV-cache based) and parametric (fine-tuning-based) adaptation methods on five knowledge-intensive benchmarks. We show that in the oracle setting, Cartridges (KV) are the most accurate injection method at nearly every storage budget, outperforming parametric methods by 10 points. Compaction (KV) matches Cartridges only at low compression rates, lagging behind the parametric methods by 10 points at rates higher than $50\times$. In the more realistic multi-document retrieval scenario, Cartridges are the only method that matches in-context learning (ICL), leading the parametric methods by 29 points and Compaction by 15 points. Nonetheless, Cartridges are also the only method, besides full fine-tuning and large MLP adapters, that suffers from catastrophic forgetting, i.e., a 6% performance degradation on control benchmarks, with 13% in coding.

AI.tldr: The paper compares different ways to inject new knowledge into LLMs and finds KV-cache-based Cartridges are generally the most accurate at a given storage budget, but they can cause catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: LLMs need up-to-date or task-specific knowledge that is not present in their pre-training data. There are multiple ways to provide this new information—via context, via parameter updates (fine-tuning), or via latent representations like KV caches—but each has different trade-offs and it is unclear which is best under realistic constraints. The paper aims to systematically, and in a controlled way, compare these approaches on knowledge-intensive tasks.
AI.method: The authors run controlled experiments on five knowledge-intensive benchmarks, comparing representation-based adaptation methods (primarily KV-cache based approaches like Cartridges and a compressed variant called Compaction) with parametric adaptation methods (full fine-tuning and various adapter sizes). They measure accuracy under different storage budgets and compression rates, and they evaluate both an oracle setting (where the best possible document/knowledge is assumed available) and a more realistic multi-document retrieval setting. They also test for catastrophic forgetting using separate control benchmarks, including coding tasks.
AI.result: In the oracle setting, KV-cache Cartridges consistently outperform parametric approaches across almost all storage budgets, with around a 10-point accuracy advantage. Compaction, a compressed KV approach, only matches Cartridge performance at low compression; beyond 50× compression, its accuracy drops, trailing parametric methods by about 10 points. In realistic multi-document retrieval, Cartridges are the only method that matches the performance of in-context learning (ICL), outperforming parametric methods by 29 points and Compaction by 15 points. However, Cartridges, like full fine-tuning and large MLP adapters, show catastrophic forgetting, with roughly 6% degradation on control benchmarks and up to 13% degradation on coding tasks.
AI.conclusion: KV-cache based Cartridges are a highly effective way to inject new knowledge into LLMs, providing superior accuracy across storage budgets and in realistic retrieval scenarios compared to both compressed KV methods and parametric fine-tuning. However, they share an important drawback with heavy parametric adaptation methods: catastrophic forgetting on unrelated tasks. Compressed KV methods such as Compaction offer better storage efficiency but lose accuracy at higher compression ratios. Overall, the paper highlights a key trade-off between performance, storage, and preservation of existing capabilities when choosing a knowledge injection method for LLMs.

title: ECHO: A Matched-Contrast Benchmark for Context-Sensitive Turn-Taking in Full-Duplex Dialogue
summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems must distinguish interruptions that require yielding the floor from backchannels that permit continued speaking. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate events independently and may therefore reward fixed action preferences rather than context-sensitive decisions. We introduce ECHO, a paired diagnostic benchmark for Chinese full-duplex turn-taking. ECHO pairs examples with the same overlap transcript but contrasting preceding multi-turn dialogue contexts, with one requiring Yield and the other Keep. It additionally includes off-talk examples for diagnosing unnecessary yielding. We introduce pair accuracy, which requires correct decisions on both members of a pair and assigns no credit to constant-action policies. Experiments on multiple full-duplex systems show that most exhibit a pronounced bias toward \textsc{Yield}, performing substantially better on interruptions than on backchannels, while another system remains comparatively balanced. These findings demonstrate that interruption-only evaluation can overestimate practical turn-taking reliability. ECHO and its metadata will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: ECHO is a new benchmark for evaluating full-duplex Chinese dialogue systems’ ability to distinguish interruptions from backchannels using paired contexts and a stricter pair accuracy metric.
AI.motivation: Current full-duplex spoken dialogue benchmarks evaluate overlapping speech events in isolation, which can reward fixed preferences (e.g., always yielding the turn) instead of context-aware turn-taking decisions. There is a need for a diagnostic dataset that tests whether systems genuinely use dialogue context to decide whether to yield or keep speaking when overlapped.
AI.method: The authors construct ECHO, a Chinese full-duplex turn-taking benchmark where each example is part of a pair sharing the same overlap transcript but differing in the preceding multi-turn dialogue context. In one context the correct system behavior is to yield the floor; in the other it is to keep speaking. They also add ‘off-talk’ examples where the user is not addressing the system, to test whether systems avoid unnecessary yielding. They define pair accuracy as the evaluation metric, which only counts a pair as correct if the system makes the right decision (Yield vs Keep) in both examples, preventing constant-action strategies from scoring well.
AI.result: When evaluating several existing full-duplex systems on ECHO, the authors find that most systems show a strong bias toward yielding the floor, performing much better on interruption-type overlaps than on backchannels. One system is more balanced between yield and keep decisions. This reveals systematic behavior patterns that prior, interruption-focused benchmarks did not capture.
AI.conclusion: ECHO exposes that many current full-duplex dialogue systems rely on a yield-biased strategy and do not reliably distinguish interruptions from backchannels based on context. Consequently, benchmarks that focus only on interruptions overestimate real-world turn-taking robustness. The authors will publicly release ECHO and its metadata to facilitate more accurate evaluation and future research on context-sensitive turn-taking.

title: Enhancing Accessibility of Medical Texts through Large Language Model-Driven Plain Language Adaptation
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Published in the Proceedings of the Thirty-Third Text REtrieval Conference (TREC 2024), Plain Language Adaptation of Biomedical Abstracts (PLABA) track
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of making complex healthcare information more accessible through automated Plain Language Adaptation (PLA). PLA aims to simplify technical medical language, bridging a critical gap between the complexity of healthcare texts and patients' reading comprehension. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), such as GPT and BART, have opened new possibilities for PLA, especially in zero-shot and few-shot learning contexts where task-specific data is limited. In this work, we leverage the capabilities of LLMs such as GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-pro, and LLaMA for text simplification. Additionally, we incorporate Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) techniques to enhance adaptability and robustness in PLA tasks. Key contributions include a comparative analysis of prompting strategies, finetuning with QLoRA on different LLMs, and the integration of MoA technique. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of LLM-driven PLA, showcasing its potential in making healthcare information more comprehensible while preserving essential content.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using large language models and a mixture-of-agents setup to automatically simplify complex medical texts into plain language, improving patient comprehension while preserving key information.
AI.motivation: Patients often struggle to understand technical healthcare documents, which harms communication, adherence, and decision-making. Manual plain-language rewriting is costly and doesn’t scale. With recent progress in large language models, there is an opportunity to automate plain language adaptation for medical texts even when little task-specific training data is available.
AI.method: The authors apply several LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-pro, LLaMA) to text simplification for healthcare content under zero-shot and few-shot prompting. They systematically compare prompting strategies, perform parameter-efficient finetuning using QLoRA on different LLM backbones, and integrate a Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) framework, where multiple models or variants collaborate to produce more robust simplified outputs.
AI.result: Experiments indicate that LLM-based approaches can generate simpler medical texts that maintain essential clinical meaning. Comparative analyses suggest that certain prompting strategies and QLoRA-finetuned models improve simplification quality, and that the MoA setup further boosts adaptability and robustness across PLA scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven plain language adaptation is a promising solution for making complex healthcare information more understandable to patients. Combining careful prompting, lightweight finetuning, and mixture-of-agents techniques yields effective simplification while preserving critical medical content, suggesting practical applicability for patient-facing health communication tools.

title: Right Tool, Right Job: Native-Language Evaluation, Tokenizer Sensitivity, and Methodological Findings from a French-Only BabyLM
comment: Accepted at BabyLM Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: We submit MéTRON-FR, a 125M GPT-2 pretrained on 92.47M words of French, to the BabyLM 2026 Strict track. It scores 85.97 +/- 0.17% on QFrBLiMP (a native Quebec-French benchmark of grammatical minimal pairs) and 62.80% on the BabyLM-weighted leaderboard. A cross-lingual GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation) protocol that combines French task-data translation with rank-16 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) produces a sharp task-type gradient: relational tasks gain measurably, while world-knowledge tasks regress. Bilingual Lexicon Induction aligns the French embeddings to GPT-2 at p@1 = 68.84 +/- 8.61%, 18X above chance, suggesting cross-lingual alignment tracks acquired grammatical competence rather than training duration. An ablation study shows that single-token zero-shot scoring is dominated by tokenizer and template artifacts at the child scale, motivating tokenizer-swap sensitivity, placebo-controlled prompting, and native-language minimal-pair benchmarks as standard diagnostics.

AI.tldr: MéTRON-FR is a 125M-parameter French GPT-2 model evaluated in the BabyLM 2026 Strict track, showing strong grammatical competence in Quebec French, mixed cross-lingual transfer on GLUE-style tasks, substantial embedding alignment with English GPT-2, and revealing that common zero-shot scoring practices are unreliable at small scales, motivating more careful evaluation protocols.
AI.motivation: To investigate how a small French GPT-2 model (child-scale) acquires grammatical competence, how well it transfers to English-like downstream tasks via cross-lingual methods, and to critically assess standard language modeling evaluation techniques (especially zero-shot scoring) for small, non-English models.
AI.method: 1) Pretrain a 125M-parameter GPT-2 model (MéTRON-FR) on 92.47M French tokens. 2) Evaluate grammatical knowledge using QFrBLiMP, a Quebec-French minimal-pair benchmark, and compute an overall BabyLM-weighted leaderboard score. 3) Use a cross-lingual GLUE-like protocol by translating GLUE tasks into French and fine-tuning with rank-16 LoRA to probe task-type performance differences. 4) Perform Bilingual Lexicon Induction to align MéTRON-FR’s French embeddings with English GPT-2 embeddings and measure p@1 alignment accuracy. 5) Conduct ablations on single-token zero-shot scoring to identify artifacts from tokenization and prompting templates, and test sensitivity via tokenizer swaps, placebo prompts, and native minimal-pair benchmarks.
AI.result: 1) MéTRON-FR achieves 85.97 ± 0.17% on QFrBLiMP, indicating strong grammatical discrimination in Quebec French, and 62.80% on the BabyLM-weighted leaderboard. 2) Cross-lingual GLUE with LoRA reveals a sharp gradient: relational reasoning tasks improve with adaptation, while tasks that depend on world knowledge degrade. 3) Bilingual Lexicon Induction reaches p@1 = 68.84 ± 8.61%, about 18 times above chance, implying substantial cross-lingual embedding alignment. 4) Ablation shows that single-token zero-shot scoring at this child scale is heavily confounded by tokenizer and prompt-template effects rather than genuine model competence.
AI.conclusion: A small French GPT-2 model can develop strong grammatical competence and substantial cross-lingual embedding alignment with an English GPT-2, but cross-lingual transfer to downstream tasks is uneven, benefiting relational tasks more than world-knowledge tasks. Standard single-token zero-shot evaluations are unreliable at this scale due to tokenizer and prompt artifacts, so future work should adopt diagnostics like tokenizer-swap sensitivity checks, placebo-controlled prompting, and native-language minimal-pair benchmarks for more robust evaluation.

title: What Breaks Under Pruning in Smart Homes, and When? Evaluating LLM Degradation Across Architectures and Task Complexity
summary: Pruning can reduce the deployment cost of large language models (LLMs), but its impact on context-grounded tool calling remains poorly understood. We systematically study pruning-induced degradation in smart-home tool calling across four LLMs spanning dense Transformer, dense hybrid, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, together with depth, width, hybrid, and expert pruning methods. After post-pruning supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we evaluate more than 19,500 instances from three smart-home datasets. Beyond aggregate task accuracy, we characterize degradation along two dimensions: action components (i.e., operation, device, argument, and value) and task complexity. Our results show that dense models have narrow safe pruning regions followed by sharp degradation, while MoE models tolerate substantially more pruning. Pruning degrades grounded specificity before schema-level intent, and aggressive dense pruning can induce systematic over-refusal. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating pruning beyond aggregate accuracy when selecting pruned LLMs for reliable tool execution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how pruning affects large language models’ ability to do accurate, context-grounded tool calling in smart-home scenarios, across different architectures and pruning methods, and finds dense models degrade sharply while MoE models are more robust and that aggregate accuracy hides important failure modes.
