AI.motivation: While pruning is widely used to reduce the cost of deploying LLMs, its specific effects on context-grounded tool use—especially fine-grained smart-home actions—are not well understood. Practitioners typically rely on aggregate accuracy metrics, which may miss subtle but safety-critical degradations such as wrong device arguments, loss of specificity, or over-refusal. There is a need to systematically characterize how different pruning strategies and architectures affect reliable tool execution.
AI.method: The authors evaluate pruning-induced degradation in smart-home tool calling across four LLMs with diverse architectures: dense Transformer, dense hybrid, and mixture-of-experts (MoE). They apply several pruning strategies—depth, width, hybrid, and expert pruning—and then perform post-pruning supervised fine-tuning (SFT). They measure performance on more than 19,500 examples from three smart-home datasets. Instead of only looking at overall task accuracy, they decompose performance along two axes: (1) action components (operation, device, argument, value) and (2) task complexity, to understand nuanced failure modes.
AI.result: Dense models show only narrow “safe” pruning regions after which performance drops sharply, whereas MoE models can be pruned much more aggressively with less degradation. Pruning tends to harm grounded specificity (e.g., correct arguments/values) before it harms higher-level schema intent (e.g., choosing the right operation or device). For dense models, aggressive pruning can cause systematic over-refusal, where the model declines to act instead of executing tools. These effects are visible when analyzing components and complexity, but are not always clear from aggregate accuracy alone.
AI.conclusion: Pruning can significantly and non-uniformly affect LLM tool-calling behavior, especially for dense architectures, and aggregate accuracy metrics are insufficient to capture these effects. MoE models are more tolerant to pruning, while dense models rapidly lose reliability beyond narrow pruning ranges and may develop problematic behaviors like over-refusal. For deploying pruned LLMs in tool-intensive domains such as smart homes, it is crucial to evaluate component-level performance and task-complexity-dependent behavior, not just overall accuracy, to ensure safe and reliable tool execution.

title: When Should LLMs Abstain? Chain-of-Self-Questioning for Selective Risk Control
summary: Large language models can produce fluent answers when their factual support is weak. This paper introduces Chain-of-Self-Questioning (CoSQ), a prompt-only framework that makes answer commitment conditional on an explicit assessment of the information required to answer a question. We evaluate three CoSQ variants under seventeen conditions on the 817-item TruthfulQA multiple-choice validation set using eleven open-weight and hosted model families. In the final balanced-option protocol, Grounded-CoSQ at τ=0.90 reduces the mean unconditional wrong-commitment rate from 13.1% under chain-of-thought prompting to 8.9%, a 32.1% relative reduction, while increasing answered accuracy from 86.9% to 89.7% and answering 87.6% of questions. Both improvements hold for all eleven models and at every evaluated threshold. Critical-CoSQ and Adaptive-CoSQ provide neighboring operating points with 88.6% and 86.5% coverage, respectively, while remaining more reliable than the baseline. A secondary Natural Questions Short-Answer evaluation provides convergent open-form evidence. These findings show that self-assessment can support explicit, tunable answer-or-abstain decisions when an unsupported commitment is more costly than referral or review.

AI.tldr: Introduces Chain-of-Self-Questioning (CoSQ), a prompting framework that makes LLMs explicitly assess whether they have enough information to answer, reducing incorrect confident answers while maintaining or improving accuracy and coverage.
AI.motivation: LLMs often give fluent, confident answers even when they lack sufficient factual support, leading to unreliable and misleading outputs. Existing prompting methods like chain-of-thought improve reasoning but do not adequately control overconfident wrong answers. There is a need for a simple, prompt-only mechanism that allows models to decide when to answer and when to abstain, especially in settings where unsupported answers are more harmful than deferring to humans or other systems.
AI.method: The authors propose Chain-of-Self-Questioning (CoSQ), a prompting framework in which the model first explicitly evaluates what information is required to answer a question and whether it has that information, then decides whether to answer or abstain. They design three variants: Grounded-CoSQ, Critical-CoSQ, and Adaptive-CoSQ, which differ in how they assess and threshold confidence or groundedness. They run 17 evaluation conditions on the 817-item TruthfulQA multiple-choice validation set across 11 different open-weight and hosted LLM families, comparing against chain-of-thought prompting. They vary a groundedness threshold τ and measure wrong-commitment rate (incorrect but answered), accuracy among answered questions, and coverage (percentage of questions answered). They also perform a secondary evaluation on Natural Questions Short-Answer to test the approach in an open-form QA setting.
AI.result: In the main TruthfulQA evaluation, Grounded-CoSQ at threshold τ=0.90 reduces the mean unconditional wrong-commitment rate from 13.1% under standard chain-of-thought prompting to 8.9%, a 32.1% relative reduction. At the same time, answered accuracy increases from 86.9% to 89.7%, with the model still answering 87.6% of questions. These gains are consistent across all eleven evaluated models and for all tested thresholds. The other CoSQ variants—Critical-CoSQ and Adaptive-CoSQ—offer different trade-offs between coverage and reliability, achieving 88.6% and 86.5% coverage respectively while remaining more reliable than baseline chain-of-thought. The Natural Questions Short-Answer evaluation shows similar qualitative improvements in an open-form QA setting, supporting the generality of the approach.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based self-assessment via Chain-of-Self-Questioning allows LLMs to make explicit, tunable answer-or-abstain decisions, significantly reducing overconfident wrong answers without sacrificing—and even slightly improving—accuracy and coverage. The method is model- and provider-agnostic (prompt-only), works across diverse LLM families, and is particularly valuable for applications where the cost of unsupported or incorrect commitments is higher than the cost of deferral for human review or additional validation.
